1. “Government deficits don’t necessarily cause inflation. They are funded by the sale of T-bills and bonds.”

Yes, but if demand for those bonds is weak, the central bank steps in as the lender of last resort, printing money to purchase them, which can lead to inflation.

2. “Even an expanding money supply does not dictate the inflation rate. As we saw last year, we can have inflation even when the money supply shrinks, and this year we have much lower inflation even with a growing money supply.”

Yes, but inflation often lags behind changes in the money supply—it can take time for new money to fully circulate and impact prices.

3. “Moderate inflation is NOT bad and does not destroy purchasing power (unless you keep your wealth all in cash).”

Inflation does destroy purchasing power. Investing in assets that grow faster than inflation, like stocks or real estate, can keep you ahead of it. They don’t avoid inflation, they just try to beat it.

Mr. Money Mustache October 30, 2024, 7:23 pm

I think hybrids were great as a transition technology, because they helped our gas cars become more efficient back when batteries were too expensive to make an affordable all-electric car.

For example, in 2013, electric car battery packs cost about $780 per kWh to build, meaning my Tesla Model Y’s 80 kWh pack alone would have cost $62,000!

Today (2024 as I write this) that battery pack number is about $100, so my battery is only $8k of the car’s price. And since an electric car no longer needs an engine, transmission, exhaust system or all the other junk that comes with combustion, we now see electric cars have become LESS expensive than gas cars of equivalent quality/performance (the model Y is in the low $40s brand new, and under $30k used)

With the combination of easy+cheap home charging plus a bunch of nationwide fast charging networks (Tesla’s is still the best by far), there is no reason to have to settle for a hybrid – unless you’re shopping in the cheaper end of the used market. An under $10k used Prius with low miles is still a great frugal car if you can find one!

Avoid Nissan Leafs since their charging standard is no longer used and their batteries are air cooled, leading to far more degradation than other EVs that have active cooling. If you’re looking at Chevy Bolt’s make sure the battery modules were repaired per the recall. One of the best things about them is that your house is your “fuel” station. If you don’t have at home charging available it can be more of a challenge (unless your work has chargers).

Thanks for writing back! I always appreciate hearing your thoughts.

There are plenty of people who say SS does NOT keep up with inflation:

“Though the COLA is supposed to keep up with inflation, it’s missed the mark in eight of the last 15 adjustments, according to a recent analysis by The Senior Citizens League, an advocacy group, which looked at the annual increases prior to the one for 2025. Over the past five years, only the 2023 adjustment has beaten the rate of inflation. The COLAs lagged inflation by as much as 1.1 percentage points the other years.

“Social Security benefits have lost 20% of their buying power since 2010, according to the league. Those who retired that year would need a boost of $370 a month, or $4,440 a year, on average, to regain the lost value.

“The automatic annual cost-of-living adjustment is one of Social Security’s most essential and unique features. It is intended to ensure that benefits do not erode over time,” Nancy Altman, president of Social Security Works, an advocacy group, said in a statement. “However, the formula currently used to calculate annual COLAs under-measures the expenses that Social Security beneficiaries face. “What’s more, senior citizens typically don’t receive the full adjustment. https://www.cnn.com/2024/10/10/politics/social-security-cola-increase/index.html#:~:text=Though%20the%20COLA%20is%20supposed%20to%20keep%20up,2023%20adjustment%20has%20beaten%20the%20rate%20of%20inflation.

This. CPI-W is used on SS, which is known to outpace what is generally referred to as a more accurate reflection of the real cost of goods people endure, CPI-U.

Also, lots of people are retired with pensions which are adjusted by either a flat % or not adjusted at all, and these retirees have seen serious pain from inflation, even if their stock portoflio has done well. As a practical matter there is no such thing as a “fixed income” in the United States, unless some unfortunate retiree stuck their entire net worth under their mattress on the day they bid their employer farewell. Social Security receives annual cost of living adjustments. Defined benefit pensions almost always adjust for inflation. Private retirement account can and should be very easily invested in interest bearing securities or the stock market. Heck, even a no risk money market account has paid around 5% annually for the last couple of years.

I’m a city dweller with a desk job, so take this analysis for what its worth. Also, a farm or ranch is a business, so a approaching it from a personal finance perspective may not be the right way to look at it.

From what I understand most small farms and ranches in the US aren’t profitable. Based on my parents’ neighbors and many of the sources I’ve read, I think this is because farming and ranching is often a cultural identity and a lifestyle choice, and these properties aren’t being run as an efficient business. They’re hobby farms run by rich dentists, or their owners identify as “cattle ranchers” whether or not the market supports that identity and without a diversified, efficient business plan to maximize the profitability of the entire enterprise.

Here are some Mustachian principles I think apply to farms, ranches, and people who live in rural areas.

Trade the pickup truck for a smaller, less expensive, and preferably used vehicle that does the job better and drive it as little as possible. For everything else, buy a bike or small (used) sedan. There are shades of rural, but a lot of transportation needs can still be met by bike or electric bike. I rode my ebike about 40 miles yesterday to run errands in the city. I grew up in the sticks, and I’d have had a lot more freedom if I’d had an ebike. An electric cargo bike may able to be substituted for a four-wheeler or pickup truck for a lot of on farm transportation. The bike I have can basically carry the weight of two people. If you’re moving a dozen 40lb bags of feed around, that’s a max of four trips by electric cargo bike. Bikes are low, so loading one is faster and easier than throwing bags up into a pickup truck bed.

When it comes to farm equipment and purchases of all kinds, ask if you really need the equipment or if its just a status symbol. Can the job be done with muscle power. If you need the equipment, can you buy it used or substitute a less flashy alternative. Financing for farm equipment is similar to financing for a new car. Probably a money hole.

Every single farm input needs scrutiny and optimization. Fertilizer that washes into the river is money going down the sewer. This includes water, fertilizer, pesticides, etc. Spraying money at the problem isn’t solving it.

Cut your Cash-Leaking Umbilical Cord. If you moved to the country to enjoy the country, why do you need 500 channels of entertainment?

Focus on your Circle of Control, not your Circle of Interest. You can’t change the global cattle market, but you can decide whether to add sheep and goats, get paid by a land conservancy, host duck hunters, market your beef to yuppies at farmers markets, or do any number of other things to increase the profitability of your property.

Reduce grocery trips and expenses by growing your own food and trading with neighbors. Put in some fruit trees and a kitchen garden. Raise some chickens. Trade for milk. This should be one of the big advantages of living in the countryside in farm country.

That’s just a quick look, but I think a lot of the Mustachian principles apply in rural areas too.

#8691. This Year’s NYC Marathon Proved Different Strategies Can Lead to Victory

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

I’m sure I could think of a couple of thousand ways, many of which include espresso, to spend a Sunday morning in New York City than running 26.2 miles through all five boroughs. But on Nov. 1, nearly 60,000 people decided to run the New York City Marathon—again—like they have every year since 1970. Some were chasing a championship. Some were chasing a personal best. Others probably just wanted to finish before their feet decided to go on strike. And there are hosts of runners dressed in all kinds of costumes just out for a jog. And the crowd keeps everyone well cheered on. No matter who it is.

The men’s winner was Andreas Almgren of Sweden, who covered the course in two hours, six minutes, one second. And I’m going to put an asterisk next to it because this was his first marathon. Not his first race, obviously. Almgren arrived as the reigning world half-marathon champion and European 10,000-meter champion. He’d spent years developing the engine. He just hadn’t taken it out for this particular 26.2-mile test drive.

The lead pack stayed together deep into the race, and Almgren waited until the final mile to make his decisive move. Italy’s Yemaneberhan Crippa finished second, thirteen seconds behind him, and Kamohelo Mofolo of Lesotho was third. Defending champion Benson Kipruto wound up fourth. That’s quite a debut, particularly on a course that includes bridges, hills, crazy potholes and enough turns to get you lost.

Before anybody decides the lesson is to skip marathon preparation, understand what a debut means here. Almgren wasn’t some guy who woke up last Thursday and discovered running shoes. He had world-class credentials at shorter distances. Moving up required applying an already extraordinary aerobic foundation to a longer event. A marathon is not merely two half-marathons stapled together. Fueling, pacing, muscular endurance, and how you respond after mile twenty all become rather important when your body starts negotiating terms of surrender.

The women’s race was even more entertaining near the finish. Kenya’s Sheila Chepkirui reclaimed the title she’d won in 2024, finishing in 2:24:36. Defending champion Hellen Obiri was in the fight late, but American Jess McClain came charging from behind and passed her in the closing meters. Chepkirui won, McClain took second in 2:24:42, and Obiri was third one second later. McClain became the first American woman on the New York podium since 2018.

And if you think the only interesting athletes are the ones with the smallest numbers on the clock, the wheelchair divisions cranks them out! Switzerland’s Marcel Hug won his eighth New York title in 1:28:14, edging American Daniel Romanchuk by one second. Catherine Debrunner, also Swiss, won the women’s wheelchair race in 1:40:02, nearly eight and a half minutes ahead of Tatyana McFadden. Same city, same event, completely different demands on the athlete. The upper-body power, equipment handling, and tactical judgment involved deserve more attention than they usually get.

Then there’s Mildred Baker, an 80-year-old Bronx resident who took up running in her late seventies and completed her first marathon in 7:03:49. Seven freakin’ hours! No, Almgren is not the only champion. That’s the point. The marathon can be a world championship-level knife fight at the front and a personal expedition at the back. And a trade in between. You can appreciate both extremes without pretending they’re the same athletic achievement.

Secondly, I must admit that l like the way this race exposes a certain kind of gym stupidity: the assumption that only one type of physical performance counts. A Swedish speed merchant conquered a distance he’d never raced. An American woman stole second place in the final strides. An 80-year-old finished something most people wouldn’t even start. You’re actually, in one Sunday event, looking at the entire definition of fitness.

The ultimate domestic travel rewards benefit for families and couples

Imagine this: you book a flight for yourself, and your spouse — or your best friend, or your mom — flies with you for the cost of taxes alone. Not a discount. Not a sale. Completely. Free. For up to two full calendar years. That's the Southwest Companion Pass, and it is, without question, the single most powerful perk in all of domestic travel rewards. The ChooseFI community has a saying: if you only ever pursue one travel rewards strategy in your life, make it this one. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A round-trip Southwest flight from Denver to Cancún might run $400 per person. A family of four flying during spring break? You're looking at $1,600 cash. But with the Companion Pass, you pay for two tickets and the other two fly free — cutting your out-of-pocket cost in half, every single flight, for nearly two years. Run the numbers over a year of typical family travel and you're looking at **$2,000 to $8,000 in total value** from a single benefit. The CPP (cents per point) range here — **1.5 to 5.9 cents per point** — is what makes this genuinely remarkable. Southwest's Rapid Rewards program values points at roughly 1.4 cents toward any flight. But the Companion Pass doesn't just redeem points efficiently; it *doubles the value of every redemption you make while it's active*. That's the pricing inefficiency the loyalty system has quietly built in, and the FI community is uniquely positioned to exploit it. Think about what 135,000 points normally buys: roughly $1,890 worth of Southwest flights. Solid, but not earth-shattering. Now attach the Companion Pass, and those same points — redeemed strategically over two years — effectively unlock $3,780 or more in flight value for your household. No blackout dates. No seat restrictions. No change fees. Just book, fly, repeat. This isn't a first-class lounge or a lie-flat bed over the Pacific. It's something arguably more valuable for the FI-minded family: **sustainable, repeatable, nearly free domestic travel** that works with your actual life.

The Companion Pass isn't a points redemption — it's a status benefit. That distinction is everything, and it's the insight that separates people who get this from people who miss it entirely.

Here's how it works: Southwest grants the Companion Pass when you earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. Once you hit that threshold, you designate one person as your companion, and that person flies with you on every flight — paid or points — for the remainder of that calendar year plus the entire following calendar year.

The key word is "earn." Points transferred in from partners count. Credit card signup bonuses count. Shopping portal purchases count. Almost every way you accumulate points counts toward the 135,000 threshold — except points purchased directly from Southwest.

The pricing inefficiency here is a calendar arbitrage opportunity. If you earn the Companion Pass on January 2nd, you get it for the rest of that year and all of the next year — nearly two full calendar years of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it on November 15th, you get roughly 13 months. The strategy is to time your credit card signup bonuses to post in January, maximizing your benefit window.

Most ChooseFI members build their 135,000 points through a combination of strategies:

Chase Ultimate Rewards → Southwest Rapid Rewards (1:1, Instant) Chase transfers to Southwest at a 1:1 ratio and the transfer is instant — points appear in your Rapid Rewards account within minutes. This makes Chase points (earned on cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Ink Business cards) the most efficient fuel for this strategy.

Marriott Bonvoy → Southwest Rapid Rewards (3:1, 1-5 days) Marriott transfers at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Southwest point), and transfers take 1-5 days. This is a less efficient path — use it only if you have a surplus of Marriott points and no better option.

The most reliable path to 135,000 points is stacking Southwest credit card signup bonuses. Southwest's consumer and business cards frequently offer bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points each. A couple who each opens one card, or one person who opens both a personal and business card, can often hit the threshold with signup bonuses alone — before spending a dollar on the portal.

Since Southwest charges no fuel surcharges on award flights and points never expire, there's no penalty for building this balance over several months. The Rapid Rewards program is revenue-based with dynamic pricing, meaning points cover the full fare including taxes — no hidden redemption fees to erode your value.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account and your Southwest Rapid Rewards account and tally your existing points. You need 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points earned in a single calendar year to trigger the Companion Pass. Note: points already sitting in your Rapid Rewards account from prior years don't count — you need to earn 135,000 in the target calendar year.

The optimal window is October through December of the prior year. Apply for Southwest credit cards (personal and/or business) so that your signup bonuses post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Verify with Southwest's current card offers — signup bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points are common. A couple can each apply for a card; a solo pursuer can apply for both a personal and a business card if they have qualifying self-employment income.

Call Chase or Southwest after your first statement closes to confirm when points will post. Timing is everything.

Once your signup bonuses post, calculate how many points you still need. If you're short:

Southwest will notify you by email once you've crossed 135,000 qualifying points. Log into your Rapid Rewards account at southwest.com and navigate to "My Account" → "Companion Pass" to confirm the benefit is active.

You can designate — and change — your companion up to three times per calendar year. Name your most frequent travel partner first. Go to southwest.com, log in, and find the Companion Pass section to add their name and contact information.

Searching is simple: go to southwest.com and search any route. Toggle between "$ Dollars" and "Rapid Rewards Points" to see your cost. When you book with points and your companion is designated, Southwest will automatically prompt you to add your companion to the same flight. Your companion pays taxes only — typically $5.60 each way for domestic flights.

Pro tip: Southwest opens its booking window 330 days in advance. For peak travel like spring break or holiday weeks, set a calendar reminder and book the day the window opens.

The Companion Pass works because Southwest treats it as a status benefit rather than a points redemption. Most airline companion programs require you to burn miles for the second ticket or limit usage to specific fare classes. Southwest flips this model: once you earn the pass, your companion flies on every single flight you take — paid or award — for the remainder of the qualifying year plus the entire following calendar year. The only cost is taxes. Because Southwest has no blackout dates, no fuel surcharges, and no change fees, the pass amplifies in value with every trip you take. The January-earning calendar arbitrage is the key optimization that turns a good benefit into an extraordinary one.

Let's make this real. It's March, and your family of four wants to spend a week in Orlando this July — theme parks, pool time, the works.

A quick search on southwest.com shows round-trip flights from Chicago Midway to Orlando for $320 per person. For four tickets, that's $1,280 cash. Standard family travel math: painful but doable.

You have the Companion Pass active, earned back in January. You book two tickets: yours at 22,000 Rapid Rewards points (worth ~$308 at 1.4 cents per point), and your spouse's ticket at $5.60 in taxes as your designated companion. Your two kids? You use 44,000 more points for their tickets. Total out-of-pocket: 66,000 points + $11.20 in taxes.

Let's value those 66,000 points at their Chase transfer cost — you transferred them 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards, where they were worth roughly $825 in travel via the portal. But by pairing them with the Companion Pass, your spouse flies free, effectively doubling your points' purchasing power on this trip.

Cash price: $1,280. Your cost: 66,000 points + $11.20. That's a CPP of roughly 1.9 cents per point on the base redemption — but accounting for your companion flying free, the effective CPP on the entire trip rockets to 3.8 cents per point. Well within the 1.5–5.9 cent range where this sweet spot lives.

And here's what makes Southwest specifically wonderful for families: no change fees. Book in March, change in June when your kid's baseball tournament schedule shifts, rebook without penalty. No one in the FI community is paying $200-per-person change fees.

The experience itself? Economy class on Southwest, open seating, snacks, and friendly crew. It's not lie-flat business class to Tokyo — but that's not the point. The point is your family of four flies to Florida for a week, and the flights barely register on your annual budget. That's FI-level travel.

Time your credit card applications so signup bonuses post in January of your target year. A bonus that posts January 5th gives you until December 31st of the following year to use the Companion Pass — nearly 24 months of 2-for-1 flights. This single timing decision can mean the difference between 13 months and 23 months of value.

The Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal (rapidrewardsshopping.com) awards points on purchases at hundreds of retailers. Even after you've earned the Companion Pass, continuing to earn Rapid Rewards points means more flights at lower point costs. Treat it like a cashback portal and check it before any online purchase.

Southwest opens availability 330 days in advance. For Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and summer weekends in popular markets, set a calendar reminder and book the exact morning the window opens. Southwest doesn't have blackout dates, but high-demand flights sell out in Wanna Get Away fare class — the cheapest points tier — quickly.

You can change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. If your life situation changes — a different travel partner, a new relationship, a child aging into a separate ticket — use this flexibility. Just don't burn all three changes frivolously.

Purchased points do not count toward the 135,000 qualifying threshold for the Companion Pass. Don't make this mistake when you're close to the threshold — transfer from Chase instead.

Some people try to earn the Companion Pass in November or December. You'll get it for only a few weeks before the calendar resets. The math simply doesn't work. January earning is the only strategy worth pursuing.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards Performance Business Credit Card (or similar business cards) have separate signup bonuses that stack with personal card bonuses. If you have any self-employment income — freelancing, a side hustle, a rental property — you likely qualify. This is often the fastest path to 135,000 points for a single applicant.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The Southwest Companion Pass was practically invented for the FI-minded family. If you have a consistent travel partner — a spouse, a partner, a parent you visit annually — and you fly domestically more than two or three times a year, this benefit will transform your travel budget.

Minimum points to get started: You need to earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. In practice, this means you either need access to Southwest credit card signup bonuses (which requires good to excellent credit, typically 700+) or a substantial existing balance of Chase Ultimate Rewards points to transfer at 1:1.

How it fits the FI strategy: The Companion Pass is a force multiplier. Every dollar you would have spent on a second ticket stays in your investment accounts instead. Over a two-year Companion Pass window, a couple who takes six domestic trips per year could easily bank $2,000-$4,000 in travel savings — real money that compounds.

Who this is NOT for: Solo travelers get zero benefit from the Companion Pass. International travelers who primarily fly non-Southwest routes won't find much use here. And if you're averse to economy class or require a specific airline's premium cabin, this redemption isn't your path.

The Southwest Companion Pass earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is almost entirely about the *earning*, not the booking. Once you have the Companion Pass, booking is literally the simplest award experience in travel rewards: search southwest.com, find your flight, click "Add Companion." There are no partner airlines to navigate, no availability calendars to decode, no call centers to endure. It's a 5/5 on ease of booking for a reason. The moderate rating comes from **three earning challenges**: **1. The credit requirement.** Southwest credit cards require good to excellent credit. If you're early in your credit-building journey, this strategy may need to wait 12-18 months while you strengthen your profile. **2. The timing discipline.** Earning the pass is straightforward, but earning it in January takes planning. You need to apply for cards 2-3 months in advance and coordinate signup bonus posting dates — something most people have never had to think about. **3. The 135,000-point threshold.** This is a real number. It requires intentional credit card strategy, not casual spending. For a single applicant without a business card, it may require supplementing with Chase transfers or portal activity. **How to overcome these challenges:** - Start planning in **October or November** for a January earn target - Check whether you qualify for a Southwest business card — it dramatically simplifies reaching the threshold - Use the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal year-round to passively accumulate qualifying points If you've successfully applied for a travel rewards credit card before and you have a consistent travel partner, you can absolutely do this. The ChooseFI community has helped hundreds of families earn the Companion Pass — and not one of them regretted the effort.

Open a personal and/or business Southwest credit card so that signup bonuses of 50,000 to 75,000 points each will post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Call to confirm when points will post after your first statement closes.

Once signup bonuses post, calculate your gap. Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards at 1:1 (instant) to fill any shortfall. Use the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal for additional earning on everyday purchases.

After Southwest confirms your Companion Pass, log in to southwest.com and designate your travel partner. Book flights as normal — Southwest will prompt you to add your companion for taxes only ($5.60 each way domestic).

Set calendar reminders for Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and summer travel. Southwest opens its booking window 330 days in advance. Book the morning the window opens to lock in Wanna Get Away fares at the lowest point costs.

The Companion Pass is valid for the remainder of the calendar year in which you earn it plus the entire following calendar year. If you earn it on January 2nd, you get nearly 24 months of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it in November, you get roughly 14 months. This is why timing your earning to January is the critical optimization.

Yes. Signup bonuses, spending on Southwest cards, points transferred from Chase Ultimate Rewards, and points earned through the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal all count as qualifying points. The only points that do not count are those purchased directly from Southwest.

Yes. The Companion Pass works on both cash-purchased flights and flights booked with Rapid Rewards points. Your companion pays only taxes — typically $5.60 each way for domestic flights — regardless of how you booked the ticket.

Southwest allows you to change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. Log into your Rapid Rewards account on southwest.com and update the companion information in the Companion Pass section. Plan strategically since you only get three changes per year.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Southwest Companion Pass is the single most powerful domestic travel rewards benefit available to FI-minded families and couples. At a cost of 135,000 qualifying points — achievable through credit card signup bonuses and Chase transfers — you unlock nearly two full years of 2-for-1 flights on every Southwest route with no blackout dates and no change fees. A family of four taking six domestic trips per year can realistically save $2,000 to $4,000 annually, money that goes straight back into your investment accounts. Time your earning to January, stack your signup bonuses, and designate your most frequent travel partner. This is the redemption that makes domestic travel a rounding error in your FI budget.

#8686. Bodybuilder AJ Ellison Shares 3 tips for Fat Loss After 50

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

IFBB Pro and Masters Men’s Physique Competitor Adam J. Ellison may be 50 years old, but he has a physique that would make most men half his age green with envy. Fortunately, the proud father of three kids says that it is still possible to drop fat while juggling the responsibilities of work and family, as he shared his “No B.S. guide” on Instagram.

AJ Ellison knows that fat mass tends to increase while lean muscle decreases with age, and science suggests that the slow down in metabolic rates could play a significant role as to why it is harder to drop body fat as we age, but that doesn’t mean that we should ditch our physique goals  as we mature. Ellison, now 50 years old, is still winning competitions on stage, and looked phenomenal as he topped the Master’s 50+ Men’s Physique category at the 2026 IFBB Masters World Championships. He even placed second in the 40+, meaning that AJ is still hanging with those who are up to a decade younger than himself. With all that in mind, here are his tips for dropping stubborn fat.

“Fat loss doesn’t start in the gym, it starts in your kitchen,” wrote Ellison. “You can’t out-train a poor diet.” The big man also said that he makes sure to consume plenty of protein. “Aim for 50 to 70g of protein at every meal. Build every plate around protein first. Fill the rest with whole foods.”

“Most men try to burn more calories. That’s backwards,” said Ellison. “Protect your muscle first.” While muscle does not burn calories directly, the presence of more muscle tissue means that there is a greater level of energy required in the body, leading to a greater calorie requirement.

To build muscle, the competitive bodybuilder suggested that we “Lift 3 to 4 times every week,” and added that for hypertrophy, “Progress your lifts whenever possible.”

“Cardio is a tool. It isn’t the foundation,” believes Ellison, who utilizes cardiovascular training to support his efforts without making it the center of his ethos. “Strength training should always come first,” wrote the master, for his almost 900K Instagram followers.

To make sure that cardio is part of the mix, “Add 8,000 to 10,000 daily steps,” enthused Ellison. “Use cardio to support recovery, not to punish yourself.”

Summing up, the bodybuilder noted that “Small calorie deficits beat aggressive diets,” observing that “Crash dieting teaches your body to conserve energy.” So, to get started, Ellison coached that we should aim to lose 0.5 to 1% of body fat per week, and to trust in the process. “Track your progress for at least three weeks before changing anything,” he concluded.

#8683. Stephan James Cut Weight in Order to Look Bigger for ‘I Play Rocky’

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Stephan James is no stranger to playing a real-life person on screen. The award-winning actor put his best foot forward as Olympic running legend, Jesse Owens, in Race so he understands the importance of getting in shape for athletic roles. But to play the late, great Carl Weathers in I Play Rocky, the star tells M&F that he actually cut weight in order to look like his far larger hero.

Carl Weathers was in the NFL before his big break in the movies, but once the former Oakland Raider was cast as boxing champ Apollo Creed in the original Rocky, not to mention three successful sequels, it became clear that the star could blend his physicality as an athlete with the charisma required for the big screen.

At 6’2’’ and topping the scales at around 220 muscular pounds, Weathers frame is a difficult one to replicate. “So, that was my first thought: I had to put on a lot of weight, gotta put on a lot of muscle,” says James. “I was just over 200 pounds when I found out that I was going to play him in this film. And, speaking to one of my trainers, I was telling him about this plan to just start packing on all this weight and trying to turn it into muscle. And, he was like, ‘You know what, Steph? If you just try to cut your bodyfat percentage down, then you may give yourself a better chance, giving the perspective of somebody who is even bigger than you may actually be.’”

The tactic was a savvy one. Competitive bodybuilders have long known that decreasing levels of body fat makes for a more muscular looking physique. As fat stores shrink, the skin appears tighter against the muscle, making the most of those angles, edges, and separations that create definition. And, as the waistline decreases, the upper body appears wider, making the shoulders, chest, and arms look wider.

“I was able to cut down to about 180,” shares James, who continued to train for his fighting scenes while on a calorie deficit. “It really helped just emphasize and accentuate, you know, the muscles that I had. So, I was proud of what was the end result in the film.”

The Canadian actor says that he had just two months to get in shape to play Weathers, who passed away in 2024, and was hailed as Sylvester Stallone’s favorite onscreen opponent. James tells M&F that while he was previously “not big on cardio” before gaining the role, he soon understood that the iconic boxing battles between Creed and “The Italian Stallion” would force him to embrace the grind.

“I had to get very big on it during the process of making this film,” explains James, noting that mornings would consist of a cardio and weight training session, followed by learning the craft of boxing in the afternoons. “There was so much that I didn’t know and understand,” he recalls of stepping between the ropes. “From the footwork, to the technical, punches, then starting to learn the choreography. Cardio is the number one thing that you get from boxing. So, I think all of these things helped me cut the weight really fast, helping me to shred really, really, quickly.” The hard work certainly paid off, as Rocky fans have been quick to praise the casting of I Play Rocky, the story of how Sylvester Stallone defied the odds: writing and starring in one of the biggest movies of all time.

While Anthony Ippolito has Sly’s voice and body language down to a fine art, there’s more than a passing resemblance between Stephan James and Carl Weathers. The actor, who alongside brother Shamier Anderson, champions the representation of black talent with their nonprofit, The Black Academy, explains that he has a great deal of respect for the doors that Carl Weathers opened up for future generations. “Guys like Carl helped pave the way,” he tells M&F. “For so many other actors, like myself, to be able to be a leading man, to be seen as layered, characters with heart, thoughts, emotions, charisma and charm. Even his comedic beats. It’s not lost on me what Carl meant for that time, just being a pioneer.”

I Play Rocky hits theaters in the U.S. from Nov. 20.

#8678. Why Smarter Strength Training Starts With a Better Home Gym

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Strength training can do more than build muscle. Research has linked it to better overall health and physical function, making it a worthwhile part of a regular fitness routine. But finding the time, space, and equipment to train consistently can be a challenge.

Home gyms appeal to so many lifters. You can work out on your own schedule, skip the trip to the gym, and choose equipment that fits your space. But if you’re starting from scratch, what do you really need?

Adjustable dumbbells are worth considering, especially if you don’t have room for a full rack of weights. Instead of buying a separate pair for every weight, you can change the resistance on a single set. They take up less room while supporting many of the same exercises you’d do with traditional dumbbells.

You can use them for presses, rows, curls, lunges, and more. Keep in mind, though, that adjustable dumbbells can feel different from traditional ones. Their shape, grip, and adjustment system vary by model, so consider which available weight range suits your training needs.

5 Ways to Get Started With Adjustable Dumbbells

Adjustable dumbbells have been around for decades, and manufacturers have developed different ways to make changing weights more convenient. One company in this space is PowerBlock, founded by Carl Towley in Owatonna, Minnesota, in 1993.

PowerBlock’s design uses a nested weight stack and a magnetic selector pin to change the load without requiring a separate pair of dumbbells for every weight. The system is designed to keep multiple resistance options in a compact footprint, which can be useful for lifters working with limited space.

PowerBlock offers dumbbells that are non-expandable, meaning they’re fixed in their range, and dumbbells that are expandable, meaning that you can purchase up to the weight you know you’re able to move, and as you get stronger, your dumbbells get heavier with expansion kits for the specific model.

Two models in the lineup offer different weight ranges and expansion options to accommodate lifters as their strength improves.

The Pro 100 EXP starts at 5 pounds per dumbbell and can expand to 100 pounds per dumbbell with additional weight kits. Depending on the configuration, weight increments range from approximately 2.5 to 5 pounds. Urethane-coated weight plates and grip options add versatility, while the expandable design allows users to increase the weight capacity as their strength grows. The set also helps save valuable home-gym space by replacing 30 pairs of traditional dumbbells.

The Elite USA 90 offers a similar space-saving design, with a capacity of up to 90 pounds per dumbbell. Its steel weight plates (Made in the USA) and 2.5- to 5-pound increments provide options for progressively increasing resistance. According to PowerBlock, the set replaces 28 individual dumbbells and 825 pounds of free weights in a compact footprint.

With more than 30 years in the adjustable-dumbbell market, PowerBlock says its mission is to make versatile fitness equipment accessible to people at every stage of training.

“Our focus is to provide high-quality, versatile fitness equipment for people at every stage of their fitness journey, whether they’re just getting started or continuing to pursue their goals,” says Josh Leake at PowerBlock. “Looking to the future, our goals are to keep providing premium home fitness equipment and continue to innovate to serve our customers best.”

Adjustable dumbbells can be a good fit if space is limited or you want several weight options without buying a full rack.

Before buying, compare the weight range, how the adjustment system works, the overall dimensions, expansion options, and price. Think about the exercises you do most often and whether the dumbbells will still meet your needs as you get stronger.

A useful home gym doesn’t have to be complicated. Start with equipment that fits your space, budget, and goals, then build your routine from there.

To learn more about PowerBlock’s models and specifications, visit PowerBlock.com or explore the company’s blog.

#8675. Elizabeth Van Winkle Shares How Resilience Can Help Make the Military Better

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Ask someone who serves in the military or in a civilian leadership role within the government why they are doing what they do, and there’s a good chance you will hear an answer that references the “mission.”

While the specific mission varies by role, a common thread unites them: being part of something bigger than themselves in service to the greater good of America. Feelings of patriotism, pride, and purpose are powerful motivators. But on the toughest days, many of these same leaders carry themselves forward with a fourth ‘P’: pressure.

Dr. Elizabeth ‘Elise’ Van Winkle understands each of those motivators, and she knows firsthand how heavy that fourth one can become. During a pivotal chapter in her government career, that pressure took a severe toll on her health. Now when she speaks about her career, she offers advice for anyone who may be in a similar position. Regardless of the mission in question, your health will matter.

Van Winkle acknowledged that fitness wasn’t a priority when she was younger, but that changed when she went to college and majored in psychology and English.

“That was probably my foray into fitness and health, the psychological side,” she said. “That is an important part of fitness to me.”

Van Winkle’s original focus was to enter a career in criminology and trauma, and she started that pursuit in the Boston, Massachusetts public school system for behavioral and psychiatric issues. Seeing children dealing with adverse issues and life situations was a valuable learning experience for her.

“The kids taught me a lot about resilience and heartache, perseverance, rage, and emotional darkness.”

Once she became a mother, Van Winkle opted to return to school to get her Ph.D. in research psychology, with a focus on neuropsychology. During that time, she had her second child and landed an intern position with the Department of Defense.

“My plan was to do research and data analytics on health and resilience, stay a year, and then move into work at NIH or do something in neuropsychology.”

Sometimes the best-laid plans can go awry, and Van Winkle’s career would have a meteoric rise that she did not see coming. She stayed in the DoD and worked her way up to a Senior Executive Service (SES) level throughout the next several years. Then came the 2016 election. A combination of being in the right place at the right time and the incoming changes with the Trump administration meant Van Winkle was elevated from a one-star SES to a three-star SES equivalent within a couple of weeks. Then shortly after, she was named the Acting Assistant Secretary for Readiness.

“That propelled me into a level of political leadership that I had never really been in.”

It also led to a massive increase in responsibility. The self-described “data geek” went from leading a team of 25 people with a budget of $4 million to now leading upwards of 900 civilians, military, and contractors with a budget of $1 billion. Almost immediately, an executive order gave her team 45 days to develop a readiness recovery framework that measured the readiness of the entire Joint Force and what would be needed to recover that readiness as well as appropriation lines.

Van Winkle added, “Anybody in the Department knows that when someone says 45 days, they really mean 30 because it has to go through coordination.”

Van Winkle’s trajectory may have felt like a whirlwind, but she accepted what became her own mission. She committed every waking hour that she could towards her new role and responsibilities. That also meant putting other things on the backburner like time with her kids and her own personal needs. As a result, she became sick but was undeterred. Knowing her team would not leave until she did, Van Winkle even closed up her office so her staff would leave, then snuck back on her own to continue her work.

Finally, her team put a meeting on her calendar that led her to the Pentagon Health Clinic. The physician informed Van Winkle she had three different infections and asked her to consider going to the hospital, but Van Winkle knew there were scheduled advisor meetings and a commitment at the White House in her future. So, the physician gave her antibiotics and said something that Van Winkle said haunted her.

“She said, ‘I’ve heard it before. I imagine it’s the mission.’”

Van Winkle admitted seeing every flag along the way but opted to drive right through them for the sake of her own mission. She eventually recovered, was able to resume her duties, and a permanent assistant secretary was named later on, but Van Winkle learned a lesson that she shares openly today. Regardless of what the mission is or what challenges face you, you must make your health a priority in order to succeed. Her personal experience combined with what she learned in college and throughout her career has given her a more comprehensive perspective on what optimal health and fitness really looks like.

“I now truly see fitness as crossing the elements of physical, psychological, and spiritual.”

Today, Van Winkle serves as the Industry Executive for Federal Government at Oracle, helping translate complex military needs into technology solutions that support the Joint Force.

“My job is really to help Oracle understand that government perspective, the Department of War perspective, and really translate what can be some fairly complex elements within the federal government back to the technology venture at Oracle.”

Alongside her corporate role, she frequently speaks to military audiences about leadership and resilience: a message rooted in her Pentagon experience. Her core principle is that individual health directly dictates collective unit readiness. Van Winkle also shares her knowledge and experience from her time in the Pentagon and about resilience when she speaks. As she learned through her own experience, each person’s health and resilience matters because it impacts the readiness of the larger group.

“Every member of the unit must be performing at 100 percent for the unit as a whole to perform at 100 percent.”

As important as that is, Van Winkle noted that communication and transparency about a problem is just as important because if someone in the unit is under 100 percent and does not share that with leadership, it could lead to bigger issues for the entire unit later on.

“I think leaders often presume that members understand this, but what I would hear from military members is a focus on mission above and beyond all else. And that sometimes meant that they would step over those red flags in order to maintain this facade and that everything is okay.”

She concluded, “Ignoring the problem is just setting a timer. They may be able to hold it together for a while but not forever.”

Many members of the military have shared that they don’t bring up their personal problem because they don’t want to be the reason that the readiness of the unit is compromised. In Van Winkle’s opinion, the moment the problem is ignored, readiness is already compromised.

“If a leader knows someone is struggling or someone is injured or someone is going through a crisis, they can do something about it before it becomes a full-blown issue that impacts the unit and the mission. If the leader does not know about it, you are then creating a blind spot.”

Those in commander and leadership positions should also see addressing those problems and resilience as investments into readiness because programs focused on resilience can save time and energy for the sake of the mission.

“If you wait for it to become a readiness problem, you really lose before you even begin. So preventing these things is an incredible return on investment.”

Aside from advances in technology, the military’s emphasis on readiness and well-being of the service members in recent years is going to benefit many future recruits who decide to join the Joint Force. Van Winkle advises that there are other things leaders can do to make sure those who wear the nation’s uniform can be better both physically and psychologically and therefore, more capable of maximizing readiness.

“Look closely at yourself, and think of it like a maintenance check like you do for a weapons system,” she explained. “As humans, we tend to preserve stability over instability and we strive towards homeostasis, but this often means that we don’t see what’s in front of us, particularly if it doesn’t align with how we see ourselves.”

Van Winkle also noted that life can take unexpected turns whether you are ready for them or not, and being resilient means being able to adjust when needed as quickly as possible.

“Life is masterful at creating instability, and we are constantly adjusting to the experiences that we have. If done right, it can make us stronger and more resilient.”

Finally, she suggested not being afraid to have the tough conversations that come with service, readiness, or life. The willingness to speak about it not only helps the service member. It can help the leader as well, which can lead to service members focusing more on patriotism, pride, and purpose while being better prepared for the pressure.

“It does an incredible amount to maintain morale and cohesion in the unit, and it really does prevent those bigger problems.”

M&F Senior Military Editor Rob Wilkins contributed to this Fit to Serve article.

#8671. Record 40,000 to Attend Sold-out ‘Rocky Run’ in Philadelphia

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

It’s 50 years since the original movie captured our hearts and fighting spirit in 1976, but the movie’s motivating message; that we can all push ourselves to be more than we thought we could, is still as relevant today as it ever was. With more than 40,000 runners expected to descend in Philadelphia, each of the three Rocky Run categories have sold out.

The first official Rocky Run began in 2014 with heavyweight beginnings, attracting 7,000 runners, but it has gone from strength to strength since. And, while organizers had expected around 30,000 competitors to descend in Philly this year, the final number will clock in at an incredible 40,000.

Those who are ready and set for November 14, 2026, have a choice of three categories, catering to different abilities, so that anyone can “Go For it.”

The half marathon actually combines the 5K and 10-mile runs, meeting the 13.1-mile requirement, and besides channeling your inner Rocky Balboa and going the distance, there are cool medals to be won. The 5K finisher medal celebrates 50 years of Rocky, while the 10-mile finisher medal depicts The Italian Stallion’s triumphant celebration at the top of the famous steps leading up to the Philadelphia Museum of Art. The 13.1-mile finishers is a large, heavyweight design that has “50” emblazoned on one side, while the other side has a vintage image of Rocky in training.

In addition to the Rocky Run, Philadelphia continues to show its love for the most famous fictional boxer in history. The city held its first “Rocky Day,” on December 3, 2023. No doubt, the inspirational story of one man going the distance continues to resonate around the world.

“Once again it’s a magical time of the year, The Rocky Run,” said Stallone in a recent social media post to promote the activities on November 14. Of course, Sly has been heavily active during Rocky’s 50th celebrations. He released his appropriately titled autobiography, “The Steps” and even brought back the man behind Rocky’s signature soundtrack, Bill Conti, for a live concert in New York to go along with a screening of the film. And for those, who still can’t get enough of Sylvester Stallone’s creation, the story of how a struggling actor defied the odds to become the star of one of cinema’s most successful franchises is also set to hit theaters, with “I Play Rocky” starring Anthony Ippolito as the struggling boxer given a once in a lifetime shot, and Stephan James playing Apollo Creed.

As to whether Sly will make an appearance at this record-breaking Rocky Run, fans are certainly hoping that Philadelphia’s favorite son will tread his old stomping ground once again.

#8667. Robert Strauss Has the Full-Body F45 Workout to Stay Fit over 40

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

As the General Manager of WWE’s NXT brand, a pro wrestling coach, and the owner of eight gyms across Florida, Robert Strauss understands the importance of rapid workouts to stay ripped. To that end, the man known to millions of WWE fans as “Robert Stone,” says that F45 workouts are perfect for staying fighting fit, and he proved it with a dedicated demonstration for M&F.

The F45 concept sees gym goers from all over the world following the same daily workout. “Everybody does the same workout every day, and you’re never going to do the same workout twice,” says Strauss. “It’s a 45-minute workout that includes your warmup, your workout, and your cooldown.”

Indeed, F45 workouts tackle fitness from all angles. There are focused cardio days, strength days, and hybrid days to keep each session stimulating. And, there’s often a choice of two different exercises as you move through the circuit. “So, you really can get a full body workout in, any day that you come into an F45, and you’re always going to leave drenched in sweat, I promise you that,” adds the NXT GM.

F45 sessions begin as soon as the clock activates and include short demonstrations followed by a guided warmup with dynamic stretching, to prepare yourself for the pump ahead. Then, after the main session is done, there’s a cooldown period before you tackle the rest of the day, feeling ready to bodyslam the world.

Greeting us at his Baldwin Park, FL, location, Strauss, who is the father of twin boys, explained that F45 has provided structure so that he can keep up with the next generation at both at home and in NXT. He completed the following session between duties, proving that he hasn’t missed a beat.

(In this class, there were 4 minutes for setup)

Execute each exercise for 45 seconds.Rest and transition to the next exercise for 15 seconds.

High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) sessions such as this one can easily burn more than 500 calories in 45 minutes, depending on the effort put in, and you’ll supercharge your fat burning power with Excess Post-Exercise Oxygen Consumption (EPOC) for the rest of the day.

You won’t need to walk around a vast gym space to hit all of the muscle groups either, because you’ll be completing each station while staying pretty much on the spot. This particular workout offered back and core strengthening exercises like crunches and rows, upper body testers like presses and extensions, and movements that also build the lower body with sumo stances and lying leg raises.

“One of the most inspiring things about NXT is that most of the trainees there are half my age,” says Strauss of his motivation to maintain muscle. “They are all phenomenal athletes that come from all over the world, and they are in the greatest shape. So, seeing them inspires me to continue my fitness journey. Also, I’m a twin dad to 10-year-olds, and I want to inspire them the way NXT Superstars inspire me. I want to inspire my kids so that they see their daddy is fit, and they want to be fit. It’s an important part of life for your mental and physical well-being,”

You can catch Strauss in his role as General Manager Robert Stone, stamping his authority on NXT, every Tuesday night on the CW Network in the U.S. and streaming internationally on Netflix.

#8663. At 43, Robert Strauss Continues Training to Be the ‘Dad Bod Destroyer’

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Whether you know Robert Strauss for his work as “Robbie E” in TNA or more recently, “Robert Stone” as WWE’s General Manager of NXT, there’s no questioning this exciting performer’s work ethic. Fortunately, as the father of twin boys, and owner of several gyms in Florida, Stone is showing no signs of slowing down. And, at age 43, the “Dad Bod Destroyer” tells M&F how he’s evolved in order to hang with the next generation, both on screen and at home.

Formerly a physical education teacher, Robert Strauss made his pro wrestling debut in the year 2000 and soon worked preliminary matches for WWE until he signed a major deal with Total Nonstop Action in 2010, gaining fame as the charismatic “Robbie E.”  It was during his time in TNA that Strauss won a multitude of titles, including the promotion’s TV and X Division gold.

He also lifted the tag team belts on two occasions alongside Jessie Godderz, and in that team, known as “The BroMans,” the duo even received support from seven-time Mr Olympia, Phil Heath. Of course, Strauss is no stranger to Muscle & Fitness. In 2017, he became a popular contributor with his “Dad Bod Destroyer” workouts, detailing how he stayed in fighting shape while balancing life with his twin sons Cash and Carter, who were just months old as that point. In 2026, Strauss is still making a name for himself in the pro wrestling business, by keeping a tight leash on the young superstars of NXT, but while his current role involves a desk rather than a squared circle, Strauss is always ready for action.

As Robert Stone, the world traveled grappler has maintained his fitness and physique by evolving, to stay consistent. For example, as a young lion, he was able to throw around weights with the same reckless abandon that he showed to many a hapless foe inside the ring. But at 43, and juggling his now 10-year-old twins with a hectic role as NXT GM, coach at WWE’s Performance Center, and broadcast commentator to boot, Strauss has a busier schedule than ever despite the fact that he does not currently compete. Fortunately, the performer has combined his passion with his profession and also owns eight gyms across Florida — that’s five F45 and three FS8 studios—so he’s never stuck for a timely way to stay toned.

Because F45 workouts last no more than 45 minutes, Strauss is able to get great value from his sweat equity. “You’re able to get it all in,” he tells M&F, noting that following an efficient plan has cut down his workout time without sacrificing quality. “Sometimes there are days where I don’t have an hour and a half. I don’t have two hours to get in everything, if I want to stretch out, if I want to warm my body up,” adds Strauss, appreciating the fact that F45 sessions are already planned out and ready to go. “At 43, I do need to regularly warm my body up. So, the 45 minutes is clutch, to be able to just come in and leave, and everything be done.”

For mobility, Strauss shares that FS8 workouts focus on a lighter style of resistance training for improving mobility and maintaining longevity, while still building strength. That’s because FS8 sessions combine Pilates and yoga, with a major emphasis on the core as well as controlled, meaningful movements.

Because of his commitment to crushing each workout, Strauss still looks like he could step between the ropes at any moment, and he maintains a low level of bodyfat to stay ripped, but as a mature athlete, he prefers a sustainable approach to nutrition rather than the latest fads, and this means embracing the balance. “The thing is, I really know my body,” he explains. “Mentally, I want to enjoy things sometimes. I’m not always eating a strict, clean diet. I want to have a good time with my wife or my twins. If they want to get ice cream on the weekend, I’m going to get it too, if I want it.”

The clever coach says that allowing himself to indulge also provides him with the motivation to eat cleaner for the rest of the week. “It adds fuel to the fire for my next workout,” says Strauss. Still, this athlete is keen to avoid eating too late in the evenings and particularly avoids starchy carbs and processed sugars before he hits the hay.

Strauss refuses to rule out the possibility that Robert Stone could one day return him to the ring. He certainly would not be the oldest grappler on the roster if he did. Randy Orton and The Miz are 46, CM Punk is 48, and Rey Mysterio is 51. WWE fans also know that Stauss’s colleague and SmackDown General Manager, Nick Aldis, who is 39, returned for a one-off match against Gunther at SummerSlam 2026.

“If someone pushed me past the point where I need to step in the ring again, I don’t need a week to get ready,” says the authority of NXT. “I don’t need three months to get ready… I can be ready in an hour.”

#8661. Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

“I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”

So, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!)

Among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore new places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

With all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

While my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the big-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.)

This level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

As we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

In summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a new cost too since I was self-insured back then.

My budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

This strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

First of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible plan ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze plan in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

But as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

When it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which says that,

Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

For me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

The only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I currently live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out.  I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

But I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

In the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

But for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?

I feel ya here. Hawai’i grocery costs are very, very high as well. Costco is an absolute lifesaver — in fact, the single busiest one in the world is in the Iwilei neighborhood here in Honolulu!

A good one I like to do, since I don’t own a car, is offer my Costco membership up for anyone who doesn’t have one but is willing to pick me up and drop me off with groceries. I pay for their things and mine, and then they’ll just toss me the money back with venmo/cashapp/zelle or just plain cash.

If any Canadians are in the house and really strapped for cash, I recommend this as a frugal, carpool-esque solution!

Agree. Canadian who shops at Costco in Ontario, Canada. I make a list. I check my stock at home. I don’t duplicate stock. Costco usually has one fruit or one vegetable on sale each week. Fresh or frozen. We buy the sale fruits and vegetables. Costco usually has a protein on sale each week. Fresh or frozen. We by the sale protein: chicken, beef, fish, tofu. Certain times of the year, we stock up on organic soup, canned salmon, frozen salmon. These go on sale at Costco, one to four times per year. Kirkland Signature frozen salmon goes on sale once or twice per year. Costco matches the price of milk when the other grocery stores have a sale on milk. They don’t advertise it. We have done this about 6 times in 2024. We stock up on milk when this happens. Costco has clearance groceries. Ends in 97 pricing. We stock up on clearance groceries at that time. Nothing wrong with the groceries. Either Costco is getting a new supplier of the same product or they are changing the packaging. I see people buying at Costco paying regular price. We strategically wait for Costco sales and Costco clearance. We eat well and buying very little junk food. We shop when the warehouse has the least amount of people. We ask the employees when it is least busiest. And at Christmas, Costco opens at 8 am. For about 2 weeks. No crowds. I wish I worked at Costco, so I could get the employee discount on the stock. lol.

Mr. Money Mustache January 17, 2025, 9:24 am

I read that many of the people in that (wealthy) part of LA were forced to self-insure partly because the insurance companies weren’t willing to cover such a high wildfire risk. At a certain level of wealth, the cost of repairing or rebuilding a house isn’t a big deal but I’m sure there are many people left behind and struggling.

For the rest of us, it’s really just a probability game: if you can’t afford the consequences of a fire or disaster, either buy insurance or stick to a less expensive house. If you ARE getting insurance, do the math on whether the premium is worth the coverage.

Homeowners also includes liability protection if someone is injured on your property and for certain off-property related claims, like if you injure someone with your bicycle, or get sued for slander or libel. Also it generally would be required before one could have an umbrella policy for higher liability coverage. Maybe this is more of a U.S. mindset, than an Canadian one where there are fewer outlandish personal injury judgments, but for me having insurance to protect my net worth is an important consideration. So I carry la homeowner’s policy for asset protection.

This is a very good point. I am a retired insurance regulatory lawyer, and homeowners insurance just covers much more than the house. It covers YOU for liability. If you get sued, it also hires a lawyer to defend you and pays any judgement against you up to the policy limits. It also provides loss of use coverage to pay for the hotel you have to live in if your house becomes uninhabitable AND pays to replace the contents of your house, like your furniture, appliances, and clothes.

You write that, “Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.”

You don’t have home insurance?!?! Say if your house burns down? Isn’t it worth it to have insurance to cover that catastrophic loss? I pay a small amount monthly for this benefit. Mr. Money Mustache January 17, 2025, 9:21 am

Yes, for many people house insurance is a solid plan. And if you have a mortgage on that house, it’s mandatory because the lender wants YOU to pay to protect THEIR collateral.

As you get older and wealthier, and especially if you live in a not-that-expensive house like my current one, it’s worth it to continually rework the math. In my case I came up with these thoughts:

– if my house burned down, I’d be rather pissed but the actual cost of rebuilding would not affect my ability to stay retired – and the foundation would probably survive, which cuts the rebuilding costs by another $50k or so – and I’d rebuild it into a much cooler house – and I’d be the builder and hire all my carpenter friends to work alongside me, because that’s my favorite thing to do anyway!

Another factor is just the “sleep at night” question. If having insurance helps you sleep better at night, that increases the value for you as well. In my case, I sleep like a worry-free log every night anyway :-)
