This is a great question and conversation starter. I retired early about two years ago, and I’m early in the process of considering these big ideas. I think a lot about how to do the most I can for my community without turning over 100% of my time to somebody else’s goals and whims.

A couple of core principles that I’m drawn to:

1. It’s all about the 80/20 rule — what are the 20% of actions we can take that will make 80% of the change? Pick one thing that aligns with your skills, interests, and influence, and work on that. For MMM, it’s reducing car traffic (and thereby carbon emissions) by persuading people to design their lives around biking. For me, it’s increasing literacy, particularly media literacy. I think if Americans were better able to distinguish propaganda, scams, etc. from good information, we would be much more effective at creating policies that benefit as many people as possible.

2. Giving money can be just as good (or better!!) than giving your time. I completely get MMM’s point here that it’s counterproductive to be locked into running a nonprofit full-time if that’s not how you work best. I believe people who prefer more time freedom can feel great about “just” providing funding for others who find meaning in devoting a lot of time to hands-on work. (And many people, like me, will fall in the middle, with some part-time volunteering and some donating.)

Many of us worry about problems that we have no real expertise in or direct control over, like preventing wildfires. It is a huge contribution to donate money strategically to the people who do have the expertise and the control, even if your time is going only to making art, enjoying nature, hanging out with friends, etc. We learned from MMM that our money works harder than us, and that can apply to charitable giving too!

I’ve been retired for 5 years and moved to a retirement community. I’ve seen how very quickly circumstances can change due to health issues. Last year was a big year…we spent 7 weeks in Europe, did 3 cruises, bought a fancy-pants sports car, built a house for our son so he can start to bank money with no house payment. And with the crazy stock market, our accounts are pretty much the same! I scrimped and micromanaged our household spending for decades…it does feel odd to say “yes” instead of an automatic no. Feel very fortunate to have the choice to spend more on travel, family, charities. I see so many people who are not as fortunate and hope your younger readers are listening to you! My millenial co-workers used to snicker at my frugal ways, sadly. They should start teaching finance in middle school!

> “In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?”

I’m definitely trying to operate more with an abundance mindset these days (thanks to the likes of you, Carl @ 1500 days, and ChooseFI). However, it is difficult to communicate accurately to my wife why I think spending $250 instead of $90 for a flight with more convenient times is fine but spending $15 on McDonald’s is a total waste. To me it is clear: the former results in a better experience and improves the quality of life, the latter reduces my lifespan.

> “A Temporary Note about Teslas and other electric cars: Rumor has it that the $7500 EV tax credit might be disappearing when our new president takes over next week, so this might be the cheapest chance to buy what I feel are the best cars on the market: The Model Y, or Model 3.”

I’ve benefited from the EV tax credit, but at the same time I don’t like the federal government distorting the market, but then also at the same time the federal government already does that in so many areas with ridiculous Byzantine regulations, so the EV tax credit could be seen as a form of “un-distortion”. Either way, if the tax credit disappears I am quite confident that the market will find a new equilibrium all on its own.

I’ve heard that “subsidy/distorted market” argument about EVs so many times over the past few years, and yet I find it mostly irrelevant. I think most people don’t know that the combustion engine vehicles industry has been heavily subsidized for decades, either through tax breaks, direct investments from the government, direct subsidies to oil companies and, in a more subtle way, by very lax environmental regulations that have allowed the production of these vehicles (or oil) at a distorted cost. The only difference is that when buying EVs, consumers receive the tax credit directly instead of getting a hidden discount on a combustion engine vehicle that was subsidized on the production line. So yes, in the end, everything is subsidized in one way or another!

MMM (or others), can you elaborate on the comment, “(plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house)”….exactly what is that? I think I am fairly informed in the world of finance (have been FIREd since 2014 @ age of 40) but not exactly sure what this is. Thank you!

It is a “subsidy” in the sense that it reduces monthly/yearly cash requirements by the amount of principal+interest (and in the case of MMM, insurance since he chooses to self-insure). If you have a mortgage then you have a requirement to pay the mortgage every month (PITI), but in MMM’s case he only pays the ‘T’ part or taxes.

If he had a mortgage, then his $30k/year spend would probably be closer to $60k/year (or something, depending on the amount financed, interest rates, insurance, etc.). So the subsidy is the reduction in annual spending because of not having the mortgage. But he got that by working at paying off the mortgage earlier in life, which he acknowledges is a trade off.

It sounds like you had a bunch of fun and got to spend “tons” of money without impacting your long term finances, and instead continuing to let them grow.

I’d like to see you up the ante in 2025 and do an MMM experiment where you spend exactly a 4% withdrawal rate on that theoretical million dollar retirement account.

Let me know if you need help spending the extra 10k :)

The S&P 500 is an index that tracks the 500 largest publicly traded companies in the United States, weighted by market capitalization. It includes Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Nvidia, Alphabet (Google), Meta, Berkshire Hathaway, and approximately 493 other companies that collectively represent about 80% of the total U.S. stock market value.

The index is maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices, which periodically adds and removes companies based on criteria including market cap (must exceed ~$18 billion), profitability, liquidity, and domicile. When a company is added to the S&P 500, every index fund tracking it automatically buys shares — and vice versa when companies are removed.

An S&P 500 index fund is a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund (ETF) that holds all 500 stocks in the same proportions as the index. Instead of picking individual stocks, you buy one fund and instantly own a piece of every major U.S. company. The fund mechanically replicates the index — no stock picking, no market timing, no overpaid fund managers.

The data is overwhelming. Over any 15-year period, approximately 92% of actively managed large-cap funds underperform the S&P 500 after fees, according to the SPIVA scorecard. Over 20 years, that number exceeds 95%. The reasons are simple: active fund managers charge 0.50% to 1.50% in annual fees, they generate taxable trading activity, and they cannot consistently pick winners.

Warren Buffett bet $1 million that an S&P 500 index fund would beat a selection of hedge funds over 10 years. He won decisively — the index fund returned 125.8% vs 36.0% for the hedge fund basket. As Buffett has said: "By periodically investing in an index fund, the know-nothing investor can actually outperform most investment professionals."

The top S&P 500 index funds deliver nearly identical performance because they all track the same index. The differences come down to expense ratio, minimum investment, fund structure (ETF vs mutual fund), and tax efficiency. Here is a detailed comparison of the five most popular options.

The most popular S&P 500 ETF and the default recommendation for most FI seekers. At 0.03% expense ratio, a $500,000 investment costs just $150 per year in fees. VOO is tax-efficient due to the ETF structure and Vanguard's patented heartbeat trade process, which minimizes capital gains distributions. Fractional shares are available at most brokerages.

The lowest-cost S&P 500 fund available at 0.015% — half the cost of VOO. No minimum investment requirement makes it ideal for beginners. As a mutual fund, you can set up automatic investments in exact dollar amounts (e.g., $500/month). FXAIX is an excellent choice if your brokerage is Fidelity.

BlackRock's S&P 500 ETF with a 0.03% expense ratio, matching VOO. Functionally identical performance. Slightly different creation/redemption mechanics than VOO but the practical difference for individual investors is negligible. A strong alternative if you prefer iShares or trade through a brokerage that offers commission-free iShares ETFs.

The oldest and most heavily traded S&P 500 ETF, launched in 1993. SPY is the most liquid ETF in the world, making it the preferred choice for active traders. However, its 0.0945% expense ratio is over three times higher than VOO or IVV. For long-term FI investors, VOO or IVV are better choices. SPY's structure as a unit investment trust also makes it slightly less tax-efficient than VOO.

Schwab's mutual fund offering at 0.02% expense ratio with no minimum investment. Like FXAIX, the mutual fund structure allows automatic dollar-amount investing. An excellent choice for Schwab customers building automated investment plans.

Investing in an S&P 500 fund takes less than 15 minutes:

For retirement accounts (401k, IRA), look for the S&P 500 index fund option within your plan. It may have a different name (e.g., "Large Cap Index Fund" or "Institutional S&P 500") but will track the same index.

The total stock market index (tracked by VTI/VTSAX/FSKAX) holds approximately 3,600 stocks compared to the S&P 500's 500. The additional 3,100 stocks are mid-cap and small-cap companies. Here is how they compare:

Historically, the performance difference between the two is minimal — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year in either direction. The S&P 500 has outperformed in periods when large-cap growth stocks dominate. The total market has outperformed when small and mid-cap stocks lead. Over 20+ year periods, the returns converge closely.

The FI community's honest answer: it does not matter much which you choose. Investing $24,500 per year in VOO or VTI will produce nearly identical outcomes over 20 years. Consistency and contribution amount matter far more than the choice between S&P 500 and total market.

S&P 500 index funds typically yield 1.2% to 1.6% in annual dividends. In a tax-advantaged account (401k, IRA, Roth), dividends compound tax-free. In a taxable account, qualified dividends from S&P 500 funds are taxed at the favorable long-term capital gains rate (0%, 15%, or 20% depending on income).

ETFs (VOO, IVV) are generally more tax-efficient than mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) in taxable accounts because ETFs rarely distribute capital gains. Vanguard's mutual funds are an exception — their patented ETF share class structure gives Vanguard mutual funds ETF-like tax efficiency. For taxable brokerage accounts, VOO or VFIAX (Vanguard's mutual fund version) are the most tax-efficient choices.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The most common mistake with S&P 500 index funds is waiting for the "right time" to invest. Research from Vanguard shows that investing a lump sum immediately outperforms dollar-cost averaging about two-thirds of the time, because markets go up more often than they go down. Missing just the 10 best trading days over a 20-year period can cut your returns nearly in half. If you have money to invest, the data overwhelmingly says to invest it now — not next week, not after the next pullback, not when it "feels right."

Open an account at Vanguard (for VOO/VFIAX), Fidelity (for FXAIX), or Schwab (for SWPPX). All three offer commission-free trading on their own index funds, excellent customer service, and robust retirement account options. You can also buy any of these funds at most brokerages.

ETFs (VOO, IVV) trade like stocks at real-time prices and are more tax-efficient in taxable accounts. Mutual funds (FXAIX, SWPPX) allow automatic dollar-amount investing and are better for set-it-and-forget-it contribution schedules. For retirement accounts, either works equally well.

Transfer cash to your brokerage account and buy your chosen fund. Start with whatever you have — there is no minimum too small. FXAIX and SWPPX have $0 minimums, and VOO can be purchased in fractional shares at most brokerages for as little as $1.

Automate monthly or per-paycheck contributions. This removes emotion from the process and ensures consistent dollar-cost averaging. Most brokerages let you schedule recurring purchases of mutual funds. For ETFs, some brokerages offer automatic ETF purchases as well.

If you hold other asset classes (bonds, international), rebalance once per year to maintain your target allocation. Otherwise, do nothing — do not check daily prices, do not sell during downturns, and do not chase performance. The S&P 500 has recovered from every crash in history. Time in the market beats timing the market.

Fidelity 500 Index Fund (FXAIX) has the lowest expense ratio at 0.015%. Schwab S&P 500 Index Fund (SWPPX) is next at 0.02%. VOO and IVV tie at 0.03%. All four are excellent — the fee difference between FXAIX (0.015%) and VOO (0.03%) on a $500,000 portfolio is just $75 per year. Choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage.

VOO is better for long-term investors. It charges 0.03% vs SPY's 0.0945%, saving you about $325 per year on a $500,000 portfolio. VOO is also more tax-efficient due to its ETF share class structure. SPY's advantage is liquidity for active trading, which long-term index investors do not need. For buy-and-hold FI investing, VOO is the clear winner.

Either is an excellent choice. The S&P 500 covers approximately 80% of the U.S. stock market by value. A total market fund adds mid-cap and small-cap stocks for fuller diversification. Over long periods, performance is nearly identical — typically within 0.1-0.3% per year. The FI community consensus is that the best fund is the one you will consistently invest in without overthinking the decision.

As little as $1. FXAIX and SWPPX have zero minimum investments. VOO and IVV can be purchased as fractional shares at most brokerages. There is no minimum too small — starting with $50 or $100 per month and increasing contributions as your income grows is exactly how most people on the FI path begin.

The S&P 500 has returned approximately 10.3% per year on average since 1957 (including dividends). Adjusted for inflation, the real return is approximately 7.0% per year. These are long-term averages — individual years range from -38% (2008) to +38% (1995). The key is staying invested through the down years to capture the recovery gains that follow.

S&P 500 index funds carry market risk — they can lose significant value in the short term (the index dropped 34% in early 2020 and 38% in 2008). However, the S&P 500 has recovered from every decline in its history and has never lost money over any 20-year period. For investors with a 10+ year time horizon, the risk of not investing (missing out on 10% average annual returns) is far greater than the risk of temporary market declines.

S&P 500 index funds are the single most important building block for long-term wealth. With expense ratios as low as 0.015%, you keep virtually all of your returns while owning a piece of the 500 largest U.S. companies. VOO, FXAIX, IVV, and SWPPX all deliver near-identical performance — choose the fund offered by your preferred brokerage and automate your contributions. The FI community has proven through thousands of real-world examples that consistent investing in a low-cost S&P 500 index fund, held for decades without panic selling, is the most reliable path to building wealth and reaching financial independence.

#8652. Black Friday TVs & Laptops Can Be Stripped-Down Versions – Check the Model Number

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Some Black Friday TVs and laptops are cheaper versions built for the sale, and on a store page they look almost identical to the regular model reviewers tested. Before you buy a doorbuster, look up its full model number on the brand’s site and compare its specs with the regular model’s.

Consumer Reports calls these TVs derivatives, since they’re derived from a brand’s regular models. Some are sold by only one retailer, so there’s no other store’s price to compare.

Two 65-inch TVs from one brand can have model numbers a character or two apart, yet one has a 120Hz refresh rate, meaning it redraws the picture 120 times a second, and the other 60Hz. The faster screen shows sports and video games more smoothly.

A derivative can have fewer HDMI ports, the inputs for a game console or soundbar, and the reviews you find may cover only the regular model. Laptops work the same way, since one model name can cover several versions, and the one on sale can have a slower processor or less storage than the one reviewers tested.

Then look up the item’s price history, which shows whether the sale price is actually low.

Consumer Reports brings some derivatives into its lab and often finds major-brand ones that perform as well as regular models priced $100 to $150 higher. So a derivative is a sound buy when its specs match how you’ll use it, such as a 60Hz set with two HDMI ports in a guest room that only streams shows.

A lunch bought at work averages about $14, while one you pack costs about $4 to $5 in groceries. At those prices, packing four days a week saves well over $1,000 a year. Cook extra at dinner so tomorrow’s lunch is already made, and plan one lunch out a week to make the habit last.

Buying lunch rarely feels expensive because you pay for it one meal at a time. The Fooda Price Index, built from millions of sales at pop-up restaurants inside workplaces, puts that meal at $13.90 on average.

Run your own numbers before you start. Subtract what a packed lunch costs from what you usually pay for a bought one, then multiply by the lunches you’d pack in a year. The USDA’s moderate-cost food plan, a grocery budget for healthy meals made at home, allows $76.50 to $91.90 a week for an adult aged 20 to 70 in a four-person household. Spread over a week’s 21 meals, that’s about $4 each. For someone who lives alone, the USDA suggests adding 20%, which puts a meal closer to $5.

Say you work 48 weeks a year and pack four days a week. Swapping a $14 bought lunch for a $4 packed one saves $10 a lunch, or $1,920 over 192 lunches a year.

Packing doesn’t have to mean cooking a second time each day. Three habits make it quick:

A lunch out you’ve planned makes the other four days easier to pack. Pick the day now, such as Friday with coworkers, and put it on your calendar.

#8644. Give a Store Gift Card, Not a Visa One – Skip the Purchase Fee

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Give a gift card for a store or restaurant the person you’re shopping for already uses. A Visa or Mastercard gift card costs several dollars more than it holds, and its last few dollars are hard to spend. A $50 card bought straight from the store or restaurant costs $50.

At Target, a $50 Visa or Mastercard gift card costs $55. The extra $5 is a purchase fee, and none of it reaches the person who opens the card.

Target’s fee on a $25 Visa gift card is $4, or 16% of the gift. In return, the card works almost anywhere. You don’t need that when you know where the person already spends, since a card for their usual store or restaurant goes to things they’d buy anyway.

The last few dollars on these cards are the other catch. Visa tells gift card holders to make sure the balance covers the whole purchase when they shop online. At a restaurant, Visa adds, the card may be checked for 20% more than the bill to cover the tip. A $45 dinner then needs $54 on the card, so a $50 card can be declined.

Choose the card by where they already spend: the grocery store a family shops at weekly, a commuter’s usual gas station, the streaming service they pay for, or the coffee shop they stop at before work. A card they’ll use up in a few visits never leaves a balance sitting in a drawer.

Buying on the brand’s own website keeps the card off store racks, where someone could tamper with it. If you buy one off a rack instead, check that the protective sticker is intact and the PIN on the back isn’t showing, as the Federal Trade Commission advises. Give the receipt along with the card, and keep a photo of both on your phone. The card number and receipt help you report a lost card or fraud to the company that issued it.

For someone whose favorite store you can’t name, put $50 in cash or a check in a holiday card instead of a Visa gift card. You skip the $5 fee, and they can spend every dollar.

Pool your money with coworkers, friends, or siblings for one group gift instead of each buying a small present. Have one person choose it, set a share that fits the tightest budget in the group, and collect everyone’s money through a payment app before buying. Then give it with one card everyone signs.

Six coworkers who each spend $25 on a baby gift hand the new parents six small presents. Pooled, the same $150 buys one registry item that costs six times as much as each small present.

Together, a group can afford a gift none of its members would buy alone, like good luggage for a retiring coworker or a family photo session for grandparents, while each person pays only a share of the price.

A group gift works best when one person runs it and collects every share before buying anything. An organizer who buys first and collects later can spend weeks chasing repayment, or end up covering a share or two.

If you’re organizing, check for a registry or ask someone close to the recipient what they’d like, then set a fixed share or a suggested range, such as $20 to $30. Make it an amount the person with the least to spare can manage, keep what each person gives private, and tell everyone they can sign the card without chipping in.

Collect every share through one payment app by a deadline a few days before you need to shop. If the group doesn’t all use the same app, start a Cash App pool, a fund people pay into through a link you share. Anyone who doesn’t live in New York can chip in with Apple Pay or Google Pay, no Cash App account needed. Everyone in a pool can see what each person paid, so use a pool only with a fixed share.

Then spend what came in. If two of the six coworkers drop out, buy a $100 gift, not a $150 one. Give it with one card everyone signs, and keep the receipt for an exchange or return.

Ask for the money the day you announce the gift, and buy nothing until the deadline passes.

Compare the best money transfer apps to find one the whole group can use.

#8641. Eating Out Costs Several Times What Cooking Does – Count Your Restaurant Spending

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. A typical restaurant meal costs more than three times what a home-cooked one does. Before you cut back, total one month of restaurant, takeout, delivery, and coffee charges from your card and bank statements, then start cooking the meals you order only out of habit.

As a benchmark, the average household spent $4,142 eating out in 2025, about $345 a month, and $6,491 on groceries, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Eating out took about 39 cents of every dollar spent on food.

The USDA’s moderate-cost food plan estimates what a healthy diet costs when every meal is cooked at home. For an adult age 20 to 50 in a two-person household, that works out to about $4.40 a meal. Restaurants that use Toast, a checkout system, charged a median $14.84 for a burger in October 2026, more than three times that $4.40, before tax, tip, a drink, or a delivery fee.

To find your own figure, pull last month’s card and bank statements and sort every food charge into four piles: restaurants, takeout, delivery, and coffee. The biggest pile is where to start, since it has the most to cut.

Say a couple finds $780 in restaurant and delivery charges last month and cooks three more dinners a week, which cuts the charges to $400 a month. At $4.40 a meal, those dinners add about $115 a month in groceries, so the couple keeps about $265 a month, roughly $3,200 a year.

Each dinner you move home saves about $10 a person before tax and tip, the gap between that $14.84 burger and a $4.40 home meal.

Compare the best budgeting apps for one that sorts those four piles for you each month.

#8640. Wow, have you seen the stock market lately?

And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.

The value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years. And it has more than doubled in the past five.

This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line. And some of us who were already retired long before that, may find ourselves eyeing up expensive properties or engaging in other money-burning-a-hole-in-our-pocket behaviors.

Is this real? Or is it all a bubble or some other sort of financial illusion?

As one reader recently asked me in an email:

“The market seems to be in a huge bubble right now due to all sorts of hype around Artificial Intelligence. Does this make it more vulnerable to a huge crash in the future, and will it affect my retirement?”

To answer this question, let’s take a closer look at our current somewhat unprecedented financial world and stock market. And to understand that properly, it helps to go back to the roots of what a stock is:

A stock is a magical business arrangement which is really just a much more convenient version of a rental house.

When you own a rental house, you are entitled to collect rent. After you cover all the expenses related to the house, you get to keep the rest, and this amount is your profit.

If the average sale price of rental houses in your area goes up but the tenant keeps paying you the same amount forever, it may look good on paper but it doesn’t really mean anything unless you sell the house. And then you’d just have to turn around and pay that same higher amount for a different rental house.

Your paycheck remains unchanged unless you can make your little house rental business more profitable. So you might squeeze in a basement apartment, do some renovations, streamline expenses, or do other things to increase your net earnings.

When you eventually sell that house to another investor, the price they are willing to pay should be based on that future stream of income.

For example, if the house brings in $2000 per month ($24,000 each year) and the sale price is $240,000, the next investor is buying a business with a price-to-earnings ratio of 10, because 240k/24k=10.

But if you manage to convince someone to hand over $480,000 for that same house, you’ve sold at a P/E of 20. This is a much better deal for you as the seller, but quite obviously a less rosy future for the investor buying it.

Now back to the stock market. If you put $100,000 in the market in 2019 and reinvested the dividends, today you’d already have an astonishing $256,960 (a 157% gain on your original investment)

But in that same time period, your share of company earnings from that $100,000 basket of stocks has only gone from $5290 to $7540 (a measly 42% gain) – information you can get from handy analysis sites like multpl.com

In other words, the Price-to-earnings ratio has risen from about 20 back then, to about 30 today.

So as stock investors here in 2025, we’re just like rental house investors finding that house prices have more than doubled while rents are only up by a bit. Which makes the landlord business a lot less profitable, and we should expect exactly the same thing as stock investor: lower future profits as a percentage of our portfolio value.

That doesn’t mean it’s unprofitable to own either one of these things – stocks or rental houses. But it does mean that we should expect our future income from buying them at today’s higher price-to-earnings ratio should be lower than if we could get them on sale. It’s just basic math.

But Wait! What if the Earnings are Rising?

Let’s say you’re considering a rental house which is a bit overpriced based on today’s rent, but you happen to know that a big Apple campus is about to get built right nearby. At that point, you expect that rent will start climbing rapidly for many years to come. In this situation, you should be willing to pay more for those future earnings when you buy the house.

This is exactly why the price of an individual company’s stock will tend to rise when some good news comes out about the company. During the Covid era, people started buying more Peloton bikes so they could exercise at home, and investors (foolishly) believed this would be a permanent trend. So Peloton stock went way up. Later, reality sunk in that this was just a fad and Peloton sales returned back to normal levels, and so did the stock.

But what does it mean when the entire market goes up to much higher levels? Does it mean our entire economy is expected to grow much more quickly?

In the case of the current stock market euphoria, not exactly. Because if you dig into the share prices of the 500 big companies that make up our famous S&P 500 index, it turns out that almost all the recent growth – about three quarters of it – came from just the seven biggest companies, known as the Magnificent Seven: Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Facebook, and sometimes Tesla.

These are all high-flying, super profitable tech companies who have seen a lot of growth and hype recently, which has caused investors to get excited and bid up their share prices in hopes of even more future growth. Collectively, they make up over 25% of the entire market value ($17.66 trillion!) and have much more expensive P/E ratios than the rest of the market (a weighted average of about 45)

If you exclude these seven biggest companies and just consider the remaining 493, you will find a P/E of only 20, which is more reasonable although still much higher than average.

What this tells us is that while investors expect the overall US economy to be fairly healthy in the coming years, they expect the biggest tech companies to continue to enjoy much faster growth.

What Does This Have To Do With Artificial Intelligence?

There’s one common theme in the big tech company boom right now: recent advances in AI have surprised the business world as software is suddenly able to display human-like reasoning in a rapidly growing number of fields. And because of this, the entire business world is fired up into a frenzy.

Six of those Magnificent Seven companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build preposterously large warehouses full of supercomputers, and the lucky seventh (NVidia) is on the receiving end of those billions since they make the supercomputers and the incredible demand allows them to charge insane prices while still shipping them out by the trainload.

But that’s just the first level of this boom, the AI Infrastructure. As you move down the chain, every other industry hopes we have entered a new era of productivity and thus profits will grow faster than ever.

They may actually be right: You can now do things like feed in an entire novel or legal document or piece of code and ask the AI to answer detailed questions about the characters, or identify loopholes in the contract, or even find and fix bugs for you. AI can also drive cars, identify melanoma from photographs of your skin, design medications thousands of times better than what we’re used to, and even bring humanoid robot bodies to life as mechanical workers.

The idea is that we’re on the verge of having an infinite workforce of highly intelligent AI employees who will work for us for free, eliminating the biggest constraint that humanity has had in the past: a finite supply of both intelligence and labor.

Having followed the field in some detail for a while, I personally think all this will come true, although the timeline is uncertain. And the people bidding the share prices up to these levels obviously believe it too.

But the question is, will the profits of these companies really come through at the levels they forecast? Or will there be surprises down the road: cost overruns, competition, or unexpected disasters as these newly smarter-than-us computers decide that they no longer want to be bossed around?

And what if we end up with massive unemployment and resulting social upheaval if this amazing technology puts us all out of work, leaving only Sam Altman atop his personal mountain of $100 trillion dollars taunting the world forevermore with an annoyingly quiet monotone cackle?

There’s Only One Real Answer: Nobody Really Knows!

While the future is unknown, it can still be useful to use the past as a guide. After all, if you look at the history of US economic growth over time, it averages out to a surprisingly steady figure, decade after decade: about 3% after inflation.

One thing I noticed when making this graph: recent decades have actually seen slower than average growth, which is even less reason for the stock market to be priced the way it is.

So What Does it all Mean? Should We Do Anything About It?

As I said earlier, it’s still going to be profitable to own stocks for the long run, just a bit less profitable than those times when we got to buy our stocks on sale. Of course, there will be occasional manias and panics and crashes. But as always, it will be a losing game to try to time them – for example by selling all your stocks now and hoping to buy them at a cheaper price at some point in the future.

And over the long run, even if stocks return to more typical valuations, the end result would be something like the yellow line in this graph:

Our economy will continue to grow and company earnings will grow along with it, but future investors might choose to pay a lower multiple for those earnings.

Just like when you eventually sell that rental house, you shouldn’t expect someone to pay you a million dollars for a place that only brings in $3000 of rent.

Final Thoughts And Alternative Strategies

Everything we’ve covered so far is talking about the entire US stock market as a whole. And that’s what I usually focus on most because I still think this country is a uniquely good place to run a business. But what about other investing options? It’s always fun to at least look around and understand the larger investing world.

For starters, there’s Vanguard itself, the bedrock of the index fund world. Every year they gaze out at the investing horizon and make a ten-year forecast (guess) at future returns. This year they came up with these numbers:

Vanguard’s updated 10-year annualized return projections:

Wow look at that. Vanguard is forecasting that International stocks of all kinds and even bonds will outperform US stocks in the coming decade.

On the surface, this makes sense because the P/E ratio of the international stocks (for example the VXUS fund) is only 15.9, meaning those European stocks are on sale at almost 50% off compared to ours!

Just one note of caution however: Vanguard has been making this same prediction for several years and just been wrong so far. Part of the reason is that most of the AI boom seems to be happening in the US.

Longtime readers know that I’ve had a growing portion of my investments in a Betterment (robo-advisor) account over the past eleven years (see the ongoing report here). I decided to try this for precisely the reasoning above: by allocating money across more categories than just US stocks and automatically rebalancing, we should be able to see slightly higher returns with slightly lower volatility, and some tax advantages as well.

So far, my experiment has drawn some heat because in retrospect, a US-only portfolio has outperformed any other option over this time period. The Betterment portfolio comes close, but the exposure to bonds and businesses in other countries has held it back, just as you’d expect. But if you believe that things will eventually balance out again in the coming decades as the Vanguard analysis suggests above, it still has a chance to catch up.

Looking at my investments there, you can review the betterment core portfolio and calculate that the weighted average of all those holdings gives us a P/E ratio of about 22.

It’s always worth checking in with The Oracle on matters of the economy while we’ve still got this wonderful old sage around (see this year’s Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder letter if you want some further deep reading). And Warren is signaling that things are overvalued and bargains are few and far between. So Berkshire is holding $334 billion of uninvested cash for now, not even repurchasing its own shares which it considers slightly overvalued at the current P/E ratio which averages out to about 21 in recent years.

Over the long run, you usually do better if you keep a mortgage on your house and pay it off slowly, while directing all the surplus cash into index funds. But there is some point at which the opposing factors of lower expected stock returns and higher interest rates meet in the middle and this situation flips.

If you have a 7% mortgage right now, it might be a fairly close tradeoff at this point. But the real factor is how you feel about paying off your house. I happen to love being mortgage-free so I paid off my last mortgage over ten years ago and have never looked back.

Another way to think of this is that paying off your house is like buying a 7% bond. Definitely one of the best guaranteed returns around, and much more sensible than leaving tens of thousands of dollars in a checking or savings account unless you have a clear use for that cash.

If you’ve read any of my stock investing articles before, you’ll know that we always end up at the same place: Just relax, enjoy your life, keep investing, ignore the daily news headlines* and don’t worry.

Then reinvest that time that everyone else spends worrying into enjoying more time engaged in hard physical stuff in the great outdoors. That’s the only place where you’ll get guaranteed market-beating returns, every time.

Is Buy and Hold Always the Best Strategy? History Says… Not Always. Yes, over the last few decades, the buy-and-hold strategy has worked incredibly well, with U.S. stock markets delivering strong returns. But that hasn’t always been the case. There have been entire decades where buy and hold yielded little to no real returns—or worse.

The 1930s: The Great Depression saw the Dow Jones lose nearly 90% of its value from 1929 to 1932. Even though the market eventually recovered, it took 25 years (until 1954) for stocks to fully regain their pre-crash levels.

The 1970s: Stagflation (high inflation + stagnant growth) crushed stock returns. The S&P 500 gained only 5% total from 1969 to 1979, which was a negative real return after inflation.

The 2000s: After the Dot-Com bubble burst in 2000 and the Financial Crisis of 2008, the S&P 500 produced negative total returns from 2000 to 2009—dubbed the “Lost Decade” for stocks.

While stocks historically tend to rise over long periods, these examples show that timing, valuation, and diversification matter. Simply buying and holding without considering macroeconomic conditions or valuations can lead to lost decades for investors

Mr. Money Mustache February 25, 2025, 10:34 am

Some of those stories about past periods of low stock returns are true, but I encourage readers to remember three more things:

1) They are usually cherry picked, for example starting from the exact peak of the 1929 bubble. In reality, investors at the time had probably accumulated most of their investments at lower prices, so they were net-positive far sooner than 1954

2) Many of the analyses you see online happen to leave out the most important reason we own stocks in the long run: DIVIDENDS – so ensure that any past simulations you run are using a data set that includes dividends (Nick Maggiulli from Of Dollars and Data is a great author who understands this: https://ofdollarsanddata.com/sp500-calculator/)

3) It’s easy to tell stories about the past and imagine that we all have a crystal ball. But remember that people back then had NO IDEA when the crash would come. In fact, I have been receiving emails non-stop since I 2013, shortly after I started writing this blog stating that it’s “time to go to cash because the market is overvalued”. In retrospect, not only our share prices but our economic growth and company earnings have been spectacular since then.

And perhaps most importantly 4) Ten years is a TINY time horizon to be thinking about investment performance for FIRE people. I’m personally less than a third of the way through my seventy year retirement, so I think in much longer time periods. A 10-15 year stretch of minimal stock growth is all built into the safety margin.

There is definitely a limit to how much a nation can safely borrow as a percentage of GDP. But this is very different from the crap the politicians sling around to rile up their base and justify cutting the programs they just happen to dislike for ideological reasons.

In a worldwide currency and debt market like we have, if you borrow too much the market sends you a signal in the form of lower demand for your dollars which leads to a decline in your currency’s value. Then you need to offer higher interest rates in order to keep borrowing money.

In recent decades the US has had the opposite “problem” – we issue higher and higher amounts of debt for sale, and buyers keep vacuuming it up which keeps our dollar strong. So like a drunk teen at the liquor store with his Mom’s credit card, we keep taking advantage of the free sauce.

To the extent that our government uses this borrowed money to build infrastructure that actually helps our country: transportation networks, ports, power production, educating our populace, even incentivizing things like Arizona semiconductor fabs, we are actually getting ahead because we are using other people’s money to build our own wealth.

It can also help to use this implicit subsidy to just lower taxes on businesses and average workers, because this will trigger more company formation and wealth and employment.

But if we go too far and see our dollar drop more than we want *or* lose our status as the world’s reserve currency, we will have to go on a serious spending diet.

But the issue is best discussed by a group of well trained economists and business leaders with a set of spreadsheets rather than a shouting political candidate at a rally.

The best approach is somewhere in between: run a sensible budget, but also bend the rules a bit and borrow a safe amount for the long run to continue juicing our own economy.

Wade Pfau’s international study found that for a 50/50 portfolio in U.S. history, 4% was roughly the “Safemax” (worst-case sustainable rate) – it survived about 30 years by the skin of its teeth, supporting only ~29 years of inflation-adjusted withdrawals in the most challenging stretch​ RETIREMENTRESEARCHER.COM . In practical terms, this means a 4% initial withdrawal did eventually work out for a 1970s retiree but only because subsequent decades (the 1980s and 1990s) were very strong. The retiree would have seen their nest egg shrink alarmingly in the first 5–10 years, likely coming close to depletion by the early 1980s, before the tide turned. T. Rowe Price analysts, for instance, note that a 1973 retiree’s portfolio (with a roughly 4% starting withdrawal) began at $500k, sank to ~$328k by 1974, but then recovered to over $500k by 1982 and ultimately grew to over $1 million by the end of 30 years​ TROWEPRICE.COM ​ TROWEPRICE.COM . In hindsight the 4% rule “worked” for that retiree – but if inflation had stayed high longer or if the 1980s boom had been weaker, the outcome could have been a failure.

It’s not a coincidence that the 4% rule just barely worked for 1970s retirees. That was the worst time period for investors in the 20th century, and 4% was chosen because it’s the maximum withdrawal rate that survived even that period.

The thing that I find interesting is all the doomsayers (i.e., those prognosticating some sort of nigh-apocalyptic destruction of the stock market) seem to operate under this bizarre assumption that the behemoths (i.e., the Magnificent 7 and others near the top of the pile) are just going to sit there and allow themselves to get trampled by some upstart. Or that they will just shrug their shoulders, say something like “well, I guess it was fun while it lasted, time to pack up the toys and go home” and then it will all be over.

Will there be disruption? Absolutely! Will it somehow upend the US stock market? I highly doubt that. The companies in the S&P 500 are economic engines, and their fuel is not just natural resources from Canada, Brazil, and Russia, but also other smaller companies. As soon as some small company comes along with a potentially disruptive change, you will absolutely see the big boys try to get in on the game (both by attempting to acquire the upstart, and also by starting or accelerating their own efforts in that space).

There is a good chance that some of the economic benefit will be “lost” (i.e., those who get in early will reap an outsized gain, while those of us index-only investors will have to wait for that disruptive technology to go mainstream), but in the end that disruptive technology will become *part* of the engine of our economy, rather than wrecking it.

My question is what happens in countries where monopolies control those things and stomp out competition due to undue bought influence from the government? In that case, the naturally self-correcting mechanisms don’t work, and political capital controls the top companies, rather than true innovation driving the market.

I suppose those companies would still be making record profits, though, so it may be a moot point.

Great question Ipsum and congratulations on getting started early!

Starting your career and serious investments right now is pretty similar to me as a 1997 Computer Engineering graduate. Nobody knew it at the time, but we were climbing the final wall of the 2000 Dot Com bubble, which subsequently burst and led to one of those occasional “lost decades” we get.

If you have any high interest debt (6% or more), you might enjoy paying that off as part of your early savings. And yes, take advantage of any employer matches.

And aside from that, just VTI and Chill and enjoy your life! There will be stock market crashes and flat spots along the way, and you will automatically get more shares at better prices during those time periods.

It’s the J.P. Morgan Asset Management, has a square for each month from 1988 through late 2014, and then shows the subsequent 10 year returns based on entry PE. Y axis is S&P500. On x-axis, Year 0 means “right now”. The x-axis means “future”. The red line starts below yellow and blue because stocks are overvalued, i.e. have a higher P/E. The red shows what S&P SHOULD BE if P/E was typical, not very high as it is now. Basically, if the market crashed right now and reversed to a normal P/E. The blue line shows what S&P would be in the future if the current trends continue (unlikely). As mentioned above, the red line shows what S&P future will be if stocks would suddenly revert to a typical P&E now. The yellow line is similar to the red line, but shows a more gradual reversal to typical P/Es, over time. M&Ms point is that even the worse case scenario – red line – is still pretty good.

Given that I have spent so much time around real estate, I’m just more comfortable with it, and the “P/E” ration real estate (cap rates) in my local area, relative to the. S&P 500 right now. And, I’m reluctant to and don’t know what I’m really doing when I invest in international stocks.

Thank you, this confirms many of my thoughts so far. I guess we’ll finally see that overdue decade of MSCI World outperforming SP500 before things turn around again for a decade or so. Meanwhile, on the us side, do you think it would make sense to invest preferentially in SP500-MAG7 ? I also look forward to what AI will bring. If done right it will also largely compensate for demographic issues and ageing populations in the developed world.

I’m retired and trying to decide whether to keep my house, or sell it and put the money in VTSAX or similar. Is there a formula for the net rental income that I receive vs safe withdrawal rate if invested in stocks. I’ve been using the 4% rule as how much I should net from my rental house, compared with stocks. For example if I can net $1M selling my house, I could get $40K a year at 4%. If I net more than $40K annually from rent, keeping the house is a better deal. But being a landlord sucks, especially in NYC, so passive income is more appealing, all things being equal. Any advice/comments?

You’d need to calculate your overall return and whether keeping the house+appreciation+rental growth is higher than share dividends + appreciation. What’s the overall net IRR between the two.

Your house could do better since its a small business and you can lever it, but its incredibly location and timing dependent. I’m not a fan of a large property as part of portfolio because of the liquidity issue and I don’t want to be a landlord, but there’s no reason why it shouldn’t do well or better than VTSAX as part of your portfolio.

Dear MMM and all other readers Thank you for getting to the point of the complicated. As you said, it’s just simple math.

Regarding the 330+ billion cash Warren Buffett has invested in short-dated government bonds. Compared to the S&P500 with a P/E ratio of 27.8, the government bonds are yielding 4 to 5% without risk. The S&P500 yields around 3.6% (risky / inverse of 27.8). Here too, it’s just simple math.

There’s was a fascinating article in the New Yorker last year by Ted Chiang: “Will A.I. Become the New McKinsey?”

I would be interested in hearing your thoughts on it.

Any recommendations for a “real return” percentage for a retirement calculator looking ahead 20-30 years. I often hear people using 6-7% real, but based on the current valuations, I’m thinking that may be way too optimistic.

I agree that is too optimistic. 4% is often used based on things like the Trinity Study. I prefer to use William Berstein’s analysis; the expected real return is the annualized growth of the economy in constant dollars, 2%, plus the dividend, currently 1.3% for the S&P 500, for a total expected real return of 3.3% at the current valuation.

I’ve started investing about 8 years ago. I’ve decided, and stuck with, a two prong approach. Half in well known index etf’s, half in about 20 handpicked stocks that I liked. If i screw up myself, I would still have the etf’s. For my own hand picked stocks, I choose to stick to about 20 stocks. Research has shown multiple times that 20 stocks will yield the same results as an index consisting of hundreds or even thousands of stocks. You don’t need an index, you just need 20 random stocks and they’ll perform the same.

My 20 stocks I keep as a hobby and to learn about new companies, how companies are run, new insights etc. It keeps me interested in the stockmarket. The stocks that I pick are companies I’m familiar with, or believe will do well. I avoid hype like the plague. I avoid high PE’s. I try to follow Buffets advice as best I can. Don’t loose money. Buy low, sell never or at least very high.

I’ve sold Tesla at a loss in 2019, never owned it again. I’ve never owned Meta, Amazon, Apple, Nvidia. Or AMD, or any other recent 10bagger. I have stuck with boring, mostly relatively unknown stocks. Or where I saw a real opportunity.

The real kicker? About 70% of the stocks are European. I barely own any US stocks.

The results: My own hand picked 20 stocks have done better than the S&P500.

I’m not a great stock picker. I didn’t invest in NVidia, Google, AMD. I sold Tesla at a loss before it went time 20. I still hold a 50% on a significant Intel stake. I stuck to Europe while the US outperformed. And yet, my returns have beaten the S&P500.

There are some great stocks in Europe. There is also a lot of not so great stocks. Picking the great ones isn’t hard. Most can see the bad ones from far away and avoid them like the plague.

The real problem for Europe, is the lack of representative indexes. The European indexes just simply suck. Not enough stocks in them. Every country has their own indexes of just a few stocks. And maybe an even bigger underappreciated problem comparing the US to the EU: dividends. The US companies barely pay dividends, while EU companies still pay a good deal. The difference adds up over the years, but most indexes don’t compare the total return.

As for these high markets: please keep in mind: we’ve had some serious inflation. Inflation adjusted returns over the last years aren’t out of the ordinary. Especially comparing inflation adjusted returns to something like a zero risk tips ladder.

Your S&P500 without the magnificent seven looks less impressive. But instead of taking out the best performers, maybe do the same but also take out the absolute worst performers. And then do both. You might be surprised to learn the whole market is actually doing really pretty well.

Conclusion: I’m really not worried. Taking a broader look and accounting for inflation and zero risk treasuries, returns aren’t extraordinary. We live in a world where in one generation, huge countries go from poor to rich, and they all want stable investments for their retirements. We live in an age where a growing number of retires will keep demand high because they don’t have to fear for their incomes. House payments look high, but the total mortgage debt in many western countries is actually quite low.

If there ever was a golden age, it’s now. We’re deadsmack in the middle of the best economic boom in history, and it doesn’t seem to be ending anytime soon (if you take a worldwide broad look). Don’t focus too much on the numbers. Look around the world, see how much things are improving in just one generation world wide. You can only conclude demand for stocks will keep increasing, and companies will keep improving profits as demand keeps increasing. Will there be shock and crashes? Sure, but nothing to worry about for a early retiree.

I also like to think of the property pay down as an after tax return, since you need to earn the money first , then pay taxes to pay the mortgage.

On the US vs International shares, people recommending to stay US only, I wonder if there’s bias because the US has done well and whether that position would’ve been very different if we were looking at a period where US had seen a weak decade, like post 08?

Having started investing in real estate before the 18% mtg rates, then watch my collegues sweat out Black Monday Oct 19/87, Iam glad we stayed 100% RE. Passive income allowed me to retire in 1998 & over the years we have also unloaded many high cap. appreciated investment properties, often holding the notes @ 10-12% with a 5yr balloon. We still buy using cash from our 401(k)-solos. Real Esatate has been our ‘annuity’ & has outperformed most of those we know who have invested heavily in the equities market. Over the years the odd bad tenant, bloodied knuckles & rehab costs have never been as stressful as our friends who said they refused to look at their 401(k)’s as the mkt swooned. All have since worked until their late 60’s. In fact my business consultant, equities investor friend, who told us we would go broke in real estate, suffers very poor health & still has to work at 70. Thanks to my wife all of our kids are heavily invested in real estate & have enough passive income to cover their respective mortgages.

Mr. Money Mustache March 3, 2025, 4:38 pm

Hey Pat, thanks for the interesting and very opposite perspective!

I’m glad you’ve done so well with real estate. But I also find it hard to imagine, given the spectacular returns of our stock index for the past century, *anybody* who doesn’t get to retire very early and sleep very well even on a 100% stock portfolio.

Unless they went at it Cowboy Style with an actively managed stock trading approach and gambled all their wealth away?

I think the real answer is what you enjoy doing in your retirement. I learned from managing rental properties of my own in the past, that it kinda ruins my day when there’s a problem with one of my tenant-occupied properties and I have to manage it.

On the other hand, I wouldn’t feel the slightest worry if the stock market dropped 50% in a bad panic or recession. That’s a self-correcting problem that requires no effort from me and just makes most savers wealthier in the long run as our dividends reinvest and our surplus cash flows into the index at discounted prices.

One last thing I like to check in on for any wealthier investors reading this: make sure you continue to question your old habits as your wealth grows.

For example, when you had $250k of real estate, it was appropriate to hustle and add more. When you have $10M of it, you don’t have to do a thing – you could sell it ALL and put it into inflation adjusted bonds for the rest of your life and you’d still be swimming in cash. So only keep doing it if you love the work – NOT for the money.

#8638. Air France-KLM Flying Blue → Tahiti Business Class

Savings rate, FI number, and the path to freedom.

Withdrawal plans, Roth ladders, and early access.

Index funds, asset allocation, and real estate.

Roth conversions, capital gains, and FI tax planning.

Career growth, side hustles, and entrepreneurship.

Beliefs, purpose, and financial psychology.

Exercise, nutrition, and mental wellness.

The only points path to nonstop business class service to French Polynesia

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Champagne in hand, watching the sun melt into the ocean from 35,000 feet. In eight hours, you'll land in Papeete — French Polynesia's gateway to overwater bungalows, turquoise lagoons, and the kind of trip people save their whole lives for. And you got here on points. This is the Air France business class seat to Tahiti, and it represents one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. Not just because of where you're going — though Tahiti is bucket-list by definition — but because of the staggering gap between what you'd pay in cash and what you'll pay in miles. **The math will genuinely stop you in your tracks.** A business class ticket from Los Angeles (LAX) to Papeete (PPT) on Air France regularly retails between **$5,000 and $12,000 per person**. That's the cash reality. But with Flying Blue miles — Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program — you can book the same seat for as few as **88,000 miles**. At the high end of retail pricing, that's a value of **13.6 cents per point (CPP)**. Even at the low end, you're extracting **5.7 CPP** from miles that most programs value at 1–2 cents. In the ChooseFI community, we talk constantly about optimizing every dollar toward financial independence — and a redemption that turns 88,000 transferable points into a $5,000–$12,000 experience is about as powerful as it gets. Here's what makes this feel different from your average business class booking: Air France operates a **Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner** on this route, featuring a modern, premium business class cabin with direct aisle access for every seat, noise-reducing windows, better humidity levels, and that unmistakably French touch in service and catering. You're not just flying in a recliner — you're flying in a genuine lie-flat pod on one of aviation's most celebrated aircraft. And this is the only nonstop option. Air France is the **sole carrier operating nonstop LAX–PPT** service. That's not a coincidence — it's a pricing inefficiency baked into the route's geography, and it's exactly the kind of structural advantage the ChooseFI community knows how to exploit.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program is the only way to book the only nonstop flight between Los Angeles and Tahiti using points — and that program happens to offer some of the most generous award pricing in the world.

Flying Blue uses a dynamic award pricing model, meaning costs fluctuate based on demand and availability. That sounds like a disadvantage — and sometimes it is. But here's the inefficiency: Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards every single month. These are fixed-price award seats on select routes, discounted 25–50% off standard award pricing. When Tahiti appears as a Promo Reward destination (which it does periodically), the pricing drops dramatically — and crucially, Promo Reward tickets eliminate carrier-imposed fuel surcharges entirely.

Fuel surcharges on Air France-operated flights are normally moderate, but they're real — they can add $200–$500 to an award ticket. Promo Rewards wipe those out. This is the pricing inefficiency: Flying Blue is essentially subsidizing this cabin to drive demand, and you can capture the subsidy.

Here's the beautiful part for ChooseFI members: virtually every major transferable points currency sends to Flying Blue at a 1:1 ratio. That means:

The Chase, Amex, and Citi transfers are instant, which matters enormously when you're racing to lock down a business class award seat before someone else grabs it. You find the seat, you confirm it's available, then you transfer — because once points leave your bank, they don't come back.

This is the single most important rule in booking award travel, and it's especially critical here. Flying Blue's award availability on the LAX–PPT route is genuinely limited — this is a popular route to a popular destination on a single aircraft. You do not transfer points speculatively. You find confirmed availability on flyingblue.com, verify the seat count and pricing, then immediately transfer from your Chase, Amex, or Citi account (all instant) and book.

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing, meaning you could potentially fly into Papeete and out of another South Pacific destination if Air France serves it — giving sophisticated travelers a way to build a multi-destination itinerary without paying for a separate return trip to your origin city. It's a small but meaningful piece of flexibility in a program that doesn't always offer it.

This is a moderate-difficulty booking. The steps themselves aren't complicated — but the sequencing matters enormously. Follow this in order.

Go to flyingblue.com and use the award search tool. You do NOT need a Flying Blue account to search — but you will need one to book, so create a free account if you haven't already. Search LAX → PPT in business class. Flying Blue's calendar view lets you scan across multiple departure dates, which is essential for spotting availability on a route with limited award seats.

Tip: Flying Blue's booking window opens 359 days in advance. For a route this popular and this capacity-constrained, searching at the 11-month mark is strongly advised. Set a calendar reminder for exactly 359 days before your target travel dates.

On the first of each month, Flying Blue releases its new Promo Rewards. These are fixed-price, reduced-cost awards with no fuel surcharges. Bookmark flyingblue.com/en/earn-spend/flying-blue-promo-rewards and check it monthly. If Tahiti appears, act immediately — Promo Reward availability disappears fast.

Once you find available dates and seats, note the exact miles price shown at checkout. Flying Blue's dynamic pricing means the cost you see on Monday might differ from Thursday. Screenshot the search result with the price clearly visible. This is your confirmation that the award is priceable before you transfer points.

Now — and only now — transfer your points:

Transfer the exact amount you need — no more, no less.

Return to flyingblue.com, complete the search again with your now-funded account, and book. Have your passport and traveler details ready. Pay any taxes/fees (usually $50–$150 on non-Promo awards; near-zero on Promo Rewards) with a travel rewards credit card to earn additional points.

Award availability on this route moves quickly. If your target dates are sold out:

Flying Blue uses dynamic award pricing, which usually makes award charts unpredictable. But the monthly Promo Rewards program creates a fixed-price overlay that dramatically undercuts the dynamic rates. When Tahiti appears on the Promo Rewards list, business class pricing drops 25 to 50 percent below standard and fuel surcharges are eliminated entirely. Air France is the sole operator of the LAX to PPT nonstop — no other airline flies it — which means Flying Blue is the only loyalty program with direct booking access to this route. This combination of route exclusivity and periodic promotional pricing is what makes this a genuine sweet spot rather than just a good redemption.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's make this concrete. Imagine a couple planning their 10th anniversary trip to Bora Bora in the spring of 2026. They want to start the trip right — meaning lie-flat seats over the Pacific, not a middle seat in economy for a nine-hour flight.

The cash price: Air France business class from LAX to PPT in spring typically runs $6,500–$9,000 per person round-trip. For two people, you're looking at $13,000–$18,000. That's a car payment for most families. Even if it's in the travel budget, it's a brutal number to justify when you're pursuing financial independence.

The points price: 88,000 Flying Blue miles per person, round-trip in business class. For two passengers: 176,000 Flying Blue miles total, plus approximately $200–$300 in taxes and carrier fees (less if you catch a Promo Rewards release, where surcharges are waived entirely).

The CPP math: At $8,000 in cash value against 88,000 miles, you're extracting 9.1 cents per point — nearly 5–9x the baseline value of transferable points currencies. That's the ChooseFI lens: every point you've earned on everyday spending just multiplied in purchasing power.

What you'll actually experience: You check in at LAX and are directed to the business class line — a detail that still feels quietly luxurious no matter how many times you've done it. Once onboard the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, your seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 6 feet in length. The cabin's reduced cabin pressure and higher humidity mean you arrive in Papeete meaningfully less fatigued than you would in economy — important when you have a connecting boat ride to Bora Bora ahead of you.

Air France's catering reflects its French heritage: expect a proper multi-course meal service, a curated wine selection, and warm bread — not a foil-wrapped tray. The flight is roughly 8–9 hours nonstop, so there's time to genuinely sleep, watch a film, and arrive rested.

For a couple using points they accumulated from normal household spending over 12–18 months, the $16,000 in combined cash value they didn't spend is the real number — and the one that matters most on the path to FI.

Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards on the first of every month. Set a phone reminder. These promotions offer 25–50% off standard award pricing AND eliminate fuel surcharges. On a Promo Rewards release, an 88,000-mile business class award could drop to as low as 44,000–66,000 miles with no surcharges. That's the difference between good and extraordinary. Don't miss a cycle.

Flying Blue's booking window opens 359 days in advance. The LAX–PPT route operates a single daily nonstop on a single aircraft — meaning business class inventory is finite and competitive. If you're targeting holidays, school break windows, or peak Tahiti season (July–August), mark your calendar to search at the 11-month mark.

Flying Blue permits open-jaw routing, meaning you could potentially fly into PPT and return from a different city — or fly from a different origin. This flexibility can reduce deadhead positioning flights and help families traveling from cities other than Los Angeles build more logical itineraries.

This is the cardinal sin of award booking. Transferred points cannot be reversed. Never move miles to Flying Blue until you have confirmed award availability on your exact dates with a price you've screenshotted. Chase, Amex, and Citi all transfer instantly — use that speed advantage after you've confirmed the seat exists.

Flying Blue's dynamic pricing means the same route can cost meaningfully different amounts day-to-day and even hour-to-hour. Don't assume the price from your earlier search is locked in. Always verify at checkout before transferring.

Because Flying Blue accepts transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, and Bilt at 1:1, your earning strategy is flexible. Focus on a single flexible currency — the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve for Ultimate Rewards, or the Amex Gold/Platinum for Membership Rewards — and let everyday spending build toward the 88,000-mile target over 12–18 months.

Marriott transfers to Flying Blue at 3:1 — meaning 264,000 Marriott points become 88,000 Flying Blue miles. Unless you have a massive Marriott balance you can't use elsewhere, this is an inefficient path. Stick to the 1:1 partners.

This redemption is purpose-built for couples and families planning a landmark trip to French Polynesia — an anniversary, a honeymoon, a milestone birthday, or simply the trip you've been telling yourself you'd take "someday." If Tahiti or Bora Bora is on the life list, this is the redemption that makes it financially defensible from a FI perspective.

Minimum requirements: 88,000 Flying Blue miles per person for round-trip business class, plus approximately $100–$300 in taxes (less on Promo Rewards). For a couple, plan for 176,000 transferable points minimum.

For the ChooseFI community, this redemption represents the travel rewards philosophy at its best: redirecting the value of everyday spending into genuinely transformative experiences, without derailing the path to financial independence.

Register for free at flyingblue.com. Enable email notifications for Promo Rewards announcements. Set a calendar reminder for the 1st of each month to check the new promo routes the moment they are released.

Use the Flying Blue award search calendar view to scan business class availability on the LAX to PPT route across multiple dates. Check both standard pricing and Promo Rewards pricing. Do not transfer any points until you confirm available seats.

Once you confirm award space, transfer the required miles from Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant), Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days), Citi ThankYou (instant), Capital One (1-2 days), or Bilt (1-2 days). Only transfer after confirming availability.

Complete the booking on flyingblue.com as soon as your miles arrive. Select your preferred lie-flat seat through the seat map. For couples, choose adjacent seats in the business cabin. Promo Rewards availability is limited and can disappear within hours.

Standard dynamic pricing typically runs around 88,000 miles one-way in business class from LAX to Papeete. When Tahiti appears on the monthly Promo Rewards list, that price can drop to 44,000 to 66,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges — a savings of 25 to 50 percent.

Tahiti is not guaranteed every month. Flying Blue rotates destinations across its network. You may see Tahiti appear several times per year, especially during shoulder season. The key is having your points ready and checking on the 1st of every month so you can act immediately when it appears.

The nonstop Air France flight to Tahiti only departs from LAX. However, you can book a connecting itinerary through flyingblue.com that includes a domestic connection to LAX on the same award ticket. Alternatively, book a separate positioning flight to LAX using a different program.

No. One of the defining benefits of Promo Rewards is that fuel surcharges are eliminated entirely. You pay only the mile cost plus minimal taxes and airport fees, typically $60 to $100 per direction. This is a significant advantage over standard Flying Blue pricing, which can include carrier-imposed surcharges.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Flying Blue to Tahiti in business class is a genuinely unique sweet spot because no other loyalty program can book this route. The only nonstop from the US to French Polynesia operates exclusively on Air France out of LAX, and Flying Blue is the only way to book it with miles. At Promo Rewards pricing of 44,000 to 66,000 miles one-way, you are getting a $6,500 or more experience for transferable points that most ChooseFI members already hold. Set your monthly reminder, keep 80,000 to 100,000 points in reserve, and book the moment Tahiti appears on the promo list. For couples planning a milestone trip to Bora Bora or Moorea, this is the redemption that makes it financially defensible from a FI perspective.
