From its humble beginnings in 2008 to today, Bitcoin’s history has been relatively short but very eventful. The original protocol for this popular digital currency was created in 2008 by Satoshi Nakamoto, believed to be a pseudonym for an unknown developer or group of developers.

Nakamoto launched the Bitcoin network just a year later and began mining the currency— an estimated 1 million bitcoins were mined in the early years.

The creator(s) of this first-of-its-kind asset developed the cryptocurrency in response to the Great Recession of 2007-2009, spurred by a distrust of the traditional banking system and concerns about its stability.

Given the recent values of Bitcoin, it’s hard to believe the currency first started trading on exchanges in 2010 at under $0.10. Since then, it’s experienced astronomical growth and some pretty wild price swings.

At its most recent high, one bitcoin was worth over $64,000—a far cry from trading for pennies in its earliest days.

Whether you’re thinking of investing in Bitcoin or you’ve held this cryptocurrency for several years, it’s fun to look back at this groundbreaking asset’s history. Read on for insights on Bitcoin milestones, historical returns, and how its returns compare to those of other assets.

Since being created, Bitcoin has experienced several milestones. Here’s a look back at some of the most significant moments in the short history of this cryptocurrency:

While Bitcoin isn’t exempt from the volatility cryptocurrencies often experience, it’s delivered some impressive returns over the years. Here’s a look at Bitcoin’s annual returns from 2010 to 2022:

And here’s a look at monthly returns, if you feel like getting a deeper dive:

While Bitcoin has experienced some wild monthly price swings and a couple of years where its value has declined, you can see that its declines have been eclipsed by some incredible gains. Now let’s explore how Bitcoin’s value has changed over 10, 5, 3, and 1 years.

Let’s say you bought one bitcoin on August, 3rd 2013, for $1,106.75, its price at the time. If you held that one bitcoin until August 3rd, 2023, it would’ve been worth $29,310.44, and your total ROI for the 10 years would be 2,546.8%.

We’ll also assume you purchased one Bitcoin for this example. A single bitcoin was valued at $965.31 on August, 3rd, 2018, and its value climbed to $29,310.44 by August 2023. Using our calculation above, your total ROI for those five years would be 294.1%.

A single bitcoin was valued at $11,246.20 in August 2020, and its value climbed to $29,310.44 at the end of 2021. Your total ROI for those three years would be 160.6%.

If you purchased a single bitcoin in August 2022, you would’ve paid around $22,626.83. In one year, that value would’ve increased to $29,310.44. Your total returns for that year would be 29.54%.

Instead of buying one bitcoin, let’s say you decided to invest $1,000 into Bitcoin. Here’s a look at how this $1,000 investment would’ve performed if you bought and held your Bitcoin for 10, 5, 3, and 1 years.

While Bitcoin’s earliest investors would have benefitted the most from buying and holding their Bitcoin, those who’ve invested recently also fared well.

If you’re curious how Bitcoin returns compare to those of other asset classes, here’s how its annual and total returns compare to gold, real estate, and the S&P 500.(Spoiler alert: Bitcoin outperformed all three assets by an enormous margin.)

If you compare Bitcoin’s returns to gold’s returns, you’ll notice a stark difference. Bitcoin has an average annual return of 1,576% and a total return of 18,912% from 2010 to 2022, while SPDR Gold Shares had an average annual return of just 5.14% and a total return of 61.67% over the same period.

Let’s see if real estate fared any better compared to Bitcoin. The cryptocurrency delivered a whopping 1,576% average annual return and an 18,912% total return from 2010 to 2021, while the Vanguard Real Estate ETF had an average annual return of 13.49% and a total return of 161.91% over the same period.

So, real estate saw slightly higher returns than gold, but it still didn’t come close to Bitcoin’s returns.

The S&P 500 didn’t fare too much better in its head-to-head with Bitcoin. From 2011 to 2023, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF delivered an average annual return of 15.74% and a total return of 173.14%. While those numbers aren’t too shabby, Bitcoin’s average annual return for the same period was a whopping 819%, and its total return was 9,012%.

We’ve analyzed how Bitcoin compares to gold, real estate, and the stock market, but how does it stack up against some of the best-performing stocks? Here’s how this popular cryptocurrency stacks up against major companies like Amazon, Apple, Berkshire Hathaway, JP Morgan, Microsoft, Visa, and Walmart.

We looked at the average annual and total returns for each asset. This data assumes you bought the asset in 2010 and held it until 2023.

While some investors may be skeptical about cryptocurrency, citing concerns over market volatility and a high risk of loss, Bitcoin’s performance over time paints a rosy picture. With its longevity and astronomically high returns, Bitcoin has been worth the risk for many investors—especially early adopters.

Of course, historical performance doesn’t guarantee future returns. So if you’re considering investing in cryptocurrency, only invest what you can afford to lose.

#8630. Cutting Back on Family Gifts – Propose a New Rule Before Anyone Shops

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. If your family’s gift giving has outgrown your budget, say so plainly, weeks before the first gift is bought. Then propose one new rule, such as gifts for the kids only, a price cap, or a year off from presents. A specific plan is easy to say yes to, and no one gets caught off guard.

The relative you’re dreading telling may be relieved to hear it. In Drive Research’s 2026 holiday survey, 32% of holiday shoppers said they feel pushed to spend more on gifts than their budget comfortably allows.

So raise it as a change that saves everyone time and money, not as a hardship you have to explain. A vague apology singles you out. The others keep swapping gifts, and you still get presents you feel you owe back. A specific rule for the whole family puts everyone on the same footing.

Timing matters as much as the wording. The National Retail Federation’s 2026 holiday survey found that 43% of holiday shoppers planned to start shopping before November, so propose a rule for holiday gifts by early October. After October, send the proposal before Thanksgiving weekend, since 64% of consumers in the survey said they were likely to wait until then to do most of their shopping.

For a family or friend group that swaps gifts at every birthday, propose the rule a few weeks before the next one. Say it in person or in one group message, so everyone hears the same plan at once.

Pick one rule, the smallest change your budget needs:

Keep a fallback ready for anyone who objects. Picture a sister who texts her four siblings in early October to propose kids-only gifts and a family dinner out. Three write back relieved. The fourth still wants to swap gifts, so she suggests a $25 cap for anyone who keeps giving.

Then keep to the rule yourself, and expect a relative or two to give anyway. Thank them warmly, but don’t buy a gift back, since that restarts the exchange you just ended.

#8629. Order Takeout Direct and Pick It Up – Skip the App’s Markup & Fees

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Place takeout orders on the restaurant’s own website or app, then pick them up. On a delivery app, a menu markup, a service fee, a delivery fee, and a tip can add a third or more to the food’s price. Pay for a delivery membership only if your delivery fees come to more than $10 a month.

Part of that extra cost is in the menu prices, not the fees. Restaurants pay the apps a commission on each delivery order, 15% to 30% of the subtotal on DoorDash’s published plans, and DoorDash says many set different prices for delivery.

Say a restaurant lists a $36 dinner at $40 on the app, the app charges a 15% service fee and a $2 delivery fee, and you tip the driver 15%. With a $6 service fee and a $6 tip, that’s $54 before tax. Picked up from the restaurant at its own prices, the same dinner costs $36 before tax, so delivery through the app costs $18 more, half the food’s price.

That 15% is DoorDash’s service fee on most orders in California, Chicago, New York City, and six other places. Elsewhere, DoorDash is moving to a fee based on distance and order size. It can also add a fee to small orders. Uber Eats charges delivery and service fees too. Grubhub drops both on restaurant orders over $50, but any markup and the tip remain.

To pay the restaurant’s own prices, order on its website or app, or by phone, and pick it up. Join its rewards program, if it has one, so the order earns points. In an app, switching to pickup drops the delivery fee and the tip, and DoorDash’s terms for restaurants call for pickup prices to match in-store prices.

A delivery membership saves money only on deliveries you’d order anyway. DashPass and Uber One each cost $9.99 a month or $96 a year and waive the delivery fee and cut the service fee on eligible orders over a set minimum. If your delivery fees on such orders came to more than $10 last month, waiving them alone would have covered the $9.99 monthly price. Check whether you carry one of the credit cards that include DashPass before you pay for it.

On your next order, open the restaurant’s own site, price the same meal for pickup, and compare that total with the app’s.

When I became an accredited investor, I found myself among an elite group with the financial means and regulatory clearance to access investments that many couldn’t. This opened doors to exclusive realms like hedge funds, venture capital firms, specific investment funds, private equity funds, and more.

Even though I had this “exclusive access” it took me a while to start investing in alternative asset classes.

The Securities and Exchange Commission states that as an accredited investor, I possess a level of sophistication that equips me to craft a riskier investment portfolio than a non-accredited investor. While this might not be universally true for everyone, in my case, I had demonstrated the financial resilience to bear more risk (see barbell investing), especially if my investments took an unforeseen downturn.

One of the intriguing aspects I discovered was that investment opportunities for accredited investors aren’t mandated to register with financial authorities. This means they often come with fewer disclosures and might not be as transparent as the registered securities available to the general public.

The underlying belief is that my status as a sophisticated investor implies a deeper understanding of financial risks, a need for less disclosure of unregistered securities, and a conviction that these exclusive investment opportunities are apt for my funds.

On a personal note, as a practicing CFP®, I haven’t always worked with accredited investors. Early in my career, I didn’t quite grasp the allure. However, as time went on, I began to see the broader spectrum of investment options available to accredited investors.

As I learned more the clearer it became why this realm was so sought after. The variety and potential of these exclusive opportunities were truly eye-opening, reshaping my perspective on the world of investing.

An accredited investor is an individual or a business entity that is allowed to trade securities that may not be registered with financial authorities. They are entitled to this privileged access because they satisfy one or more requirements regarding income, net worth, asset size, governance status, or professional experience.

The concept of an accredited investor originated from the idea that individuals or entities with a higher financial acumen or more resources are better equipped to understand and bear the risks of certain investment opportunities.

Historically, the distinction between accredited and non-accredited investors was established to protect less experienced investors from potentially risky or less transparent investment opportunities.

Regulatory bodies, such as the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), have set criteria to determine who qualifies as an accredited investor, ensuring that they have the financial stability and sophistication to engage in more complex investment ventures.

To be classified as an accredited investor, one must meet specific criteria set by regulatory bodies:

Here’s a rundown of some of the top investments for accredited investors…

Fundrise has revolutionized the real estate investment landscape. By democratizing access to real estate portfolios, it allows individuals to invest without the complexities of property management or the need for vast capital. The platform’s innovative approach provides exposure to a traditionally lucrative, yet often inaccessible, sector of the market

Through Fundrise, investors can access a diversified range of properties, from commercial ventures to residential units. The platform’s expert team curates these portfolios, ensuring a balance of risk and reward. With its user-friendly interface and transparent reporting, Fundrise has become a top choice for many venturing into real estate investments.

Investors start by choosing a suitable investment plan on Fundrise. Once invested, the platform pools the funds with other investors and allocates them across various real estate projects. As these properties generate rental income or appreciation in value, investors receive returns in the form of dividends or appreciation.

Equitybee offers a unique platform that bridges the gap between private companies on the cusp of going public and potential investors. This innovative approach provides a golden opportunity for investors to tap into the potential of startups and other private firms before they make their public debut.

The platform’s primary focus is on employee stock options. By allowing investors to invest in these options, they can potentially benefit from their appreciation as the company grows. With a vast array of companies, from emerging startups to established giants, Equitybee presents a diverse range of investment opportunities.

Investors browse available stock options from various companies on Equitybee. Once they choose an option, they invest their funds, which are then used to purchase the stock options from the employees. If the company goes public or gets acquired, the investor stands to gain from the increased value of these stocks.

Percent stands as a beacon in the vast sea of the private credit market, illuminating a sector often overshadowed by traditional investments. This burgeoning market, valued at over $7 trillion, consists of companies borrowing from non-bank lenders. Percent offers a unique vantage point into this market, allowing investors to diversify their portfolios beyond typical stocks and bonds.

The allure of Percent lies in its ability to offer shorter terms and higher yields, combined with investments that are largely uncorrelated with public markets. This makes it an attractive proposition for those looking to step away from the volatility of traditional markets.

Upon joining Percent, investors are presented with a plethora of private credit opportunities. After selecting an investment, funds are pooled with other investors and lent out to companies seeking credit. As these companies repay their loans, investors earn interest, providing a steady income stream.

Masterworks paints a vivid picture of art investment, blending the worlds of finance and fine art. Traditionally, investing in art was a luxury reserved for the elite. However, Masterworks has democratized this, allowing individuals to buy shares in artworks from world-renowned artists.

The platform’s strength lies in its expertise. From authentication to storage, every facet of art investment is handled meticulously. This ensures that investors can appreciate both the beauty of their investments and the potential financial returns.

After registering on Masterworks, investors can browse a curated selection of artworks. They can then purchase shares, representing a fraction of the artwork’s value. Masterworks take care of storage, insurance, and eventual sale. When the artwork is sold, investors share the profits based on their ownership.

Yieldstreet stands at the intersection of innovation and alternative investments. It offers a smorgasbord of unique investment opportunities, ranging from art to marine finance. For those looking to venture beyond the beaten path of traditional stocks and bonds, Yieldstreet presents a tantalizing array of options.

The platform’s allure lies in its curated selection of alternative investments, each vetted by experts. This ensures that while investors are treading unconventional grounds, they’re not stepping into the unknown blindly.

Investors begin by browsing through the diverse investment opportunities on Yieldstreet. After selecting their preferred asset class, their funds are pooled with other investors and allocated to the chosen venture. Returns are generated based on the performance of these assets, be it through interest, dividends, or asset appreciation.

AcreTrader, as its name suggests, brings the vast expanses of farmland to the investment table. It offers a unique opportunity to invest in agricultural land, combining the stability of real estate with the evergreen nature of agriculture. With the global population on the rise, the value of fertile land is only set to increase.

The platform meticulously vets each piece of land, ensuring only the most promising plots are available for investment. This rigorous process ensures that investors are planting their funds in fertile ground, poised for growth.

Investors peruse available farmland listings on AcreTrader. After selecting a plot, they can invest, effectively owning a portion of that land. AcreTrader manages all aspects, from liaising with farmers to ensuring optimal land use. Investors earn from the appreciation of land value and potential rental income.

EquityMultiple is a testament to the power of collective investment in the real estate sector. By leveraging the principles of crowdfunding, it offers a platform where multiple investors can pool their resources to finance high-quality real estate projects. This collaborative approach allows for diversification and access to projects that might be out of reach for individual investors.

The platform’s strength lies in its curated selection of real estate opportunities, ranging from commercial spaces to residential properties. With a team of seasoned real estate professionals at the helm, EquityMultiple ensures that each project is vetted for maximum potential and minimal risk.

Upon joining, investors can explore a variety of real estate projects. After committing to a project, their funds are pooled with other investors to finance the venture. Returns are generated through rental incomes, property appreciation, or the successful completion of development projects.

CrowdStreet stands as a pillar in the commercial real estate investment domain. With its vast experience and industry connections, it offers a platform where investors can tap into prime real estate projects across the nation. From bustling urban centers to tranquil suburban locales, CrowdStreet provides a diverse range of investment opportunities.

The platform’s expertise ensures that each project is meticulously vetted, offering a blend of potential returns and stability. For investors looking to delve into commercial real estate without the hassles of property management, CrowdStreet is an ideal choice.

After registration, investors can browse a myriad of commercial real estate offerings. Upon investing in a project, CrowdStreet manages the investment, providing regular updates and ensuring optimal project execution. Investors earn returns based on the project’s performance, be it through rentals, sales, or project completions.

Mainvest offers a refreshing twist in the investment landscape, focusing on the heart and soul of the American economy: local businesses. From quaint cafes to innovative startups, Mainvest provides a platform where investors can support and benefit from the growth of small businesses in their communities.

The platform’s community-centric approach ensures that investments are not just about returns but also about fostering local economies. For those looking to make a difference while earning, Mainvest presents a unique opportunity.

Investors can explore various local businesses seeking capital on Mainvest. By investing, they essentially buy a revenue-sharing note, earning a percentage of the business’s gross revenue until a predetermined return is achieved.

Vinovest uncorks the world of wine investment, offering a blend of luxury, history, and financial growth. Fine wines have been a symbol of opulence for centuries, and Vinovest provides a platform where this luxury becomes an accessible investment.

With a team of wine experts guiding the way, the platform ensures that each wine is not just a drink but an investment poised for appreciation. From sourcing to storage, Vinovest handles every facet, ensuring the wine’s value grows over time.

After signing up, investors set their preferences and investment amounts. Vinovest then curates a wine portfolio based on these preferences, handling sourcing, authentication, and storage. As the wine appreciates, so does the investor’s portfolio.

Arrived Homes offers a fresh perspective on real estate investment, focusing on the charm of single-family homes. While skyscrapers and commercial complexes often dominate real estate discussions, single-family homes offer stability, consistent returns, and a touch of nostalgia.

The platform’s strength lies in its focus. By concentrating on single-family homes, it offers investors a chance to tap into a stable real estate segment, benefiting from both rental income and property appreciation.

Investors browse available properties on Arrived Homes. After selecting a property, they can invest in shares, representing a portion of the home’s value. As the property is rented out, investors earn a share of the rental income. Additionally, any appreciation in property value benefits the investors.

RealtyMogul stands tall in the commercial real estate investment landscape. It offers a platform where diversification meets opportunity, presenting a range of commercial properties for investment. From bustling office spaces to serene residential complexes, RealtyMogul provides a plethora of options for investors to expand their portfolios.

The platform’s prowess lies in its dual approach. Investors can either dive into non-traded REITs or make direct investments in specific properties. This flexibility ensures that both novice and experienced investors find opportunities that align with their investment goals.

Upon joining RealtyMogul, investors can choose between REITs or direct property investments. Their funds are then channeled into these real estate ventures. Returns are generated through rental incomes, property sales, or successful project completions.

The world of accredited investing is dynamic and ever-evolving. Emerging trends suggest a shift towards democratizing investment opportunities, with regulatory bodies considering more inclusive criteria for accredited investor status. This shift aims to balance the need for investor protection with the recognition that financial acumen can come from experience and education, not just wealth.

Furthermore, technological advancements are playing a pivotal role. The rise of blockchain and tokenized assets, for instance, is creating new avenues for investment and might reshape the landscape of opportunities available to accredited investors.

As the line between traditional and alternative investments blurs, the future promises a more integrated, inclusive, and innovative environment for accredited investors.

Understanding the role and opportunities of accredited investors is crucial in the modern financial landscape. While the distinction offers privileged access to unique investment opportunities, it also comes with increased risks and responsibilities.

As the world of investing continues to evolve, potential accredited investors are encouraged to stay informed, conduct thorough research, and seek professional advice. The realm of accredited investing, with its blend of challenges and opportunities, promises exciting prospects for those ready to navigate its complexities.

#8627. Varo Advance Review – $8 per $100 With $800 in Deposits, $20 Without

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Take a Varo Advance for a one-time gap before payday if your paycheck already lands at Varo. With $800 in deposits there this month or last, it costs $8 per $100 borrowed, with up to 30 days to repay. Without them, the fee is $20 per $100, so don’t open an account just for it.

Varo Advance works only inside a Varo Bank Account, where each advance lands as soon as it’s approved. Qualifying customers can borrow on the same day Varo approves their account.

For a Varo customer paid $800 a month there, a $200 advance for up to 30 days costs $16, a fair price for a one-time need, though one every month adds up to $192 a year. Anyone paid into another bank should compare cash advance apps that work with that bank, some of which charge nothing for a transfer that takes a few business days.

#8626. Hyatt Category 4 Free Night Certificate — Card Perk Sweet Spot

Savings rate, FI number, and the path to freedom.

Withdrawal plans, Roth ladders, and early access.

Index funds, asset allocation, and real estate.

Roth conversions, capital gains, and FI tax planning.

Career growth, side hustles, and entrepreneurship.

Beliefs, purpose, and financial psychology.

Exercise, nutrition, and mental wellness.

The simplest high-value card perk in travel rewards — no points math required

Picture this: you walk into a stunning hotel lobby — maybe it's the Hyatt Regency Kyoto, maybe it's the Andaz Maui at Wailea, maybe it's a chic Hyatt Centric in the heart of a city you've always wanted to explore. You hand over your World of Hyatt card at check-in, and the night is on the house. Not because you're a high roller. Not because you spent $50,000 on a credit card. Because you crossed a spending threshold you were hitting anyway, and Hyatt rewarded you with a free night certificate that covers any Category 1–4 property in the entire portfolio. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about travel rewards done right: identifying the moments where a credit card benefit perfectly intersects with your normal life, and extracting maximum value with minimum complexity. ## The Math That Makes This a No-Brainer Here's the value proposition in plain numbers. Category 4 Hyatt properties — places like the Thompson Nashville, the Hyatt Regency Maui, or the Andaz San Diego — regularly command **$200 to $400 per night** in cash. On peak dates, holiday weekends, or in premium markets, that number climbs even higher. Your free night certificate covers any of these properties at no additional points cost. None. Zero. This isn't a discount. It's a full, unrestricted free night at properties that charge real-world luxury rates. Why does this represent a genuine pricing inefficiency? Because Hyatt's Category 1–4 certificates are earned through a flat spending threshold — $15,000 on the World of Hyatt Credit Card in a calendar year — and can be redeemed at properties whose nightly rates vary enormously. A Category 4 certificate costs the same to earn whether you use it at a $150 roadside property or a $400 resort. The system rewards you for targeting the high end of the range every single time. For a household already putting everyday spending on a rewards card, $15,000 across a full calendar year is often an achievable benchmark. Groceries, utilities, insurance premiums, quarterly tax payments — it adds up faster than you think. And when it does, Hyatt drops a certificate in your account that can deliver **$300–$400 in hotel value** without spending a single additional point. In the World of Hyatt program — consistently rated the **best hotel loyalty program for value per point** — this certificate is one of the most quietly powerful perks on any hotel card in the market.

The core mechanism here isn't a transfer partnership exploit or a routing rule loophole. It's simpler and more durable than that: Hyatt's Category system creates a ceiling, not a floor. When you earn a Category 1–4 free night certificate, you're not locked into a $150-a-night budget motel. You're handed a key that opens any door in that range — and some of those doors lead to genuinely spectacular properties.

Hyatt operates on a fixed award chart, ranging from 3,500 points for a Category 1 night all the way up to 45,000 points for a Category 8 night. Unlike programs that use dynamic pricing (where award costs swing with cash demand), Hyatt's chart is static. A Category 4 property costs the same 15,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in February or New Year's Eve.

Your free night certificate functions exactly like those 15,000 points — but you earned it through card spending, not through a points balance. This means the certificate has a defined and predictable value: whatever a Category 4 property charges in cash on the night you use it is exactly what you're getting for free.

The pricing inefficiency exists because Hyatt assigns categories based on average nightly rates across the year — but peak-season rates at desirable Category 4 properties can blow well past that average. A Hyatt Regency in a major city might be Category 4 because its average annual rate qualifies, but on a conference weekend or holiday weekend, that same room might cost $350–$400. Your certificate captures that peak-season value without any upcharge.

While this sweet spot is certificate-based (no points required), World of Hyatt integrates beautifully with two major transferable currency programs:

This matters for your broader strategy. If you want to stack a certificate with a separate points redemption — say, booking multiple nights where the first is covered by the certificate and subsequent nights use transferred points — you have two strong, flexible on-ramps into the Hyatt ecosystem. Chase Ultimate Rewards is the workhorse of the FI community's travel rewards stack, and having Hyatt as an instant 1:1 partner makes it one of the most actionable transfer relationships in the game.

Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award redemptions — a meaningful distinction compared to some airline programs where surcharges can swallow most of your savings. Your certificate redemption is clean: one certificate, one free night, no surprise fees at checkout beyond standard resort fees (which, to be fair, do apply at some properties — more on that in Pro Tips).

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. As a World of Hyatt Credit Card holder, your card activity will naturally keep your account active, so expiry is rarely a concern for cardholders. But if you ever cancel the card, make sure you use your points and certificates before they age out.

Booking a World of Hyatt free night certificate is genuinely one of the easiest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's the complete walkthrough from certificate to check-in.

Log in to your World of Hyatt account at hyatt.com and navigate to your account dashboard. Under the "My Certificates & Awards" section, confirm your Category 1–4 free night certificate is present and note its expiration date. Certificates are typically valid for 12 months from issuance, so don't let it sit unused. If you don't see it and you've crossed the $15,000 annual spend threshold on your World of Hyatt Credit Card, allow a few days for it to post after your statement closes, or call Chase to confirm.

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search function. You can filter by World of Hyatt category — specifically, search for Category 4 properties in any destination you're targeting. Don't shortchange yourself by defaulting to a Category 1 or 2 property out of habit. The certificate works at any Category 1–4 property, so always target the top of the range. Look for properties with high nightly cash rates — this is where your certificate delivers the most value.

Once you've identified a target property, search your dates on hyatt.com and switch the search to "Use Points." Category 4 properties will show award availability for 15,000 points per night. If award availability shows for that date, your certificate will cover it. Hyatt's booking window opens 395 days in advance, so for peak travel dates — holidays, major events, popular travel seasons — you can and should book the maximum window out.

Proceed through the booking process. At the payment step, you'll see an option to "Apply Free Night Award" or select your certificate from your account. Select the Category 1–4 certificate. The system will apply it and your total cash charge drops to $0 for the room rate (plus taxes and any applicable resort fees).

Hyatt award availability at popular properties can be limited during peak periods. Your tactical options:

Hyatt operates on a fixed category system where each property is assigned a category from 1 to 8 based on the brand and location, not the current market rate. This creates a structural pricing inefficiency: a Category 4 property in a high-demand market like Maui or Kyoto charges the same certificate cost as a Category 4 in a mid-tier city. Your free night certificate works at all of them equally. Unlike hotel programs with dynamic pricing where the cost of a free night fluctuates with demand, Hyatt's fixed chart means you can target the highest-value Category 4 properties without paying more. The card's $95 annual fee is one of the lowest in the premium hotel card category, yet the certificate alone delivers $250 to $400 or more in value — a return that makes the math trivially easy for any FI-minded household.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's make this concrete with a real example that represents exactly how this certificate shines.

The Andaz San Diego is a boutique lifestyle hotel in the Gaslamp Quarter — rooftop pool, stylish rooms, walking distance to everything downtown. It's the kind of hotel that signals a real trip, not just a place to sleep. On a standard weekend night, cash rates run $250–$350 per night. During Comic-Con, a Padres playoff weekend, or a major convention, rates push past $400.

Cash cost: $300 (conservative weekend estimate) Certificate cost: 0 points, 1 Category 1–4 free night certificate Your out-of-pocket: $0 for the room rate

You earned this certificate by crossing $15,000 in annual spending on the World of Hyatt Credit Card — a threshold many households reach through regular everyday spending over 12 months. The certificate posts automatically, you search availability on hyatt.com, and you apply it at checkout in about five minutes.

You're not redeeming into a budget experience. The Andaz brand sits at the upper-upscale tier of the Hyatt portfolio. You check in through a host model (no formal front desk), settle into a room with thoughtful design, and wake up knowing that $300 night cost you nothing extra beyond your normal spending.

If you hold World of Hyatt elite status — Discoverist, Explorist, or Globalist — that status applies to certificate bookings exactly like paid stays. Room upgrade requests, early check-in, late check-out: all the same benefits apply.

In every case, your one certificate delivers more value than most points redemptions in any hotel program. And you earned it without touching your points balance.

Your certificate works identically at a $150/night Category 4 property and a $400/night Category 4 property. Always search for the properties with the highest cash rates in your target destination. Use hyatt.com's rate display to compare award availability against current cash pricing — this directly shows you the value you're capturing.

Hyatt's booking window opens 395 days in advance. For properties in high-demand markets — Maui, New York, Chicago during peak season — award inventory gets claimed fast. Set a calendar alert to search exactly 395 days before your target dates and book the moment the window opens.

Your certificate covers one night. If you're staying multiple nights, stack it strategically: apply the certificate to the highest-cost night (often a Saturday) and book the remaining nights with World of Hyatt points transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards at a 1:1 ratio. This hybrid approach maximizes the value of every currency you're using.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of inactivity. As a cardholder, your spending activity resets this clock automatically. But if you ever pause card use, make a small Hyatt purchase — even a $1 on-property charge — to reset the timer and protect your balance.

Hyatt does not waive resort fees on award and certificate bookings at all properties. Before booking, check whether your target property charges a daily resort fee — these can run $25–$50/night and will appear on your final bill. Factor this into your value calculation, especially at resort properties in Hawaii or Las Vegas.

The $15,000 spend threshold should come from natural household spending, not manufactured purchases. In the FI community, we optimize around spending you're doing anyway — insurance premiums, tax payments, groceries, utilities. If you're buying things you don't need to hit the threshold, you're eroding the value of the certificate.

Certificates issued by Hyatt are typically valid for 12 months. Mark the expiration date in your calendar the moment the certificate posts. An expired certificate is $300+ in value that simply disappears — one of the most painful mistakes in travel rewards.

This sweet spot is built for the everyday FI household that's already spending $15,000 or more annually on a single credit card and wants to redirect that activity toward a meaningful travel benefit. You don't need a large points balance. You don't need to understand transfer partners or award chart math. You earn the certificate by spending, you apply it at checkout, and you get a free night at a genuinely nice hotel.

You need: the World of Hyatt Credit Card, $15,000 in annual card spending, and a World of Hyatt account. No minimum points balance required — this is a card perk, not a points redemption.

If your annual spending is significantly below $15,000 on a single card, this particular mechanism won't trigger. In that case, the World of Hyatt Credit Card still earns Hyatt points on spending and delivers a Category 1–4 certificate on each card anniversary — so it retains value, just through a different path. Also, if you're deeply committed to a non-Hyatt hotel program, the benefit is obviously less useful without a library of Hyatt properties in your regular rotation.

## Rated: Easy (4/5 Beginner Friendly) This is one of the most accessible sweet spots in the entire travel rewards ecosystem, and that's by design. The certificate mechanism removes the two biggest friction points in traditional points redemptions: **finding the right number of points** and **navigating complex transfer timing**. You earn the certificate passively through spending, it posts to your account automatically, and the booking process on hyatt.com is as intuitive as booking any other hotel stay. ## What Makes It Easy - **No transfer required** — the certificate lives in your World of Hyatt account, ready to apply at checkout - **Fixed pricing** — Category 4 is Category 4 everywhere in the world; no dynamic pricing surprises - **Simple availability search** — hyatt.com's award search is clean and straightforward ## The One Genuine Challenge: Availability at Popular Properties The only real friction point is award inventory at high-demand Category 4 properties on desirable dates. Hyatt limits how many award rooms it releases per night, and popular properties in destinations like Hawaii or New York fill quickly. **Three ways to beat this:** 1. Search 395 days in advance when fresh inventory releases 2. Build a shortlist of 3–5 Category 4 properties in your target region so you have backup options 3. Stay flexible on dates — midweek nights almost always have more award availability than weekends If you can approach this with even modest date flexibility, you will find great options. The Hyatt portfolio at Category 4 is large and geographically diverse, and there is almost always a compelling property available somewhere you'd actually want to go. For anyone new to travel rewards, this certificate is the perfect first redemption — low complexity, high reward, and a genuinely memorable hotel stay to show your household what this strategy can deliver.

Log in to hyatt.com and check My Certificates and Awards after your card anniversary. Note the expiration date — certificates are typically valid for 12 months. If it does not appear within a few weeks of your anniversary, contact Chase.

Search hyatt.com for Category 4 hotels in your target destinations. Compare the cash rate against the free certificate value. Target properties where cash rates exceed $300 per night — these deliver the highest return on your $95 annual fee.

Hyatt opens its booking window 395 days in advance. For popular Category 4 properties in Maui, New York, or Kyoto, set a calendar reminder and book the day the window opens. Apply your certificate during the booking process on hyatt.com.

Use the free night certificate for the most expensive night of your stay (typically weekends or peak dates), then book remaining nights with World of Hyatt points at 15,000 points per Category 4 night. This combination stretches your overall lodging value significantly.

Category 4 includes well-known properties like the Andaz Maui at Wailea, Hyatt Regency Kyoto, Andaz San Diego, Hyatt Centric locations in major cities, and many Thompson hotels. The full list is available on hyatt.com by filtering the award chart. Category 4 is the sweet spot tier where property quality is high but the award cost remains accessible.

The World of Hyatt credit card automatically issues a Category 1-4 free night certificate each year on your card anniversary. A second certificate is earned after you spend $15,000 on the card in a calendar year. No special action is required beyond holding the card and meeting the spending threshold for the bonus certificate.

Yes. The free night certificate is valid for any available standard room at a Category 1-4 property, including weekends and holidays. There are no blackout dates. However, standard room availability may be limited during peak periods, so booking early is recommended.

The certificate expires 12 months after issuance and cannot be extended or refunded. If you know you will not use it, consider booking a refundable reservation at a Category 4 property to hold the value, then cancel and rebook if your plans change. Do not let it expire unused — the value easily exceeds the annual fee.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Hyatt Category 4 free night certificate is the most accessible sweet spot in travel rewards. You do not need to understand transfer partners, award charts, or complex booking strategies. You hold the World of Hyatt credit card, the certificate arrives on your anniversary, and you redeem it at a hotel where cash rates run $250 to $400 or more per night. The $95 annual fee pays for itself three to four times over with a single use. For FI-minded households that consolidate $15,000 or more in annual spending on one card, the second certificate doubles the value. This is the card perk that turns skeptics into believers — simple math, real savings, no tricks required.

#8624. How to Navigate the Tariff Circus

Quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well. Back in February 2025, the market put the perfect cap on a multi year climb before stepping onto the wild roller coaster we’re currently riding. Since then it has seen some of the steepest drops and recoveries in history, losing a full 20% of its value at the bottom while somehow managing to end up right back near the peak as I’m writing this.

And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.

As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.

As I write this, we still don’t know the outcome of the worldwide tariff and trade battle that our unpredictable government has unleashed upon the world. But we’re already seeing the results: businesses are bracing for massive changes, currencies and interest rates are reacting, and regular investors like you and me are wondering what the future holds for our early retirement funds. Surveying my own group of friends, the reactions span the whole range of emotions from “this is a giant Nothingburger” to “we’re all totally screwed.”

So what’s the real answer? To get closer to that, we should start with the most basic question of:

A tariff is just a sales tax charged by our government on goods which are imported into the country.  They are paid by whoever is doing the importing – meaning you if you order something like an e-bike directly from a company in China, or by companies like Amazon, Walmart, or Apple which import products from other countries by the shipload.

But in the end, the tariffs aren’t paid by China or Amazon or Apple. They are paid by you, the end consumer, because if their cost of goods increases, a retailer is of course going to raise their prices to continue to make a profit.

Tariffs also affect companies directly: if Home Depot wants to build a new store or Chevron needs a new oil rig, the tariffs on imported steel, copper, lumber and a million other components will raise the cost of these construction projects. And they raise the cost of housing, because most of the building materials in houses come from multiple countries as well.

On average, tariffs will result in higher prices for everything just like any other broad-based sales tax. And just like most other taxes, the overall effect is to slow the economy and reduce our spending power. On the positive side, all that tax money flows into the government’s pocket which could help fund the national budget and even reduce the deficit.

Of course, every government needs at least some tax revenue to function, so it makes sense to use some mix of sales, income and corporate taxes to get there. The most important part is that the levels need to be as low as possible while still keeping the country running well, and as fair and predictable as possible, so that people and businesses have an incentive to work hard and the ability to plan far into the future.

And that’s where our current tariff regime gets it completely backwards. Donald Trump is throwing around random, extremely high tariff numbers as threats, then walking them back and changing them on an almost daily basis..

Whoa, that Sounds Mostly Bad – Is There a Good Side of Tariffs?

Sometimes, a country will use tariffs to protect their own domestic industries. For example, if you put a tax on imported Hondas, then General Motors cars will gain a competitive advantage – so GM will make more money. In this example, most consumers end up losing due to increased prices and decreased selection. But at least domestic auto manufacturers and their employees are happy.

This can be strategic (for example we might want to slap a tax on imported fighter jets to make sure Boeing and Lockheed can remain in business, for national defense purposes.) Or it can be corrupt (a politician might receive funding from kingpins in the steel industry, and in return then push through tariffs on imported steel to protect the profits of US steelmakers.)

And this isn’t just a Trump or Republican thing either – Joe Biden used tariffs during his terms in an attempt to please swing-state voters. One of the worst examples was a tax on imported solar panel components (which Trump has since raised even further, proving that Boneheadedness can be Bipartisan). These are sheets of cheap glass that literally pump the cheapest energy and easiest wealth into your country for 30 years as soon as you plug them in. Cheap energy lowers everyone’s cost of living while also boosting industry. There is no good reason to block such wealth from flowing across your borders.

Let’s go back to that hypothetical tax on Hondas, and let’s say it’s a big one like $5000. At that level, many buyers will start heading over to the GM dealer next door to consider what he’s selling. Sure, the GM cars may not be as good, but for five grand some people are going to settle in order to save some money.

Because of this, GM’s sales go up. So they hire more employees and build more factories. They might even develop some new models and new technologies in response to all that new demand. More people learn advanced skills and in the best case it becomes a virtuous circle.

But in exchange for this boom in the auto industry, everyone else has to pay more for slightly shittier cars and trucks. Higher vehicle prices means Amazon will have to spend more on their delivery fleet, so they will raise prices slightly on everything they sell. Somewhere a startup company or a medical breakthrough will be just a bit less likely to happen, because they are operating in an environment that is just a bit more expensive and a bit less efficient.

On top of that, with GM liberated from the hassle of competing with Honda, it will have less incentive to innovate and streamline itself. So its overall trajectory will be slower and less efficient even if its profits are higher.

This big picture effect is why most economists agree that tariffs should be used very sparingly. They almost always cause unexpected damage, decrease overall employment and slow down an economy, but sometimes (like for food security or national defense) those costs are worth paying.

So Why is Donald Trump Throwing Around Tariffs Like They Are The Best Thing Ever?

This has been confusing to almost everyone. If you take him at his word, he appears to have a Bizarro Opposite Universe belief system about economics. Donald has claimed in speeches that the tariffs will somehow make us wealthier. He’s focusing on the first-order effects like GM hiring more workers, while completely ignoring the fact that everything else in the country gets less efficient in exchange.

But when he announces larger tariffs, share prices go down, because everyone who actually runs or invests in US companies knows that of course they will make less money on average. When tariffs are paused or reduced, share prices go back up. Yet he keeps wielding the threats and we go back and forth.

It seems to be obvious to everyone except Donald himself that Tariffs are just a national sales tax rather than some clever sneaky strategic weapon, which leads to various theories that okay, maybe he knows that too but is just pretending in order to gain some influence.

So right now our entire economy is subject to the whims of a single person.. And as long as this is the case, we’re just the same as any other dictatorship – something our constitution was supposed to prevent with the whole “three independent branches of government” thing.

But presidents have tried to break out of their constitutional cage and get more power many times in the past, and this is just the latest example. The real test will be if our system eventually manages to stop this abuse and put itself back in balance as it always has in the past. You can already see this fight beginning to play out in our court system, in this Economist article:

Even without the 145% nonsense numbers that were thrown around a few months ago, they are still far higher than they have been in the last 75 years or more. While it would be hard to pin down the current numbers in a stationary blog post like this one, the key thing to remember is that our current US economy is built around very low tariffs and relatively free trade.

Why haven’t I noticed Prices Going Up Yet?

While the US economy is fueled by a constant stream of cargo ships, as a whole we function like the biggest cargo ship of all: we have a huge inventory and it takes a while to change directions.

So in normal times, we already have several months of inventory of most things in the country. And then when all this drama started, importers started placing even more orders to stockpile things in advance before the tariffs hit. And now that they are in place, we’re importing a lot less stuff.

For now, we’re still using up the stockpiled inventory, but imports have dropped significantly so we’re quickly running out of cheap goods. If that happens, we will probably start seeing shortages and price increases throughout this summer or fall. For some things like plastic party trinkets, we can do just fine without. But if we lose access to core useful things like tools and machinery, the economic consequences will be much less fun.

The most important phrase to remember in US politics and economics is the phrase “This too shall pass.” The only mystery right now is that we don’t know exactly how it will pass. So we could sketch out a few scenarios:

1) The current crazy-high tariffs really do stick around:

I personally think this is the less likely scenario because nobody really wants it. But just as a thought experiment, it might go something like this:

2) They do end up being just a negotiating tactic and we go back to mostly low tariffs.

In other words, the best way to win the tariff game is not to play it.

Just as much of US prosperity is built upon our huge population of 330 million people living in 50 states with open borders and no trade restrictions, all (friendly) countries of the world can benefit from the free exchange of goods, services and even people. We’re all human beings and if we treat each other with a collaborative respect, we all grow richer.

I started writing this article on April 2nd, when Donald announced his “Liberation Day” and the stock market reacted with the biggest drop since 1932. Some people panicked and locked in big losses despite decades of warnings from your favorite financial bloggers, like this unfortunate soul in the comments to a JL Collins post:

But as I watched over the next two months, we have bounced our way back up – with each drop in proposed tariffs triggering a corresponding increase in stock prices (a measure of investor enthusiasm of how bright our future looks).

Right now, the US stock market is just about back to its all-time high. This doesn’t match with our current level of tariffs, which are still about seven times higher than they were before the circus opened. But it shows that investors believe it’s all going to end with a truce and a resumption of free-ish international trade.

If they’re wrong, the roller coaster ride will still have some more fun in store for us. But as long as we eventually end our current experiment in “emergency” tariff dictatorship and get back to functioning as a democracy, things should be just fine in the long run. I’m still 100% invested myself, so that’s where I place my bet.

The Biggest Lesson: Don’t Form Your Opinions Based on News Headlines

Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us, with just a bit of sizzle and spice to pull in our attention. Unfortunately, nowadays the priorities have flipped where the primary goal is attention, and accuracy carries little or no weight. Even a totally inaccurate article makes money for the publisher.

So while Democrats and Republicans like to do battle over which media sources are biased, in reality they’re all wrong: all click-funded commercial media is biased – sometimes politically but even more importantly biased towards generating outrage and fear, because those generate more money.

1) Either ignore the media completely and focus on your own life, or

2) Become a subject matter expert on things you really care about, and then read the original sources whenever you want to learn about something.

I mostly practice option #1, but as a science and technology nerd I get into #2 in just the areas I find most interesting. And it’s amazing how the more deeply you understand a subject, the more you see just how wrong most media stories are about your area of expertise. Which means they’re probably pretty wrong about almost everything.

So as always, with this lesson learned it’s time to shut down that phone and laptop, exhale all our worries and get back outside with your real-life family and friends. See you in a few months!

Why We Are Not Really All Doomed – the original all-purpose MMM article which explains why we never really have to worry about the long-term economic future.

There’s one more possible reason for the tariffs that you didn’t mention: Trump might be running a giant pump-and-dump scheme on the entire U.S. economy.

Great question – I tried to cover this in the article under the heading, “Why haven’t I noticed prices going up yet?”

First of all, most of the tariffs (or threatened tariffs) haven’t even hit yet.

But even when they do, the end result will be a bit unpredictable. Importers can of course shift supply to countries with lower tariffs or even domestic suppliers. Consumers will also react to rising prices by scaling back their spending, which shifts prices back down the supply/demand curve a little.

In the extreme case, high tariffs can even cause a recession which lowers demand for almost all goods and services, which means that prices for domestically produced services with elastic pricing might go down and bring the overall inflation numbers back in check. In other words, some people lose their jobs so on average there’s less money being spent on restaurants -> restaurants have to lower their prices.

Might be semantic, but maybe tariffs are not “inflation”. It would be like saying that a VAT would be inflationary. Instead, this is a one-time step-function change in the cost of goods, then inflation (velocity) resumes on the new cost base. Oren Cass had an interesting blog article on this last week. At least food for thought – he posits that economists don’t actually think tariffs are inflationary.

100% the case. Inflation is caused by an increase in the money supply, by definition. It means your purchasing power is worth less. A one-time increase in a specific category of goods of 15% is not “inflation.” Meanwhile, every time the government uses printed (or digitally entered) dollars to spend trillions they don’t have, inflation grows massively and compounds, and for some reason, the majority of people don’t bat an eye.

A great analogy for inflation would be something like this… You are in charge of the county fair. There are a bunch of vendors of popcorn, cotton candy, and ride like ferris wheels, etc. You print tickets that visitors can use to acquire these goods and ride these rides, and the vendors set their own ticket prices. You and your friends discover you can give yourselves tickets and get more popcorn and ride more rides since you own the ticket machine. With the flood of tickets, the vendors realize they can (and need to) raise their prices. This is inflation. And it doesn’t matter if it’s due to your and your friends doing it for yourselves, or just doing it because of more guests coming to the fair (for “growth”).

I think the definition of inflation is a rise in prices not a rise in money supply. Money supply is one factor in that, but so is the overall supply and demand of everything that is for sale. Money supply is increased or decreased as needed in reaction to what’s happening with prices, in order to keep prices more stable, if the system is well managed.

In your county fair example, you are holding the number of vendors and the items and quantities for sale as a constant while increasing the number of tickets. In reality the fair’s mini-economy will grow and shrink over time, and if the ticket supply were forced to always stay constant the ticket prices of rides, popcorn and cotton candy would move up and down significantly in reaction.

“I think the definition of inflation is a rise in prices not a rise in money supply.”

Well, that’s the problem – that is wrong. A rise in prices is a symptom of inflation. It is not inflation nor is it the cause of inflation. Inflation is similar in concept to dilution.

No it’s not wrong. Inflation is prices going higher as time passes. The causes of inflation are debatable, but “inflation” is a word that refers to prices going up regardless of the cause.

It’s possible for money supply to increase without inflation. Japanese deflation and lost decades are a prime example.

I believe that the answer lies in the gig economy and with self-employed workers. There are some 50 million Americans working gig work, self-employed, or who work as contractors. But the employment report shows it as a net positive.

That’s a really good point. Even outside of the business world, on a personal level it takes up mental energy.

Thank you for raising this point. The lack of concern about the impacts on businesses has been a real source of frustration for me.

My day job has given me a window into some industry sectors, including during Trump 1.0 and the trade war then. I always remember the small US steel manufacturer one of my colleagues spoke with at that time, when researching some of the impacts of steel tariffs.

The company was an important employer in its local area, producing steel canisters that it sold to a global slate of companies (so it was an exporter, and also sold domestically). Its main input was a particular type of steel pipe made in China (so it was also an importer). After Trump implemented steel tariffs, this small firm was suddenly paying an additional $250 million (back in 2018/2019; do your own inflation math as to what that would be today) at the US border before it could pick up a shipment.

It wasn’t going to be able to afford to stay open if it couldn’t get the administration to give it a tariff exemption (something Trump 1.0 was more willing to do, although the time involved to apply and, hopefully, get some sort of relief (many didn’t) meant companies were shelling out cash in the meantime). Why? Because not only did it not have a way to source the pipe in the US (steel is made to specification and you often can’t just readily swap things out), it couldn’t afford to do that because with a global client base, it needed to keep its pricing competitive (its customers could seek out non-US sources, unaffected by tariffs, for canisters instead).

We do actually have a manufacturing sector in the US. Most companies in that sector are small and midsized firms (fewer than 500 workers; often much smaller) and these may be important employers locally (although most employment in the industry overall is via the smaller number of very large firms); many are family firms. All sizes of manufacturer may import a raw material, a component or a finished good (including capital equipment for their facilities). When we tariff, we end up hurting our own manufacturing sector along the way. I lost track of the steel canister-maker’s fate, but I’ve never forgotten its difficulty, as just one illustration of tariff impacts that aren’t about the CPI.

But there’s also no real controversy (among people who study this stuff) in saying that tariffs tend to raise prices somewhere along the way, although it can take several months and may not be a straight $1 for $1 increase for end-consumers (although it often, eventually, is). I agree that it doesn’t create a prolonged rise in inflation (which is a rate of increase), but it does tend to eventually raise prices over a certain period and they then stay at that higher level. That’s actually part of how tariffs work, by putting a new floor under prices, reducing price competition.

And there are spillovers well beyond the firms initially impacted. For instance, US makers of tin plate, used in can-making, were hit by Trump 1.0’s steel tariffs, which jacked up their input costs (whether they continued with imports or switched to domestic sources — especially since domestic steel makers raised their own prices after tariffs were imposed on imports, an approach they’ve continued with in the latest trade war). This then made foreign-produced end-products such as canned food more attractive, because the pricing was better due to the lower production costs for non-US producers of tin plate. In other words, not only did US tin plate manufacturers suffer, but so did their US customers, as those companies’ customers looked elsewhere. (Trump’s much-broader trade war this time could offset some of this, by making imported canned goods more expensive, as well, depending on how things play out, which, in turn, would affect things like grocery store margins, etc.)

I also want to add that one of the biggest problems worrying the manufacturing industry for years, including pre-pandemic, has been the difficulty firms often face in filling the jobs they already have, and the difficulty they expect to face in filling jobs they expect to have due to a looming wave of retirements. This is due to several reasons: a skills gap (applicants not having the desired skill-sets); geographic miss-matches (jobs in one place, potential workers in another); problems with drug use in some communities (applicants are often expected to pass drug tests in order to operate machinery; the opioid epidemic has truly clobbered some communities in manufacturing areas); lack of interest among younger people in going into manufacturing or other production sectors (definitely something we need to work on; lack of exposure and training in K-12 is part of the trouble there, although the appeal of other types of work has also pulled potential workers elsewhere — maybe AI taking white collar jobs will sort that out?); and an increasing tightness in the overall US labor market due to demographics (ie, retirements on the aggregate, although jobs involving manual labor often see retirements at earlier ages, skewing the problem for those industries).

To finally conclude this overlong comment — which still barely scratches the surface; I didn’t even go into the tariff (and trade war) impacts on US shipping and logistics sectors tied to global trade, including imports — a major and rarely-discussed downside of tariffs is simply that it’s so difficult to readily see the ways they thread through an economy and create a drag on firms’ employment, wages/benefits, expansion plans, financing options, earnings and stock prices, and, yes, on consumer spending. The hits to businesses are often below the radar — especially since many companies don’t want to attract the anger of protectionists (unions; certain parts of the progressive wing; the Trump administration) by openly admitting how tariffs hurt their business. So people who aren’t trade geeks are understandably oblivious to real effects of these types of policies. As Cullen Roche over at Discipline Funds has repeatedly put it, with tariffs, you have less economic growth than you would have had — you just don’t know it.

The Biden administration and Dems in Congress (and sometimes even GOPers in Congress at that time, in some rare moments of bipartisanship) did several good things to directly support certain manufacturing and other production sectors (in my world I knew about policy for clean energy-related manufacturing; the defense industry; critical minerals; computer chips). Trump and the GOP have reduced or eliminated a chunk of that, unfortunately. But the recent tax bill did include some useful items for manufacturing. The GOP could do even more to directly support the sector, if manufacturing jobs are the real goal of all this, without the downsides of tariffs. (To be clear, this is not a political argument that I’m making; I didn’t like the tariffs imposed during the Biden admin, any more than Trump’s.)

This is an interesting analysis. The way I summed it up to an acquaintance is that Trump is playing with fire. In the end, it may be that we have something nice and shiny as a result. However, it is just as likely (if not more) that this whole thing is a dumpster fire and in the end it will just a smoking heap of ash.

However, the more fundamental problem here is that the reason that things like this (i.e., Trump unilaterally going tariff-nuclear, which is actually quite similar to what Biden did trying to illegally wipe out student loan debt, it’s just that Trump’s actions are at a different order of magnitude) is because Congress actively refuses to do their jobs. In the last several decades they have rather been rather determined to pass really loose/broad laws and specifically leave the “details” to the executive branch (either as some nebulous presidential power, or via some rule-making provision for an executive agency). This was bad but not terrible as long as we were electing presidents who were within a standard deviation of the ‘center’ of the political spectrum. However, Trump is a major outlier, and now it is readily apparent that Congress’ approach of letting the executive branch decide most things for itself isn’t actually a really good idea.

Even going back to the difference between Trump’s use of tariffs and Biden’s student debt cancellation efforts, it is clear that Biden’s policy, while objectively of very dubious legality, didn’t move the macroeconomic needle. Trump’s policies, on the other hand, even if they turn out to be completely legal (which I’m not sure they will), are rather painful object lesson on why Congress needs to actually do their jobs with a bit more effort.

A stray bit of additional perspective: A good friend of mine lost a large swath of her extended family when covid churned through northern Italy in the first year of the pandemic. Communities in their area suffered terrible losses that upended the social fabric overall, in addition to the grief suffered by specific families.

This also happened in many parts of the US, with certain kinds of communities hit particularly hard (groups that tend to live with extended family were especially vulnerable; non-hispanic white middle- and upper-class America is least-likely to live that way, so people from that type of background may not have seen much of this directly).

Given what NYC itself went through early in that first year, it also wouldn’t surprise me if NYT staffers genuinely felt horrified at what was happening. My friends and colleagues living in NYC certainly felt that way, based on what they were seeing and experiencing directly themselves.

So yes, it’s absolutely true that all forms of heart disease combined remained the number one cause of death in both 2020 and 2021, followed by all cancers combined. But I suspect that many people whose families and communities were gutted by covid would agree with the NYT that the toll from that new cause of death was terrible, and that it was something worth being concerned about, even if covid alone ended up being the third-leading cause of US deaths in both of those years, after which broad herd immunity finally set in.

Also, if anyone has an idea for how to fund newspaper journalism such that eyeballs aren’t the thing, I know several very good journalists who would *love* to hear what it is. (Pricier subscriptions can’t be the answer; not if you want to pay decent salaries and thus keep people around so that you have a good mix of entry-level people and experienced folks, and not if you want to include small and regional news outlets in your funding model — you could never charge enough for subscriptions for a local or even regional paper for that to cover all costs and still have a decent staff, both in terms of actual size and experience mix. This applies to both digital and hard-copy papers.)

If you do not think that the NYT serves a political agenda, the you are naïve.

And while I think that Pete’s nostalgic comment (“Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us…”) is equally naïve, he recognizes that today news organizations are driven by getting eyeballs on their content. The thing is, it’s always been like this. Certainly, the intensity has varied with times and places, but yellow journalism (the type of sensationalism that characterizes nearly 100% of mass media coverage today) originated in the 1880s in NYC. Back then the NYT didn’t lower themselves to that level, but it’s pretty obvious that today they are down there and they deserve to be compared to the likes of FoxNews, MSNBC, and so forth.

I think a useful comparison that illustrates something important about the NYT is to look at its news articles and compare them with those in the Wall Street Journal (owned by News Corp, by the way, as is Fox News). Both the NYT and WSJ are dealing with a crazy-ass environment for “newspapers” vs back in the day. And both approach their news journalism in a similar way, even if the specific type of news story they do may differ.

At the same time, nothing could be more different than their respective opinion sections — both the editorials by their editorial boards and those by columnists and guests are 180-degrees opposite from each other much of the time.

In other words, in terms of political-ish stance, they are radically different. In terms of journalism? Pretty similar: fact-based, attempting to give a full picture, and corrections if someone messes something up. They entertain if they can, but it’s secondary to information provision.

I can’t say the same about Fox News (which I used to watch some years ago, but stopped when I realized I was never really going to get a full picture of anything since it wasn’t their style). They are really an entertainment-first entity, and they are facing fierce competition from Newsmax, which has made it less and less appealing for them to say anything they think their viewers might not want to hear. (That said, I’ve found the online version of their sister product, Fox Business, to be helpful at times. Just as I like CNBC’s “state of freight” pages for some aspects of tariff impacts on shipping and warehousing. Written! Not the videos/cable shows for either of these. There’s usually more information in written material, and the potential for more nuance. (Not always fulfilled, alas).)

I think that there is a case to be made that sales taxes, above all other taxes, are the most “just” taxes. The idea is that sales taxes are the form of taxes that give the individual tax payer the greatest degree of economic freedom. Don’t want to pay so much in taxes? Then just buy less stuff!

This sort of thing is very difficult with other forms of taxes, because there aren’t reasonable ways to reduce property taxes, and in some cases (i.e., gentrification) your taxes can increase by huge amounts even if you do nothing at all but sit at home. Income taxes, excise taxes, and tariffs live in a bit of a middle ground (they provide a bit more economic freedom, but are still more difficult than sales taxes to deal with in terms of accomplishing the “I want to pay less tax” objective).

I agree wholeheartedly. Income tax punishes you for working. Property tax is pretty crazy, because it’s based on appraised value, and you can actually be the one who created the value, i.e. you buy raw land and build a house on it completely with your own hands and your taxes go up 1000-fold. Nobody helped you, but you now owe a dramatically higher amount of tax. Extreme (and rare) example, but illustrates how bizarre this type of taxation is. And of course, if you are renting, and the property owner’s assessment goes up, this is going to be passed on with a rent increase unless there is a rent control law, which will lead to a dilapidated building in need of repair, or people leaving the area, and many other problems.

I disagree with the word “regressive.” It oversimplifies and is biased language. The thing is, the phenomenon you’re describing is simply an effect of a person being rich. The same percentage added to the sale of a good treats everyone equally – the difference is one person is rich. It’s not “hurting” the poorer person, it’s just that the rich person has a lot of money…because they’re rich. And when it comes to income taxes, “progressive” taxation is not more fair, it’s less fair. A percentage is already “progressive” because of math – 10% of $100,000 is $10,000 and 10% of $1 million is $100,000 – 10 times more tax revenue for 10 times the income. That’s completely fair. The idea of confiscating an escalating percentage is not more fair.

The math changes if you consider the marginal value of a dollar to someone who is rich vs someone who is poor. A thousand dollars more or less to someone making minimum wage is significant when measured in how much it will impact their lives. A thousand dollars more or less to a multi-millionaire with a high six figure income is barely noticeable. I agree that a simple percentage tax is more “fair” if what you’re measuring is dollars, but I think it’s less “fair” if what you’re measuring is impact on someone’s life. That said, lowering taxes helps everyone.

That’s the whole point of earning more: the marginal value changes and you can afford more. Taxes are the same as groceries, or your house bills, or anything else. Money is fungible. By raising the tax rate on higher levels of income, you’re just advocating for redistribution of wealth.

I am, yes. The more money you have the easier it is to make money until winner take all. Regulation and redistribution combat those natural effects.
