#8598. 25 Legit Ways to Make Money From Home – and What Each Pays

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Legit ways to make money from home don’t pay alike. Remote jobs and freelance work pay a real hourly rate, while paid surveys add up to pocket change. Pick the one that fits the hours, skills, and space you have, and walk away from any job that asks you to pay up front.

In the Federal Reserve’s survey of household finances for 2024, 20% of adults had done some gig work in the month before, most often selling things. Only 21% of them called it their main job.

Which way fits depends on what you have most of: spare hours, a skill, or space and things to rent out. The kind of work sets the pay. A remote job or a freelance skill pays a real hourly rate, renting earns from space or a car you already own, selling pays item by item, and online gigs like paid surveys pay pocket change.

Freelance and gig pay arrives with no tax taken out, so set aside part of every payment for taxes on your self-employment side income.

Airbnb says the typical U.S. host earned about $15,600 in extra income in 2025. If you’d rather not host guests, Neighbor says an empty garage can bring in $100 to $600 a month, rented for storage or parking. Neighbor keeps 4.9% plus 30 cents of each payout. Before you list either one, confirm that your lease, your homeowners association, and your city allow it.

Neighbor says an empty parking space can rent for $50 to $300 a month, and listing one costs nothing. Price yours by checking what garages and lots nearby charge by the month.

Turo puts its U.S. hosts’ average at $10,489 a year per car. In most U.S. markets, hosts keep 70%, 80%, or 90% of each trip’s price, depending on the protection plan they choose. Run your car through Turo’s Carculator to see what yours could earn in your market.

Selling pays once, not every month. On eBay, the fee in most categories is 13.6% of the sale’s total plus 40 cents for an order over $10, and your first 250 listings each month are free. That makes the fee on a $50 sale $7.20. Start with the item that would sell for the most.

Etsy charges 20 cents to list an item and 6.5% of each sale, shipping included, plus a payment processing fee. On a $30 piece with free shipping, the first two fees come to $2.15. Price each piece to cover materials, those fees, and a fair rate for your hours.

Retail arbitrage means buying discounted products in stores and reselling them online for more. You earn only the gap between the two prices after the resale site’s fees, and your cash sits in stock until it sells. Before you buy, look up what the same item has actually sold for online.

In an Institute for Justice survey of 775 people who sell food made in their home kitchens, median profit was $500 for all of 2016, while producers averaged 15 hours of work a week. Check your state’s cottage food law, which sets the foods you may sell from a home kitchen.

Editorial freelancers charge median rates of $65 to $75 an hour for business and marketing writing and $50 to $60 for copyediting it, according to the Editorial Freelancers Association’s 2026 rate chart. Win your first clients on Upwork, which takes 0% to 15% of each contract.

Interpreters and translators earned a median $28.93 an hour in May 2025, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Translate between the two languages you know best, starting with documents in a field you already work in, such as law or medicine.

A virtual assistant does an administrative assistant’s work from home. Secretaries and administrative assistants earned a median $23.23 an hour in May 2025, the BLS reports. Offer two or three tasks you already do well, such as scheduling, email, and travel booking.

Management consultants, whom the BLS counts as management analysts, earned a median $48.97 an hour in May 2025. Pitch your first project to a former employer or colleague who already knows your work.

Tutors earned a median $20.84 an hour in May 2025, according to BLS wage data. On Wyzant, tutors keep 75% of the hourly rate they post. Apply in the one or two subjects you know best.

Animal care and service workers earned a median $17.08 an hour in May 2025, per the BLS. On Rover, you set your own prices and, outside California, take home 80% of each booking. Offer to watch pets in your own home, so the work fits around the rest of your day.

These are jobs with an employer, and remote job websites list the openings you can do from home.

Customer service representatives earned a median $21.53 an hour in May 2025, and some employers let them work from home, the BLS says. Apply for remote openings listed on the company’s own careers page.

Computer support specialists earned a median $30.24 an hour in May 2025, and some can work from home, per the BLS. Look for remote help desk openings, and list every system and program you’ve fixed for others.

Data entry keyers earned a median $19.88 an hour in May 2025, per BLS wage data, and staffing agencies employ more of them than any other industry. Register with a staffing agency that places office workers.

Medical transcriptionists earned a median $19.43 an hour in May 2025, but the BLS expects jobs in the field to fall 4% by 2035 as speech recognition reduces the need for them. Start with a certificate program beyond high school, which the job typically requires.

These earn nothing until people find what you made, and the money grows with your audience.

A blog earns from ads and affiliate links once it has readers. The ad network Mediavine takes small blogs into its Journey program once they draw 1,000 visits in 30 days from countries such as the U.S. and Canada. Its main program waits until a site makes $5,000 a year from ads. Pick one topic you know well and publish on a schedule you can keep.

Amazon’s Kindle Direct Publishing offers a 70% royalty option on e-books priced $2.99 to $12.99. Audiobook narrators on ACX, Audible’s marketplace for them, are paid by the finished hour of audio, a share of royalties, or both. ACX says most narrators need 5 to 7 hours of work for each finished hour, so a rate of $100 per finished hour comes to $14 to $20 for each hour you work. Start with a short e-book on something you know well, priced inside that 70% band.

Udemy pays instructors 97% of the revenue from students who buy through the instructor’s own coupon or referral link and 37% from every other sale. Outline a course on a skill people already pay to learn, and send your own audience to it first.

Flippa suggests pricing a site at 2 to 2.5 times its net profit over the past 12 months, so a site netting $500 a month would list for $12,000 to $15,000. Build one that earns steadily for a year before you sell it.

These pay per task, and the work comes only when a company needs testers or survey takers.

Branded Surveys says members can expect $5 to $100 a month, depending on how often they take surveys and how many are available, which is pocket change. Most of its surveys run 5 to 20 minutes, so take them in spare minutes, and cash out once you reach 500 points, or $5.

User Interviews, which pays people for surveys, focus groups, and user tests, says its average study pays over $45, with payment within a few days of each session. Sign up and apply to studies about products you already use.

PlaytestCloud pays $5 to $9 for a typical 15-minute playtest and survey, and its onboarding session pays nothing. Sign up, finish the onboarding, and watch your email for invitations.

A real employer never charges you to get hired, the Federal Trade Commission warns, so anyone who does is running a scam. In a work-from-home scam, the charge comes as a starter kit, training, or a certification you have to buy first. Search the company’s name plus the word “scam” before you hand over money or personal details.

#8597. Air France-KLM Flying Blue — Monthly Promo Rewards

A recurring monthly opportunity to book premium cabin flights at economy-level points pricing

Picture this: you're reclining in Air France's La Première-adjacent Business cabin somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, a three-course meal on the way, and a fully flat bed waiting for you after dinner. The couple in economy paid $900 for this flight. You paid 40,000 Flying Blue miles — points you transferred from your Chase Sapphire Reserve in seconds — and the cash value of what you're sitting in is closer to $2,500 to $6,000. That gap is the entire point. Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program runs what they call **Promo Rewards** — a monthly flash sale on award seats that slashes the points price by 25 to 50% on select routes. In Business class, that can mean seats that would normally cost 80,000+ miles dropping to as low as 40,000 miles one-way. On a route where a cash ticket retails for $3,000, you're extracting **7.5 cents per point** — and on premium routes during peak travel periods, that figure can climb to 15 cents per point. To put that in FI-community terms: the average point is worth 1 to 2 cents when redeemed for cash back or basic travel. This redemption can be worth 6 to 10 times that. If you have 40,000 transferable points sitting in a Chase or Amex account, this is the difference between a $400 economy ticket and a $3,000 business class experience — for the same points. The pricing inefficiency exists because Flying Blue uses these promotional awards as a marketing tool to fill premium cabin seats on specific dates that might otherwise go out with empty seats. Airlines would rather have a loyalist in that seat than fly it empty. You, as someone who's built a transferable points balance, are perfectly positioned to take advantage of the moment they make that trade-off. This isn't a loophole that's about to close. Flying Blue has run Promo Rewards consistently for years. It's a **structural feature of the program** — one the ChooseFI community can build an annual travel strategy around. The challenge isn't finding the deal. It's being ready when it drops.

The mechanism behind Flying Blue Promo Rewards is elegantly simple once you understand it, and it separates this program from virtually every other airline loyalty play in your toolkit.

Flying Blue Has a Dynamic Award Chart — With a Monthly Override

Flying Blue moved to dynamic pricing, which typically means the program is less predictable and often less valuable than the old fixed-chart days. But here's where it gets interesting: Promo Rewards operate as a fixed-price overlay on top of that dynamic system. On the 1st of each month (or within the first few days), Flying Blue publishes a curated list of routes — often 20 to 40 city pairs — with fixed, deeply discounted mile prices. Business class seats on transatlantic routes regularly appear at 40,000 to 50,000 miles one-way. These are not dynamic prices that will creep up as demand increases. They're locked promotional rates on specific routes.

This means the program essentially gives you two separate games to play: the chaotic dynamic pricing game (usually skip it), and the monthly Promo Rewards game (always pay attention).

Flying Blue does pass on carrier-imposed surcharges for standard awards on Air France and KLM flights — this can add $200 to $500 to what should be a points redemption. But here's the critical detail: Promo Reward bookings eliminate those surcharges. You pay the miles, a small booking fee, and that's it. This is a significant hidden value that casual points users miss entirely. The published cash price comparison becomes even more favorable once you factor in that you're not paying the surcharge on top.

Flying Blue partners with every major transferable currency at a 1:1 ratio:

The instant transfer speeds from Chase, Amex, and Citi are critical here. When Promo Rewards drop and the best dates start disappearing within hours, you cannot afford a 3-day transfer window. If your points are in Chase or Amex, you can see a seat, transfer, and book in under 10 minutes.

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing — meaning you can fly into Paris and out of Amsterdam (or vice versa) on a single award, letting you plan a more dynamic European itinerary without paying for two separate tickets. The booking window opens at 359 days out, and miles are activity-based with a 24-month expiration window, so you're not racing against a clock as long as you keep your account active with occasional small transactions.

Before the 1st of any month arrives, you need to be ready. Create a free Flying Blue account at flyingblue.com if you don't have one. More importantly, ensure your transferable points — Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Citi ThankYou, Capital One, or Bilt — are linked and ready. Don't transfer anything yet. You want to see the actual Promo Reward routes before moving a single point.

Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards on or around the 1st of each month. Set a calendar reminder. Follow Flying Blue on social media and sign up for their email newsletter — they announce the month's featured routes there. The ChooseFI community forums and travel rewards deal-tracking sites will also surface these announcements within minutes of release.

When the list drops, you'll see a curated set of origin/destination city pairs with fixed Business class prices. Look for transatlantic routes from major U.S. gateways (New York, Los Angeles, Atlanta, Chicago, Miami) to European hubs like Paris (CDG) or Amsterdam (AMS).

Go to flyingblue.com and use the award search tool. Enter your origin and destination from the Promo list. Switch the cabin to Business. Search across a 30-day window if possible — the calendar view shows you which dates have availability. Act within hours, not days. The best dates — particularly weekends, school holidays, and summer dates — disappear fast.

Note: Flying Blue's search only shows Air France and KLM metal for Promo Rewards. SkyTeam partner availability is separate and won't be Promo-priced.

Do not transfer points yet. Confirm the exact flights, dates, and total miles cost. Take a screenshot. Note the flight numbers and times. Availability can disappear between the moment you see it and the moment you book, so move quickly through the next steps.

From your bank portal (Chase, Amex, Citi), initiate the transfer to Flying Blue. For Chase, Amex, and Citi, transfers are instant. Capital One and Bilt take 1–2 days, so these are less ideal for Promo Rewards' speed-dependent window. Transfer exactly what you need — Promo award prices are fixed, so there's no cushion math required.

With miles in your account, return to the award search, re-confirm your dates are still available, and book. You'll pay the fixed Promo miles price plus taxes and fees (minimal, with no fuel surcharges on Promo awards). You'll receive a confirmation email immediately.

Don't panic. Wait for next month. Or search the current month's Promo list for alternative routes — sometimes less popular city pairs have excellent availability. You can also check if the same route appears at standard dynamic pricing, but compare the CPP carefully before transferring for a non-Promo redemption.

Flying Blue moved to dynamic award pricing, which normally makes costs unpredictable and often unfavorable. But the Promo Rewards program creates a monthly fixed-price override on select routes that dramatically undercuts the dynamic system. Each month, Flying Blue publishes a curated list of discounted routes with pricing 25 to 50 percent below standard and with fuel surcharges eliminated entirely. This creates a repeatable, predictable opportunity cycle: check on the 1st, find a discounted route, transfer points instantly from Chase or Amex, and book before the best dates are taken. The structural advantage is that most casual travelers do not know about Promo Rewards or do not act fast enough — which leaves more availability for prepared ChooseFI community members who treat the 1st of each month as a mini-booking event.

Let's walk through a redemption that the ChooseFI community has actually executed.

The Route: New York (JFK) → Paris (CDG) in Business class on Air France

The Cash Price: A direct Air France Business class ticket on this route typically retails between $3,000 and $5,500 depending on the season. For this example, let's use a realistic mid-range price of $3,800.

The Promo Reward Price: 40,000 Flying Blue miles one-way, plus approximately $60–$80 in taxes and fees. No fuel surcharges — because it's a Promo award.

The CPP Calculation: $3,800 ÷ 40,000 miles = 9.5 cents per point. That's nearly 10x what you'd get using those same Chase points for cash back at 1 cent each.

You board at JFK and step into Air France's Business class cabin — the same product that Business travelers are paying $3,800+ to access. You have a lie-flat seat with direct aisle access, a curated French menu with Champagne service before takeoff, noise-canceling headphones, an amenity kit, and pajamas on longer segments. The CDG lounge is yours before departure — the Air France lounge in Terminal 2E is a genuine culinary experience, not an airport afterthought. You land in Paris rested, not wrecked.

For a couple, you'd need 80,000 miles total — both ways would be 160,000 miles. A pair of Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve cardholders who signed up in the same year could realistically have this banked between welcome bonuses and everyday spend. Transfer from Chase to Flying Blue: instant. Time from decision to booking: under 15 minutes.

You did not pay $7,600 for two Business class tickets across the Atlantic. You paid 80,000 points and roughly $160 in fees. Those points cost you, at most, $800 in credit card spend if you valued them at 1 cent each — meaning you captured $7,440 in travel value from an $800 equivalent investment in points. That's the FI multiplier that makes this program worth mastering.

Do This: Set a Monthly Calendar Reminder for the 1st

Flying Blue Promo Rewards are time-sensitive by design. The best routes with the best dates are gone within 24–48 hours of announcement. Put a recurring reminder on your calendar. Treat the 1st of each month like a mini-event.

Do This: Keep a Points Buffer in Your Transferable Accounts

Because Promo Rewards require fast action and the best transfer partners (Chase, Amex, Citi) are instant, you want at least 40,000–80,000 points already sitting in your transferable account before the announcement. Don't be in a position where you need to wait on a credit card statement to close before you can transfer.

Do This: Use Open-Jaw Routing to Maximize Your Trip

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing. Book into Paris (CDG) and out of Amsterdam (AMS) — or any combination of Air France/KLM hub cities — and you've just built a multi-country European trip into a single award booking. This is the kind of routing flexibility that turns a one-city trip into a proper adventure.

Do This: Track Multiple Months of Route Patterns

Promo routes rotate monthly, but certain routes appear repeatedly — particularly transatlantic and routes between European hubs and Africa or the Middle East. After 2–3 months of observation, you'll start to recognize patterns and can plan your travel around routes that are likely to repeat.

Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability

This is the single biggest mistake beginners make. Always confirm the specific flight, date, and cabin availability before transferring points. Miles are a one-way street — you cannot transfer them back. If availability disappears after you've transferred, you're left with Flying Blue miles that may not be useful for your target route at standard (non-Promo) pricing.

Avoid This: Ignoring Standard Award Pricing

Flying Blue's dynamic pricing outside of Promo Rewards can be punishingly expensive. A Business class seat that costs 40,000 Promo miles might cost 90,000+ miles at standard dynamic pricing. Always wait for the Promo if you can — patience pays.

The ideal earning setup for this redemption combines a Chase Sapphire Reserve (3x on travel and dining, instant transfer to Flying Blue) with an Amex Gold or Platinum (4x on dining/groceries or 5x on flights respectively, also instant transfer). Between two cards, you can accumulate 40,000–80,000 points in a single year of normal household spending.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Best For: Flexible Couples and Solo Travelers Who Plan in Advance

This redemption is purpose-built for the FI community member who thinks in systems, not spontaneous splurges. You're someone who has already built a transferable points balance of at least 40,000–80,000 points across Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, or Citi ThankYou — and who can act decisively when the right route appears.

Couples are the sweet spot. Two people, two Business class seats, one incredible transatlantic experience. Solo travelers benefit enormously too — a single seat at 40,000 miles is one of the highest-CPP solo redemptions in the entire transferable points ecosystem.

Minimum Viable Setup: 40,000 Flying Blue miles or 40,000 transferable points in Chase, Amex, or Citi. A Flying Blue account with verified transfer links. The flexibility to travel within a 30-day window of whatever routes appear that month.

**Difficulty Rating: Hard — But for Specific, Solvable Reasons** This isn't hard because the booking process itself is complicated. Flyingblue.com is a functional, English-language booking tool that anyone can navigate. It's hard because of **timing and availability** — two factors that reward the prepared and punish the passive. **What Specifically Makes This Hard:** 1. **Monthly availability windows are brief.** You have 24–48 hours from the Promo announcement to act before the best dates disappear. If you're not watching, you miss the cycle entirely and wait another month. 2. **Dynamic pricing outside of Promo is punishing.** If you miss the Promo window and try to book a standard award on the same route, you could pay 2–3x more miles. The program's value is almost entirely concentrated in the monthly Promo structure. 3. **Coordination across accounts takes discipline.** Keeping 40,000–80,000 points liquid in a transferable account, not spending them on something else, and being ready to move instantly requires real points discipline. **Three Tips to Overcome the Challenge:** - **Automate your awareness.** Sign up for Flying Blue emails and follow deal-tracking communities so the announcement comes to you. - **Keep your points liquid in Chase or Amex.** The instant transfer speeds are your competitive advantage over slower-moving transfer paths. - **Be route-flexible, not date-flexible.** You may not get Paris in July, but you might get Amsterdam in September — and that's still an extraordinary redemption. If you're willing to build the habit of checking on the 1st of each month and keeping a points buffer ready, the hard part becomes routine. The ChooseFI community has proven this works — repeatedly.

Create a free Flying Blue account at flyingblue.com and enable email notifications. Keep at least 40,000 to 80,000 transferable points in your Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, or Bilt account. Set a recurring calendar reminder for the 1st of each month.

Visit flyingblue.com on the morning of the 1st (or within the first few days) to see the new Promo Rewards routes. Scan for destinations that match your interests. Note the discounted mile pricing and travel date windows — promos typically cover travel within the next 2 to 3 months.

Use the Flying Blue award search to check specific dates on the promo routes in business class. Confirm that seats are available at the promo price before you transfer any points. The calendar view lets you scan across multiple dates quickly.

Transfer the required miles from Chase (instant), Amex (1-2 days), Citi (instant), Capital One (1-2 days), or Bilt (1-2 days). Book on flyingblue.com the moment your miles arrive. Do not wait — promo availability is limited and the best dates disappear within hours.

Promo Rewards typically offer 25 to 50 percent off standard dynamic pricing. A business class transatlantic award that normally costs 80,000 to 100,000 miles one-way can drop to 40,000 to 50,000 miles on a Promo Reward. Additionally, fuel surcharges are eliminated on promo awards, saving another $100 to $300 per ticket that would otherwise be charged on standard awards.

Chase Ultimate Rewards and Citi ThankYou are the best because they transfer instantly to Flying Blue at a 1:1 ratio. Amex Membership Rewards and Capital One both transfer at 1:1 but take 1 to 2 business days. Bilt also transfers at 1:1. Since promo availability is time-sensitive, instant transfer partners give you a meaningful speed advantage.

Yes. Promo Rewards rotate destinations each month and cover specific travel date windows, typically 2 to 3 months out. You cannot choose which routes are discounted. The strategy works best for travelers who have a list of destinations they want to visit and can match those against whatever promos appear each month rather than needing a specific route on a specific date.

The best routes with the best dates typically sell out within 24 to 48 hours of the monthly announcement. Business class availability is particularly limited. Set a reminder for the 1st of each month and check within the first few hours of the announcement for the widest selection of dates and routes.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Flying Blue Promo Rewards is the most repeatable sweet spot in travel rewards because it renews every single month. While other sweet spots are one-time plays or annual opportunities, Promo Rewards gives you 12 chances per year to book premium cabin flights at 25 to 50 percent off standard pricing with no fuel surcharges. The system rewards exactly the kind of behavior the FI community already excels at: preparation, patience, and decisive action when the numbers align. Keep 40,000 to 80,000 transferable points in reserve, check on the 1st of every month, and book the moment you find a route that matches your travel list. Over time, this single strategy can deliver thousands of dollars in business class experiences at economy-level points costs.

You can get hired with little or no experience in dozens of jobs, so choose by how much training time you can give now. Restaurants, warehouses, and delivery companies train you within weeks, while a paid apprenticeship or a short certificate program takes longer and usually leads to higher pay.

Most U.S. jobs ask for no more than a high school diploma. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) puts 59% of U.S. jobs in 2025 in occupations that typically need a diploma or less to get in, including 23.6% that need no formal credential at all.

Jobs that need no credential paid a median $36,400 that year, and jobs that need a diploma, another 35.4% of the total, paid $48,050, against $50,980 for all jobs. Jobs that typically call for a certificate from a program after high school paid $49,910, or $13,510 a year more than jobs that need no credential.

Each job below shows its median pay in May 2025 and BLS’s projected change in jobs from 2025 to 2035, against 3.5% growth for all jobs. The pay figures count only workers on a payroll, so they leave out the self-employed, including most rideshare drivers.

This list is aimed at adults starting out or changing careers. If you’re in high school, summer jobs for high school students fit your schedule better, and if you need to work from home, look for remote jobs you can do from anywhere.

These typically ask for a high school diploma at most, and you learn on the job, in anything from a few days to a paid apprenticeship of several years. Longer training usually pays more. Servers learn in a month or less and earn a median $35,230 a year, while plumbers apprentice for four or five years and earn $63,800. The longest apprenticeships lead to high-paying jobs that don’t require a bachelor’s degree.

These also typically ask for a high school diploma at most, but before you can work you need a license, a certificate, or a registration, which usually takes a short course, an exam, or both.

BLS lists a certificate from a program after high school as the usual way into these jobs, and programs run from three to six months of truck-driving school to one or two years for medical assistants. If you’re weighing one against a four-year degree, compare trade school and college on total cost against the pay each path brings.

Before you accept any offer, ask how long training lasts and whether you’re paid during it.

#8589. How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

It all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun new way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which said something like,

“Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:

Okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

So I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect

One of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:

Every time you log into the exclusive “reviewers only” Vine website, you’ll see different stuff available for the taking. Sometimes there is almost nothing worthwhile – you’ll search for “porcelain plates” and get endless pages of pink plastic disposable party plates instead. You look for a toaster for your kitchen but instead there will be just a toaster cover with a cat wearing a witch hat. WTF!?

But occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

During the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

But eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

Then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

It dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

It reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

Experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning new things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

One interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:

So I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

Thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

So here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

And of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well)

But I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

As with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:

We will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

*(Vine Gold is not all that useful as it turns out as 99.9% of the available items seem to be the same trinkets you see in the Silver tier)

After you review every product, it’s is now a USED product and the FMV is greatly reduced. Remember we are all opening and using the products to review them

The 50-20-0% rule for used products is something on the lines of:

50% FMV for name brand products 20% FMV for off brand/non branded name products 0% FMW for things you use for “business purposes for review, are broken or damaged, and are consumables that can’t be resold after opening

Using this rule, let’s say you bought $1000 worth of non branded stuff, you’d reduce FMV by $800. As the remaining resale value of the used products is now $200 using the 20% rule. You’d patties on $200, not $1000.

Edit: You are welcome to claim Amazon’s reported ETV as hobby income. Just remember:

To maintain access to vine, we are required to “do work” (aka review 60%+ of products) to get access to the products. The process of reviewing an item, results in an adjustment to the fair market value after doing so. After you review the item, the “remaining” value is not the inflated ETV.

If you don’t understand accounting, you need to be very detailed with your CPA. If you can’t be bothered with some simple accounting, you are welcome to pay your marginal tax rate for your ETV as hobby income.

From all my research and extreme warnings from my CPA, this “50-20-0%” method is not a legally recognized tax strategy and carries massive audit risk.

The products we receive are legally considered non-employee compensation given to us in exchange for the service of writing reviews.

The IRS strictly requires taxpayers to report the Fair Market Value (FMV) of this compensation at the exact moment of receipt (though in practice, Amazon’s FMV is set at tine of ordering, not receipt).

Because you take immediate ownership of the item at its full value, opening and using it to write the review is legally considered personal use. Therefore, you cannot claim business depreciation or arbitrarily lower your 1099-NEC gross income for the “wear and tear” of opening your own compensation.

My CPA explicitly stated he will not file our taxes using fabricated internet depreciation formulas to arbitrarily lower a 1099-NEC.

Here is another discussion on the TurboTax forums where someone explains exactly why you cannot use this 50-20-0 rule and that there is no accepted way to manipulate the FMV of what you receive: https://ttlc.intuit.com/community/business-taxes/discussion/amazon-vine-1099-nec-schedule-c-deductions/00/3715093

The Vine program can easily cause a significant financial impact come tax season. Because Amazon issues a 1099-NEC, the IRS system automatically assumes this is business income subject to an additional 15.3% self-employment tax. When added to a normal ~25% income tax bracket, that creates a massive tax burden. For me, even living in Texas with no state income tax, I am still looking at roughly a 40% tax burden by default, which is brutal.

You can try to claim it as a hobby to avoid that 15.3% FICA tax, but overriding a 1099-NEC, moving it from schedule C to schedule 1, requires preparation to defend since the discrepancy because it can trigger an automated CP2000 notice.

For context, last year Amazon sent me a 1099-NEC with a massive $38,000 FMV for all my 2025 Vine items. (yes, the curse of making gold which means much more allowance and expensive >$100 items, such as a $1500 Gigabyte laptop amd $1k mini split AC, and a lot of other expensive gold exclusive items)

My CPA does not want to use the hobby declaration for that $38k because the sheer volume and daily review time makes it very hard to defend, even though I have not sold anything.

Beyond the tax classification, you must be extremely careful about Amazon’s published FMVs because they are often wildly inflated. Sometimes if you wait a few months, you will find that you could have purchased the exact same product outright for less cash than you are paying in tax liability through Vine.

This is why I am giving the warning that you have to do your homework before choosing things, sivh as checking price history and comparing to similar products. Buying outright means you only buy what you actually need, the item can be returned if you don’t like it, has a real warranty when it breaks, and you do not have to waste 30-60 mins writing a detailed review.

For example, I ordered a cold press juicer, even though I already own about nine other juicers, assuming the FMV was fair. I figured getting it for 40 cents on the dollar was a good enough deal. A few months later, the retail price dropped by about 75%. I ended up paying more in taxes for an un-warrantied, non-returnable item that I wasted an hour reviewing than if I had just bought it outright down the road.

In another instance, I selected a frozen drink slushie machine with an almost $300 FMV, meaning $120 in taxes for me. I spent a lot of time reviewing it, put it away, and then pulled it out months later to actually use it and found it was not freezing properly. I attempted to contact the seller but Amazon simply stated there is no warranty on a “free” product, making my $120 tax cost completely irrelevant. I also found that they replaced that product with a near identical model at a much lower, more competitive price.

I do not believe you can safely claim depreciation the way others have said, and even claiming hobby status to avoid the extra 15.3% FICA means going directly against Amazon’s 1099-NEC filing, requiring you to be ready to defend it. That said, I am now a much wiser Vine participant. I only select items that either have a $0 FMV or a very good one that is actually at or below actual value, and only if they are items that I actually need.

Actually, you don’t take “ownership” of the item until the 6-month mark, when you get the right of disposition, (if you cannot sell it nor give it away, you don’t own it). Before that the non-consumable item is the property of Amazon that you have been contracted to use & review in return for the compensation of the item in question at that 6-month mark. The item carries no value to you until then and when it does become yours, it’s value is depreciated from whatever FMV Amazon may set for a “new” item by virtue of its being used.

#8586. Where Should I Live? – Weigh 14 Factors, Starting With What Your Pay Buys

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Choosing where to live is a money decision first, so screen each place on its prices, its state and local taxes, and what your job pays there. Then rank the other factors, from commute to climate, by how much each matters to you, and spend a month in your top pick before you sign a lease or buy.

California’s prices ran about 27% above Arkansas’s in 2024 (110.7 against 86.9), the widest gap between any two states in the Bureau of Economic Analysis’s regional price parities, which score each state’s prices against a national level of 100. For rents the gap was wider still, with California’s nearly three times those of West Virginia, the cheapest state for rent (154.3 against 54.2).

So the same paycheck buys about 27% more in Arkansas than in California, before taxes and before any difference in what your job pays in each state. That’s why the three money factors below come first: affordability, taxes, and jobs. Screen every place you’re considering on those three, then use the other 11 to choose among the places that pass.

If you don’t have a list yet, start with the best U.S. cities to live in, places where remote workers get more for their money, college towns worth moving to, or, for a move abroad, inexpensive countries.

Start with each state’s price parity, then look closer at housing. Census QuickFacts lists the median rent and home value for cities and counties side by side, though its figures average several recent years, so check current listings for the home you’d need too.

Then add up what housing would cost each month, rent or a mortgage payment plus utilities, and divide it by your monthly income. By the Department of Housing and Urban Development’s standard, which the Census Bureau uses, a household that spends more than 30% of its income on housing is cost-burdened.

Compare the whole state and local tax bill, not just the income tax. A state with no income tax can still cost you more overall if its sales and property taxes run high. The Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy’s Who Pays? report estimates the share of income that families at each income level pay in state and local taxes, state by state, so find the group closest to your income.

If you’ll keep a remote job based in another state, check your employer’s location rules and the tax bill before you move.

Look up what your occupation pays in each metro area and how many people do that work there. The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ occupational employment and wage estimates give both for every metro area.

To compare pay between states, divide it by the state’s price parity and multiply by 100. In a state at 110, for example, a $70,000 salary buys about what $63,600 buys at the national price level, before taxes. A state’s parity averages its cities and rural areas, so treat it as a rough guide.

If you plan to buy, look at how home prices have moved, not just where they stand. The Federal Housing Finance Agency’s House Price Index tracks single-family home prices by state, metro area, county, and ZIP code, so you can compare five or 10 years of history across your list. How long homes sit unsold in current listings shows how easily you could sell later. Buy only if you expect to stay long enough for owning to beat renting.

QuickFacts lists the average travel time to work for each city and county, a quick way to compare commutes across your list. If you’d rather not drive, check the transit agency’s routes and schedules to see that buses or trains go where and when you’d need them.

If you fly often, check the nearest airport’s nonstop destinations on its website against the cities you visit most, and count the drive and parking in every trip’s cost. A bigger airport an hour farther away can still save time if it flies nonstop where the closer one connects.

Look up reported crimes for each city or county police department in the FBI’s Crime Data Explorer, using the same year for every place on your list. A citywide total can hide big differences between neighborhoods, so treat it as a first screen.

Climate sets your heating and cooling bills and your insurance costs, not just how comfortable you are. FEMA’s National Risk Index shows which communities are most at risk from 18 natural hazards, from floods to wildfires, so check it for every place on your list. Where flood risk runs high, price flood insurance along with a home or renters policy.

List what you do with a free weekend, from concerts and pro sports to hiking and worship, and check that each place offers it within an easy drive. The city’s events calendar and local news show what’s on in a typical month.

Price your usual grocery list at the stores in each place on their apps or websites, and check how far the nearest full-size supermarket is. If eating out is a big part of your week, see what’s within a short drive and what it costs.

QuickFacts also shows each place’s population and how much it has grown or shrunk since 2020. Size sets how many jobs, stores, and services you can choose from, and how much traffic comes with them. A shrinking population can mean fewer of all three later, so weigh the trend along with the size. Whether the city, a suburb, or the country costs you less depends on housing, car, and commute costs added together.

Count the trips you’d make each year to see family and friends, and price them, time off included. The help you’d leave behind has a price too. If relatives watch your kids now, the Labor Department’s National Database of Childcare Prices lists paid child care prices by county.

If you have kids or plan to, compare the schools in each place on your list. GreatSchools, a nonprofit, rates schools from 1 to 10 against other schools in the same state using state data, so compare ratings within a state, never across state lines.

Check that doctors who take your insurance practice nearby, along with a hospital you’d trust. Medicare’s Care Compare lets you compare the quality of care at Medicare-certified hospitals near any address. If you buy your own coverage, HealthCare.gov previews plans and estimated prices by ZIP code before you apply.

Before you sign a lease, buy a home, or book the move, live in your top pick for a month. Airbnb hosts can discount stays of 28 nights or more, and Furnished Finder lists only rentals of 30 days or more, with no booking fee for renters.

Live an ordinary month, not a vacation. Drive or ride your commute at rush hour, shop where you’d shop, and walk the neighborhoods you’d live in at night and on a weekend.

Book the month for the season you’d like least there, such as July in Phoenix or January in Minneapolis, because you’ll live through it every year.

#8584. Price Comparison Websites – Search Now, Track What Can Wait, and Check at Checkout

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

No single price comparison site always finds the lowest price, because each kind works differently. Use a shopping search engine when you’re ready to buy, put a price tracker on anything you can wait for, and let a browser extension check for a lower price or a coupon code at checkout.

In the second quarter of 2026, online sales made up 17.1% of all U.S. retail sales, by the Census Bureau’s count, adjusted for seasonal swings. With that much buying done online, checking prices before you pay is a habit worth building.

Each kind of tool looks for a lower price at a different moment. A shopping search engine compares many stores at once and shows today’s prices side by side. A price tracker watches one item for days or weeks and alerts you when it falls to the price you set. A browser extension works while you shop and looks for a lower price or a working coupon code before you pay.

Deal websites work the other way around. They post whatever happens to be on sale, while a comparison site starts from the item you name.

Use one of these when you’re ready to buy. Search for the exact item, with its model number if it has one, and compare prices with shipping added. If the lowest price is at a store you’d rather not buy from, ask your usual store whether it matches competitors’ prices.

Google Shopping lists offers from stores that send Google their product details, so one search lines up many sellers’ prices for the same item. It can also tell you whether today’s price is low, typical, or high compared with the past three months. To have it watch a price, sign in, tap Track price, and set a target. Google then emails you and sends an alert through its app when the price drops below that target.

The catch is that offers labeled Sponsored are ads, and a store’s payment to Google can affect where they rank. A store that doesn’t list its products there won’t appear at all. Before you buy, check the final price, shipping included, on the store’s own site.

ShopSavvy compares prices at thousands of stores, online and nearby, and its free app scans a product’s barcode in a store to show whether another seller has it for less. It also charts how each product’s price has moved and can watch an item for a lower price or a restock.

Its alerts can lag. Re-checks run on the phones and computers of whoever is watching the item, and on ShopSavvy’s own servers for some large stores, so it never promises an alert the instant a price falls. A price it hasn’t seen for over 30 days carries a note that it may have changed.

Pricepirates sets eBay listings, auctions still running among them, beside offers from thousands of online stores. Its apps for Windows, Mac, iPhone, and Android are free and show no ads. Start with it for anything you’d buy used or from an eBay seller.

An auction’s price is only its current bid, which can climb before the auction ends.

A tracker suits a purchase that can wait. Tell it the price you’d pay, and it watches the price for you.

camelcamelcamel tracks prices on Amazon and emails you when an item drops to the price you name. Its charts show each item’s price history, so you can tell whether today’s price is near its recent low. The Camelizer, its free browser extension, puts the same chart on the Amazon product page.

It covers only Amazon, so it never tells you when another store sells the item for less.

BuyVia’s free app compares prices at online stores and local chains such as Walmart, Target, and Best Buy. Set an alert on an item, and it sends a push notification or an email when the item goes on sale online or in a store near you.

Its sale alerts skip Amazon, so put a camelcamelcamel alert on anything you might buy there.

An extension runs inside your web browser and reads the store page you’re on, so it can look for a better deal without a separate search. Many shopping extensions only pay cash back or test coupon codes, while these three also check what other sellers charge.

When you look at a product on Amazon, Capital One Shopping checks other sellers and shows a lower-priced match if it finds one, and at checkout it tests promo codes on its own. It also alerts you when something you viewed or bought drops in price, and a drop soon after you buy is the moment to ask the store for a price adjustment. You don’t need a Capital One card or bank account to use it.

In return, it records the pages you view, what you buy, and the price you paid. Its rewards are gift cards, not cash.

Honey, which PayPal owns, looks for coupon codes on more than 30,000 sites and tests them at checkout with one click. On Amazon, it compares sellers with shipping costs and Prime status counted, and its Droplist alerts you when an item you saved drops in price.

Droplist watches only the store you saved the item from. Honey also records the stores and pages you visit, and what you buy there, while you use it.

Price.com compares prices on new, used, and refurbished items. Its extension works at more than 100,000 stores, where it applies coupon codes and cash back at checkout, and its website can email you when the price of an item you want falls.

The extension asks for access to your data on every website you visit, not just stores.

Start with the next item on your shopping list. Search it on Google Shopping now, and if it can wait, tap Track price and set the price you’d pay.

#8581. Buy a New Car Only for a 0% Loan or a Must-Have Feature

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. Buy a two- or three-year-old car rather than a new one, since a new car loses value fastest in its first years. Go new only when the automaker offers you 0% or a low-rate loan, or when you need a safety or fuel-saving feature no used car in your budget has.

The average new vehicle sold for a record $51,109 in October 2026, according to Kelley Blue Book (KBB). KBB estimates that a new car loses about 30% of its value in its first two years and 8% to 12% a year after that.

That early loss is why a two- or three-year-old car is the better buy for most people, and keeping a car for a decade doesn’t change that by itself. A 0% or low-rate loan from the automaker is what narrows the cost gap between new and used.

Take a $45,000 new car and its two-year-old twin at about $31,500, each financed in full for five years and kept for 10 years. The loans carry October’s average rates of 7.3% for new cars and 11% for used ones, according to Edmunds. Assume each car loses 10% of its remaining value a year once it’s two years old, the middle of KBB’s range. Counting interest and what each is worth at the end, the new car costs you about $40,300 over those 10 years and the twin about $30,100. Neither total counts insurance, fuel, or upkeep, the other parts of what a car costs to own.

With a 0% loan on the new car, its total falls to about $31,400, only about $1,300 more than the twin’s $30,100. That’s about $130 a year for a car two years newer with its full factory warranty, which makes new the better buy.

The other case for new is a safety or fuel-saving feature you need that no used car in your budget has. A new electric car no longer qualifies for the federal tax credit, which ended for those bought after Sept. 30, 2025.

Before you shop, get preapproved for a used-car loan and look up the automaker’s current financing offers on its website, then total both cars the same way over the years you plan to keep one.

#8578. Where to Get Quarters – 13 Places, Starting With Your Own Bank

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. Get quarters where coins are kept in bulk. Ask a teller at your own bank or credit union for a $10 roll of 40 quarters, then try a store’s service desk or a laundromat or car wash change machine. Before you go looking, check whether the machine you need them for takes a card or an app instead.

Fewer quarters come back in change because fewer people pay with cash. The Federal Reserve’s 2026 Diary of Consumer Payment Choice found that cash made up 14% of consumer payments in 2025, about six cash payments a month per person, down from 14 a month in 2016.

A store’s register can spare only a few dollars’ worth, since it needs its coins to make change. Banks hand quarters out by the roll, and businesses whose machines run on quarters often keep a change machine. The 13 places below run from easiest to hardest.

Ask a teller, not the ATM, for a $10 roll, which holds 40 quarters, and take a few rolls if you’ll need more later. Customers usually pay just the face value, out of their account or in cash, though a few banks charge a small fee per roll. If you don’t bank there, call first, since some banks and credit unions offer coin services only to their own customers or members.

Skip the checkout lanes and ask at the customer service desk, where some stores will trade a $10 bill for a roll. Others make change only with a purchase, and then just a few dollars’ worth. A coin-counting kiosk like Coinstar won’t help, since it takes coins and pays out only a voucher for cash, an eGift card, or a donation receipt.

A big-box store’s service desk works the same way and often stays open after banks close. If the clerk needs a sale to open the register, buy something you’d use anyway, like a bottle of water, and ask for the change in quarters.

A laundromat with coin-operated washers often has a change machine that breaks bills into quarters, though a $10 or $20 bill may come back partly in smaller bills. Check the labels on its front before you feed it, since some take only certain bills and some pay out tokens that work only in that laundromat.

Self-serve car washes that take coins often keep a change machine near the bays. Check it the same way, since some pay out the car wash’s own tokens instead of quarters.

An arcade with coin-operated games usually keeps quarters in a change machine or behind the counter. Many arcades have switched to tokens or reloadable game cards, and neither works anywhere else, so check what you’ll get before you put in a bill.

Convenience stores ring up a lot of small cash sales, so their drawers usually hold quarters, and many are open late. Ask for a few dollars’ worth with a purchase, and expect less late at night, when the drawer has to last until morning.

Ask at the front register, where the line is often shorter than at a grocery store, and expect a few dollars’ worth of quarters at most, usually with a small purchase. Many drugstores stay open late, too.

Ask at the register inside, not at the pump. Buy a drink or a snack with a $5 bill and ask for your change in coins, which usually gets you a few dollars in quarters.

Ask at the counter when the line is short, and order something small if the cashier needs a sale to open the drawer. Expect a couple of dollars’ worth. If there’s a tip jar, ask whether you can trade a bill for its coins.

Pay with a bill and the change comes back in coins, often quarters, so a $1 bill for a 75-cent snack returns one quarter. Expect a quarter or two per purchase, and dimes and nickels when the machine runs low on quarters.

Any cashier has to make change when you pay with cash, so ask for yours in quarters. Pay for a $1.25 item with a $5 bill, and the $3.75 you get back can come as 15 quarters if the drawer can spare them.

Ask a friend, relative, or coworker to trade quarters for your bills, especially one who keeps a change jar or a stash for the office vending machine. Expect only what has piled up, often a few dollars’ worth.

Many washers, dryers, parking meters, and vending machines now take a card or a phone app, so check for a card reader or a sticker naming an app before you go looking for quarters. PayRange lets you pay at laundromats and vending machines from your phone, and ParkMobile does the same for street and garage parking in place of the meter. Download the app the sticker names and add a payment card at home, before you need it.

#8575. 20 Bartering & Swapping Sites – Pick One by What You’re Trading

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Books, games, household goods, services, and places to stay each have swap sites built for them, so start with the one made for what you’re trading. Before you list, check who pays shipping, what membership or fees cost, and how the site rates traders, since in most swaps you’re counting on a stranger to send their half.

A swap counts as income to the IRS even when no cash changes hands. Its Tax Topic 420 says what you receive from bartering goes in your gross income, at its fair market value, for the year you receive it.

That makes a trade worth the same care as a purchase, starting with where you make it. Each kind of trade has sites built for it, and they differ most on three things: who pays to ship, what membership or fees cost, and what protects you when the other side doesn’t deliver.

Mailed trades are safest on sites that rate their members, where a new trader can start small with people who have a trading history. Trades of bulky goods and local services happen in person, so meet in a public place.

Craigslist’s barter section lets you post what you have and what you’d take for it. Posting there is free, since barter isn’t one of the categories Craigslist charges for. Trades are local and in person, so follow its own advice and meet in a public place such as a bank or police department, never at your home.

List an item on Facebook Marketplace or in a buy-and-sell group on Facebook, and say what you’d take in trade. Listing is free. Marketplace has ratings for buyers and sellers, so check a trader’s ratings first, then meet in a public place.

Listia runs auctions in points instead of dollars. You earn points when other members buy your items and spend them on things you want, and signing up gets you your first 50 points free. Past those, your points come from listing your own things, so you’ll need to give some away before you can get much.

Everything posted on Freecycle must be free, so it’s a place to give things away and pick up what neighbors give, not to trade. Membership is free, and volunteers moderate each local group.

The Buy Nothing Project runs local gift groups in its app and on Facebook, where neighbors give and ask for things at no cost. The basic app is free, and a paid Pro tier adds extras. Before you buy something you’ll use only briefly, ask your Buy Nothing group for it.

Rehash swaps clothes and accessories by mail. A member requests a trade, and once you accept, each of you mails your side. There are no listing or trading fees, just your own postage. If a trade goes wrong, Rehash’s remedy is to give the other member negative karma, so check a trader’s karma first.

BookMooch runs on points. You earn 1 point for each book you mail to a member who asks for it, or 3 if it goes abroad, and a book you receive costs the same. Joining is free, and your one cost is postage on what you send. For every two books you receive, you must send at least one.

PaperBackSwap trades paperbacks, hardcovers, audiobooks, and textbooks by mail. Mail a book another member requests, and you can pick one from the club in return. You pay postage on what you send, and the books you receive arrive postage-paid. Each request costs a book credit plus a 99-cent swap fee. The $25-a-year Standard plan waives the fee on every request and the $15-a-year Limited plan on 30 requests a year, and each mailing you send with the site’s printable postage earns one fee-free request.

SwapaCD and SwapaDVD trade original, playable CDs and DVDs by credit. Each disc you mail earns a credit, and each disc you request costs at least one credit plus a 49-cent fee, and the sender pays the postage.

GameTZ lists the games, music, movies, and books its members have and want, flags the matches, and charges no fees to trade. Each side mails its half, then rates the other on speed, honesty, and courtesy. As a new member, you’re expected to mail your half first, so start with small trades with members who have good-trader stars.

BoardGameGeek’s math trades swap board games among many members at once. You list the games you’ll give up and the ones you’d take for each. An algorithm then decides who mails what to whom, so you end up with a game you prefer to your own or keep yours. Your main cost is shipping, which the site’s guide warns can easily top $10 for a heavy game. Each trade’s moderator sets its rules and deadlines, so read them before you enter.

In a time bank, an hour you spend helping one member earns an hour of help from any other member, whatever the work. TimeBanks.org, a charity, keeps a directory of local time banks. Because hours are the only currency, a time bank is only as useful as the services its local members offer, so look at its listings before you join.

Shared Earth pairs gardeners and farmers with landowners who have space to spare. You search listings near you and work out a plan with the landowner, such as sharing what you grow. It’s a project of the nonprofit Sustainable America and asks users for donations. The terms are yours and the landowner’s to set, so put them in writing.

HomeExchange members swap homes for vacations, either directly or with GuestPoints earned by hosting, which let you stay somewhere without matching anyone’s dates. Membership costs $235 a year for unlimited exchanges, and the site verifies members and their homes. You’ll host members in your home to earn stays, so it suits a traveler with a place others want to visit.

On Intervac, you and a family somewhere else stay in each other’s homes over the same vacation dates, so you both need plans that line up. A year’s membership costs $130, or $230 for two years, and new members get a free 21-day trial.

Couchsurfing hosts let travelers stay for free, and you can host in return. Hosting or asking for a stay takes a paid membership, and ID verification, which hosts favor, is a separate yearly add-on. Read a host’s references from past guests before you send a stay request.

Workaway hosts give volunteers food and a place to stay in exchange for about 4 to 5 hours of help a day, 5 days a week. An individual account costs $69 a year. Workaway checks every profile before it goes live but doesn’t visit every host, so vet a host yourself before you go.

GoSwap is for permanent trades of big assets, such as homes, other property, businesses, cars, and boats. A listing costs 4 credits, at 50 cents a credit. Once both sides accept a swap, each pays 500 credits, worth $250, per listing for most assets, a fee refunded only if the swap ends before its documents are unlocked. Treat a deal there like any property or vehicle sale, with inspections, a title check, and a lawyer.

On BizX, a barter exchange, businesses sell goods or services to other members for BizX dollars, each worth $1, and spend them in the network. There’s no membership fee, but BizX charges a cash fee of 6% to 7.5% on each buy and sell. Trade dollars are only good inside the network, so join only if its members sell what you’d buy.

ITEX runs a similar marketplace in ITEX dollars, open to individuals as well as businesses. It charges a 6% cash fee when you buy or sell, plus $25 in cash and 10 ITEX dollars every four weeks. As with BizX, the dollars you earn spend only with other members.

A barter exchange such as BizX or ITEX files Form 1099-B with the IRS for its members’ trades, and you should get a copy. Trades you arrange directly don’t come with a 1099-B, though people who trade services may have to file Form 1099-MISC. Either way, the IRS says barter income from your business generally goes on Schedule C, and other barter income on Schedule 1.

Write down what each trade was worth on the day you make it, since that fair market value is what you’d report as income.

#8573. How to Have a Successful Garage Sale – Plan Ahead and Price to Sell Out

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

How much a garage sale brings in depends mostly on the work you do before sale day. Pick a date, advertise it online and with signs, and price every item ahead. Then run the sale to sell everything, not to get top dollar for each item, since whatever’s left is still yours to haul away.

The money you take in won’t bring a tax bill, even when buyers pay by Venmo or PayPal, since selling your own used things for less than you paid for them doesn’t raise your taxable income, the IRS says. Payment apps have to report your sales to the IRS on Form 1099-K only when they pay you more than $20,000 in more than 200 transactions a year, the threshold the 2025 tax law restored, the Taxpayer Advocate Service notes.

Buyers choose which sales to visit from the listings and signs they see, so your advertising decides how many show up. Once they arrive, a price on every item lets them buy without waiting to ask you.

Anything that doesn’t sell still has to be stored, donated, or hauled away, so a low price that sells an item at the sale is worth more than a high one that doesn’t. A lamp you won’t sell for less than $20 and end up donating earns you nothing, while the same lamp sold for $8 puts $8 in your pocket.

When you pick the date, book a local charity’s donation pickup for the day after the sale, so whatever’s left leaves instead of going back into the garage.
