#8570. My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.

But man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here. And the more I dig into the details and the hype and controversy surrounding the field of Hormone Replacement therapy, the more I need to share the word about it to my fellow middle-aged people (both men and women).

I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid. I started vacuuming up all the training and nutrition books and magazines I could find while I was just a teenager, and that field still remains a favorite of mine over 30 years later. And if you’re a long-time reader here you’ve been reminded plenty of times of this interest, because health has always been the very heart of Mustachianism.

But a funny thing has been happening in the last ten years: even as I kept honing the healthy living habits and trying my best to improve, there seemed to be a force pulling me back almost as hard. So despite working a bit harder and smarter every year, I still felt myself riding a gradually declining tide of energy, motivation, and physical stamina.

“Perhaps this is just what it means to grow old”, I thought to myself,

Yet there was one thing that didn’t quite fit. Why was I having this decline in energy, when some of my older friends weren’t? And why was I still seeing people out there in their 50s, 60s and well beyond doing things that I felt too tired to do today?

One of these tireless friends is a guy named Kevin, who is the personification of the highly energetic successful middle-aged man. He’s a semi-retired serial entrepreneur (and extreme rock climber) who lives in Boulder.  And through an interesting twist of fate, in April of 2025 he invited me out for a hike right around the time I was doing all this wondering. And during this hike (and climb) he told me about his latest venture, a boutique men’s health company that specializes in helping men just like us get their youth back through the process of testosterone replacement therapy.

Long story short: his ideas planted a seed in my head, which led to a bunch of research and a growing interest in trying TRT myself. I had of course heard about the process, but for some reason never considered doing it until I heard Kevin’s enthusiasm: he had been on it for several years, and according to him it is a “night and day difference” in all the things you want in life: energy, focus, thinking speed, and of course physical health.

Another convenient twist of fate is that I happen to be dating an REI doctor – a Reproductive Endocrinologist and Infertility specialist who has two board certifications in exactly the relevant bodily systems that are affected by these hormones. And while she was initially skeptical that I needed more Testosterone (and in her practice she regularly sees the downsides of men taking the stuff too early in life and thus compromising their own fertility), she has followed along and helped me learn at each step of this process, eventually becoming fully in support of the program.

So I signed up as a test customer for Kevin’s new company, which is called Bolt Health. I worked with their doctor to get a baseline blood test and review my numbers compared to all the past tests I’ve collected, and as it turned out, my levels had been dropping consistently over the years, and the latest test was by far the lowest ever.

Even more telling, my age-related drop in Testosterone was correlating perfectly with my decline in energy and motivation:

The next step was a prescription for a tiny daily dose of supplemental T, which arrived at my house the next week along with instructions for how to use it. And so began the journey.

Now let’s jump forward seven months to the present day as I write this.

And wow, what a great year it has been! I only wish I had known and tried this a few years earlier, because I’m getting a lot more out of my life.

It’s not a night-and-day difference for me, but more like a 50% boost in overall youthfulness and energy. The biggest subjective change is that I just don’t have sucky tired days anymore, which was the main problem with my life before: wasting too much of my precious freedom due to not having the energy to enjoy it.

This is why I’ve become somewhat of an evangelist for hormone replacement therapy for people from about age 45 onwards. It won’t work for everyone – if your levels are already pretty high, you don’t get the same boost. Two of my male friends tried TRT and quit because they didn’t notice any benefit. But these same two guys already had plenty of energy to begin with, which is usually a sign that the body has what it needs.

It turns out I am very late to this party. Although Testosterone supplementation started out as a niche practice in the 1940s, from the 2010s onward it has been everywhere.

TRT is the reason you see every actor suddenly showing up buff overnight for their superhero roles and it’s also why so many of today’s CEOs don’t look anything like yesterday’s CEOs.

In many cases, it has gone too far with young men using it just to gain muscle for the beach or the football field, and questionable online providers (aka “Prescription Mills”) handing out prescriptions to anyone with a valid credit card – with profit as their sole motive. It became overhyped in certain pockets of Bro Culture, where every Bro eventually receives the advice “Bro! You need to get on the T!” from another Bro, and therefore does it. And some of this reputation surely contributed to my own skepticism.

But there’s a lot of valid science behind TRT, if you’re the right candidate and you take the right dosage. And because of that, I feel it is probably under-hyped in my own demographic, the Nerdy Tech Worker Semi Retired Dad contingent. And that’s why I’m writing this blog post, because there are a lot of us out there.

Many of us just tend to work with what we were given, and accept that aging means slowing down. And for those of us already enjoying an early retirement, we have the option of unlimited rest and recuperation time, so who really cares if we get tired a bit more often? After all, what better way to flex one’s wealth than with a decadent Tuesday Afternoon Nap while everyone else is stuck in the office?

While this seemingly healthy attitude has a lot of positive aspects, it can also mask a real problem which may be easily fixable. Because sometimes, the only thing that’s even better than an afternoon nap, is having the energy and motivation to go out for an afternoon hike, bike ride or adventure with friends. More energy is also pretty darned useful if you’re still raising kids or trying to do well in your career as a person over 45.

How it Actually Works (and What Happened to Me)

Distilling all of the fluffy discussion above into the simplest possible answer: TRT means using a tiny needle to inject a few drops of clear liquid just below the surface of your skin. And you do this by yourself at home, ideally once every morning.

Here’s one of the baby needles I use for my daily dose.The typical serving is less than one tenth of a milliliter, which is only a few drops.

And while the term “needle” sounds scary to some, this is very different from the monstrosities they use to draw blood from your veins. This one is so miniature that you don’t need special training to use it, and you usually don’t even feel it.

So I began doing this to myself on May 1st of this year, while keeping a daily journal of my results along the way. The results seemed to be almost immediate in all the promised areas, but I know how powerful the Placebo Effect can be so I kept my skeptic’s hat on to see what would happen in the long run.

I was seeing increased energy and motivation as well as lean weight gain through the whole spring and summer, but I remember the first truly shocking observation happened during a mountain vacation in July. I was part of a multi-family trip with lively adults, chaotic kids, early mornings, late nights with a few drinks, very intense high altitude sunshine and nonstop physical activities. It was just the type of situation that would drain my energy pretty quickly in the past.

But on day three I went out on a solo mountain bike ride to explore the area, and as I was climbing a long ascent with the blazing sun cooking me from every angle I just somehow kept having plenty of energy to keep climbing. Then I came down and joined the group for a few games of full-sun pickleball, biked back up the mountain to our cabin, and the story of unlimited energy went on from there.

“Hot Damn”, I thought to myself, “I don’t know whose youthful and tireless body I have inherited here but I’d sure like to keep it!”

In August, the Bolt Health program scheduled a follow-up blood test for me and sure enough, my Testosterone levels had been boosted from 415 to 730ng/dL, bringing me from the low side of normal to the higher side.

Many labs define “normal” as anywhere between 300 and 1000, which seems strange to me given the huge effect this hormone has on your wellbeing. It’s a bit like saying “Most cars have between 90 and 300 horsepower, so it doesn’t really matter what engine you have”

I mean yeah, either one will still get you down the road, but which one would you rather be driving?

Since then, it has just been more of the same good results. My improvements ramped up and then just stayed there – so I’m operating at a new, much higher and more enjoyable level of functioning. Energy and motivation are no longer a problem, and I even find myself willing to make longer-term plans again (before this everything beyond same-day planning felt overwhelming). And my body seems to just want to gain strength and size with any excuse. Heavy weights feel lighter and the hard manual labor I still like to spend my time on feels easier for longer. It’s nice to be young again!

When you dig into the details, hormone replacement is mired in a soup of both real and incorrect information about both its benefits and its risks. And then our well-meaning medical establishment locks this whole container of soup deep in the cabinet with a label that says, “Needs Further Study”. But if you summarize the findings on both sides of the issue, you’ll see this:

The modern American Lifestyle is a Testosterone and Health Crusher. It’s a miracle that anybody feels good ever with the crap that people do to their bodies. So if you’re not already doing all the simple, natural, outdoor things that naturally boost your health, energy, and hormone levels, you’ll want to start with these first. You can find a pretty complete list on my oft-cited Badassity Tracker page.

Since I was already doing all of these things pretty consistently, I felt ready to take the next step and at least consider hormone supplementation. But wait, there’s more!

Many of the problems above are more likely to appear when the body is flooded with too much testosterone. In the bad old days, TRT was administered by sticking a pellet beneath your skin or injecting a large amount into the butt which then gets used up over the next several weeks. One friend recounted a story of extreme moodiness when the pellet was first implanted, ramping down to tiredness by the time the hormone was all gone.

More modern providers like Bolt have fixed this problem by breaking the dose into much smaller servings which you administer each day. The idea is that your levels remain stable, and you need a lot less overall which reduces side effects.

For my part, I have not had any of the negative side effects because I was a pretty ideal candidate in the first place: 50 years old with depressed Testosterone levels but an otherwise healthy lifestyle and no risk factors.

My hope in sharing this article is to be transparent and hopefully take some of the stigma out of this subject of other people who might benefit. Because in our modern over-connected world, everybody has an opinion on your life, even when you didn’t ask them.

And it’s not just men – many women in this same age group benefit from Estrogen replacement (and there are even interesting stories about female testosterone supplementation in certain situations as this author shares). The point is that aging is normal, but in some cases there’s a pretty easy way to make it slower

The great news is that Testosterone itself is a cheap and widely available substance, typically under $50 per month even for people like me without conventional insurance or drug coverage. The expensive part (here in the US) is just the doctor stuff – consultations, blood tests, ongoing analysis and prescription renewals and so on.

The company that I used is positioned as a premium provider, bundling these services along with a bunch of other men’s health perks and deliveries for a few hundred dollars, which is expensive relative to most other parts of my budget, but still cheap if I consider the life and financial benefits of being 20-50% more energetic and productive.

If you want to be on this program, your final decision will hinge on your income, insurance coverage if applicable, whether your existing doctor can already help you, and how much service and advice you’re willing to pay for.

Note: I decided not to become a Bolt health affiliate because I wanted to write this article without conflict of interest. And I can honestly say, Bolt’s product and service seem great to me because I know and trust the people who run it. But  it’s also the only one I’ve tried. So I don’t know much about the competition and there may be other good options out there. At the very minimum, you can always try one service and switch to another if you don’t like the first one.

I’ve got lots more to say on money and early retirement, and lots of interesting projects in the works now too. So I’m thankful to have stumbled upon this booster for all aspects of life, so I can do more of everything else, for even more decades than I had expected.

I wish this same type of good fortune for you, however you create it.

Interesting. I know very little about this topic, but as I read my thoughts immediately went to the evolutionary biologist Robert Sapolsky and his book The Trouble With Testosterone. I would encourage you to go down that pathway and add it into your thinking. I’m curious what the Bolt people would say to these arguments.

It has been some time since I read the book so I got some LLM summaries to refresh me on why many evolutionary biologist consider testosterone an expensive biological tax. I’m going to paste some of it here:

In the wild, maintaining high testosterone levels is akin to driving a car with the engine red-lining. It provides short-term power for mating and fighting, but it wears down the machinery (the body) much faster. Here is a breakdown of the specific evolutionary costs Sapolsky and other biologists highlight, focusing on the immune system and metabolic “taxes.” 1. The Immunocompetence Handicap This is the central theory explaining why high testosterone is costly. The “Handicap Principle” suggests that because testosterone suppresses the immune system, only males with superior genetics can afford to maintain high levels of it. The Trade-off: Energy is finite. The body must choose between investing in survival (immunity, cell repair) or reproduction (muscle mass, aggression, mating displays). Testosterone forces the body to prioritize reproduction at the expense of survival. The “Honest Signal”: High T features (like a peacock’s tail or a stag’s massive muscles) are “honest signals” to females because they are dangerous to possess. The male is essentially saying, “Look at how strong my genes are—I can handicap my own immune system with this much testosterone and still be standing.” Parasitic Load: In wild primate studies, males with the highest testosterone often have the highest burden of intestinal parasites. Their immune systems are less efficient at fighting off low-level infections because their energy is diverted elsewhere. 2. Metabolic & Physiological Costs Beyond just the immune system, high testosterone extracts a heavy toll on the body’s daily maintenance. Metabolic Burn: Testosterone is metabolically expensive. It forces the body to build and maintain lean muscle mass which burns calories at a much higher rate than fat. In a food-scarce environment (which is most of evolutionary history), having high T is a risk; you are more likely to starve during a famine. The “Good Cholesterol” Crash: Testosterone generally lowers HDL (good cholesterol). Sapolsky notes that this is one reason why males across many species die younger than females. The hormone that helps you win the fight today clogs your arteries for tomorrow. 3. Behavioral “Taxes” High testosterone lowers the threshold for risk-taking, which carries a direct survival cost. Injury and Mortality: High-T males are more conspicuous and more likely to engage in risky confrontations. In the wild, “winning” a fight often leaves a victor injured, making them susceptible to infection (which their T-suppressed immune system is now less equipped to fight). Parental Investment: Evolutionarily, there is often an inverse relationship between testosterone and parental care. High T drives mating effort (seeking new partners) rather than parenting effort (caring for offspring). In species where offspring need high investment, high T can actually be an evolutionary disadvantage if the offspring die from neglect. Summary of the Trap The “trouble” Sapolsky identifies is that while high testosterone might help a male pass on genes (by winning a mate), it actively works against his staying alive. The Irony: Pro-TRT (Testosterone Replacement Therapy) arguments often frame high T as the key to “health” and “vitality.” From an evolutionary standpoint, nature views high T as the exact opposite: a calculated health risk taken solely to reproduce before you die.

I hope this is good food for thought and discussion. Thanks for your years of great blogging MMM!

Testosterone cypionate (most common, what MMM is using) and enanthate (another commonly used ester) have a half-life of around 10 days, meaning that 10 days after your dose about half of it will be left. After a few weeks of weekly dosing the levels stabilize (you can math this out using mg if you want). There’s zero reason to dose daily. I actually tested twice-weekly dosing vs weekly with blood testing and there was no difference in my levels. Weekly is more than fine and you won’t notice any fluctuations. It’s pretty common for people to dose every other week, but weekly is more than sufficient to maintain consistent levels.

#8569. Aeroplan Stopovers — Two Cities for the Price of One

One of the highest-value redemptions in travel rewards

Picture this: you're settling into a lie-flat business class seat somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of something cold in hand, knowing that in 48 hours you'll be waking up in Istanbul — and then, a few days later, continuing onward to Bangkok. Two bucket-list cities. One award booking. One points balance. This is what the Aeroplan stopover sweet spot feels like in practice. It's not a trick or a loophole — it's a deliberately designed feature of Air Canada's Aeroplan program that the vast majority of travelers simply don't know exists. And that gap between awareness and reality is exactly where the ChooseFI community finds its edge. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class itinerary from North America to Istanbul with a continuing flight onward to Bangkok — two long-haul segments, lie-flat seats, Star Alliance lounges at every connection — would cost somewhere between **$6,000 and $15,000 in cash**. That's a realistic retail range depending on season and how far out you book. Most people never consider it a possibility for a family vacation or a milestone trip because the sticker price puts it in a different universe. With Aeroplan, you're booking that same itinerary — the same seats, the same lounges, the same Turkish Airlines or Thai Airways product — for **75,000 Aeroplan points**. At the low end of the cash price range, that's already **8 cents per point**. At the high end, you're extracting **20 cents per point** from a currency that most people earned by putting groceries on a credit card. The pricing inefficiency here is structural. Aeroplan's partner award chart prices long-haul business class at a fixed rate regardless of cash fare fluctuations. When business class prices spike — around holidays, during peak travel seasons, during major events — your points cost stays exactly the same. You're insulated from the market. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: you've already paid for the trip in points, slowly accumulated through everyday spending, and now you're simply redeeming the stored value. The stopover itself is nearly free. Aeroplan charges just 5,000 extra miles to add a stopover city to a one-way award. That means your Istanbul layover becomes a multi-day stay — at zero additional points cost beyond that small add-on — and you haven't booked a second award at all. One booking. Two destinations. That's the entire premise, and once you see it, you can't unsee it.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you understand it, but it requires knowing three things that most travelers don't: how Aeroplan's routing rules work, what a stopover actually is in the context of an award ticket, and why Star Alliance's global network makes this scalable to almost any destination pair you can imagine.

When Aeroplan relaunched its loyalty program in 2020, it did something remarkable: it eliminated fuel surcharges entirely and published a partner award chart with fixed pricing for flights on Star Alliance carriers. This is critical. When you book Turkish Airlines business class through Aeroplan, you pay the Aeroplan fixed chart rate — not what Turkish Airlines would charge in its own currency or miles program, and not the inflated cash price. That fixed chart is the engine of this redemption.

For long-haul international business class, Aeroplan's chart prices routing through multiple regions based on your origin and destination — not every intermediate stop. This is the aha moment. Aeroplan determines your award price based on where your journey starts and where it ends, and then allows you to add a stopover in between for just 5,000 additional miles. The stopover city is priced as a pass-through for the purpose of calculating your award zone, not as a second trip.

On a one-way Aeroplan award, you're permitted to add a free stopover — meaning you can stay in an intermediate city for any length of time before continuing to your final destination. That 5,000-mile add-on is essentially the cost of a full additional destination. Compare that to booking a second one-way award from Istanbul to Bangkok, which would cost you another 40,000–55,000 Aeroplan points in business class. The math is decisive.

The routing must be geographically sensible — you can't fly backwards across the globe — but Aeroplan's allowance for multi-segment itineraries through Star Alliance hubs gives you enormous flexibility. Istanbul (IST) is a Turkish Airlines hub. Bangkok (BKK) is served by Thai Airways and several Star Alliance carriers. Both are Star Alliance partners. Both are bookable through Aeroplan at fixed chart rates with no fuel surcharges.

The best part for the ChooseFI community is how accessible the underlying points are. Aeroplan accepts transfers from four major programs:

Chase's instant transfer speed is particularly valuable here. When you find business class availability — which can disappear quickly — you want to move points immediately. Having Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency means you can search, find space, and transfer points before the availability window closes. The 1:1 ratio across all four programs means no conversion math — every point you earn translates directly to one Aeroplan mile.

Free calculator shows when you could reach financial independence — plus a savings rate tracker, expense audit, and more.

Booking an Aeroplan stopover award in business class is genuinely one of the more complex redemptions in the travel rewards world, but it becomes manageable when you break it into distinct phases. Here's exactly how to do it.

Start by deciding on your two destinations. Aeroplan stopovers work best when your intermediate city is a major Star Alliance hub that lies geographically between your origin and final destination. Classic combinations include North America to Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub) continuing to Southeast Asia, or North America to a European hub continuing to the Middle East or East Africa. Your stopover city should be somewhere you genuinely want to spend 2–5 days — this is a real trip, not just a layover.

This is the most important and most time-consuming step. You need to find saver-level business class availability on both segments independently before you book.

Once you've confirmed availability on both segments, go to aeroplan.com and use the multi-city search function. Enter your full itinerary — origin, stopover city with your intended layover dates, and final destination.

Once you've confirmed the award is bookable and are ready to complete the reservation:

Complete your booking on aeroplan.com or with a phone agent, confirm the stopover is properly reflected in your itinerary, and save every confirmation email. Verify your seats on each carrier's website immediately after booking.

A stopover is an intentional break in your journey lasting more than 24 hours at a connecting city. Most airlines treat stopovers as separate tickets, charging full price for each segment. Aeroplan is one of the few programs that allows a free stopover on round-trip awards, letting you explore a connecting city for days before continuing to your final destination. This is fundamentally different from a layover, which is a brief connection of a few hours at an airport. The stopover must be in a city served by a Star Alliance carrier on your routing, and the key is that Aeroplan prices the entire itinerary as one award, not two.

Let's build a real example so you can see exactly what this looks like on paper — and in the air.

The Route: Toronto (YYZ) → Istanbul (IST, 4-day stopover) → Bangkok (BKK) The Carrier: Turkish Airlines business class on both segments The Points Cost: 75,000 Aeroplan miles for the two segments + 5,000 miles for the stopover = 80,000 Aeroplan miles total Cash Equivalent: A comparable business class itinerary on this routing typically retails for $9,000–$12,000 in 2026, depending on when you search and how far in advance you book.

The CPP Calculation: At the midpoint cash value of $10,500 against 80,000 points, you're extracting 13.1 cents per Aeroplan mile — well inside the 8–20 cent range this sweet spot delivers, and roughly 10–13 times the value of redeeming Aeroplan miles for cash back.

The Turkish Airlines business class product on long-haul routes is consistently rated among the top business class experiences in the Star Alliance network. On the YYZ–IST segment — operated on a 787 or A330 — you'll have access to a lie-flat seat with direct aisle access, the Turkish Airlines Lounge in Istanbul (widely considered one of the best airport lounges in the world, full stop), and a meal service that reflects the airline's culinary reputation. The IST lounge alone — with its restaurant, spa, golf simulator, and sleeping areas — is worth lingering in even before your onward connection.

In Istanbul, your four days might include the Hagia Sophia at sunrise, a Bosphorus dinner cruise, and the Grand Bazaar before you head to the airport to continue your journey. You've paid nothing additional for this stay beyond the 5,000-mile stopover fee.

The IST–BKK segment puts you into Bangkok in the evening, ready for Thailand's extraordinary food, culture, and cost of living — which, for the FI-minded traveler, means your lodging and meals on the ground are remarkably affordable, stretching the value of your trip even further.

Total points cost for two lie-flat business class segments and a full European city stay: 80,000 miles, earned on everyday credit card spending. That's the entire proposition, and those numbers are real.

Book at exactly 355 days out. Aeroplan opens its booking window at 355 days before departure. The best business class availability on popular routes — especially Turkish Airlines long-haul — appears at this window and gets claimed quickly. Set a calendar reminder and be ready to search at the 355-day mark for your target travel dates.

Use Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency for this redemption. The instant transfer speed to Aeroplan is genuinely differentiating. When you find award space and need to move quickly, Chase lets you transfer and book in the same session. Amex, Capital One, and Bilt all require 1–2 days, during which your availability can evaporate.

Search availability before you transfer points. Confirm space exists on every segment before a single point moves. There's no undo button on a transfer, and Aeroplan points sitting idle in your account are fine — points transferred to an account where you can't find availability are a headache.

Call Aeroplan for complex routings. The online multi-city tool is functional but can struggle with nuanced stopover configurations. Phone agents are experienced with these bookings and have the same access to inventory. The call is worth it for an $80,000-point booking.

Leverage the open-jaw rule too. Aeroplan also allows open-jaw routing — fly into one city, depart from another. Combined with the stopover, you can design a route that visits three geographic points on a single award: fly into Istanbul, take trains or ferries to Athens, and fly home from Athens. The award prices the same way.

Don't assume partner availability matches Aeroplan's search. Turkish Airlines and other Star Alliance partners don't always make every seat available through Aeroplan's online portal. If you see space on the carrier's own site but not on aeroplan.com, call — agents can often access inventory the website misses.

Don't book inflexible connecting flights. Long-haul itineraries with tight connections are a risk. Build in at least a 3-hour connection at hub airports to protect against irregular operations that could affect your award segments.

Don't earn Marriott Bonvoy points with this redemption in mind. The 3:1 transfer ratio to Aeroplan makes Marriott a poor choice for funding this specific award. Stick to Amex, Chase, Capital One, or Bilt at 1:1.

Don't book this for a time-sensitive trip. Award availability, transfer timelines, and multi-carrier coordination mean this requires planning runway. Build in at least 3–4 weeks of lead time beyond the actual booking date.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

This redemption is purpose-built for the advanced travel rewards enthusiast in the ChooseFI community — someone who has already mastered the basics (earning transferable points, understanding award charts, booking straightforward partner awards) and is ready to unlock the next level of value.

The ideal profile: A couple or solo traveler planning a milestone trip — a significant anniversary, a sabbatical, a once-in-a-decade adventure — who wants to experience two destinations in business class without paying business class prices for either one. You're flexible on travel dates, comfortable spending time on the phone with an airline agent, and genuinely excited about the trip-planning process as part of the experience.

Minimum points balance: You'll need approximately 80,000 Aeroplan miles to complete this booking (75,000 for the award plus 5,000 for the stopover). That's achievable from a single premium credit card welcome bonus, a combination of two or three mid-tier welcome bonuses, or 12–18 months of everyday spending on a 2x transferable points card.

For the ChooseFI traveler who's been building transferable points for a year or two and wants to see what this system is truly capable of, this redemption is the answer.

This redemption is rated **Hard** — and that rating is honest. It earns that designation from three compounding challenges, not just one. **Challenge 1: Finding availability on multiple segments simultaneously.** Business class award space on popular long-haul routes is limited. Finding saver-level availability on one segment is manageable. Finding it on two connected segments, with dates that create a coherent stopover itinerary, requires persistence and flexibility. This is the primary barrier. **Challenge 2: Understanding Aeroplan's routing logic.** Aeroplan's stopover rules, multi-city booking interface, and the distinction between how partner awards are priced require more than surface-level familiarity with the program. A misunderstanding of how the stopover is added can result in a significantly higher points cost or a booking that doesn't reflect your intended itinerary. **Challenge 3: Coordinating the transfer timing.** With a 355-day booking window and fast-moving business class availability, the timing of your point transfers requires active management — particularly if you're not using Chase's instant transfer speed. ## Three Tips to Overcome These Challenges 1. **Start your availability research 60–90 days before the 355-day window opens.** Know your target route, your preferred stopover city, and your date range before you ever log into aeroplan.com. Preparation turns a chaotic search into a focused one. 2. **Use united.com as your availability research tool.** It searches the Star Alliance network and shows you realistic inventory without requiring you to commit points. 3. **Don't be discouraged by the learning curve.** Every hard redemption in the ChooseFI community gets easier the second time. Plenty of members who now book these routinely considered them impossible the first time they looked. The complexity is real — but so is the $10,000 of value sitting on the other side of it.

Pick a final destination and a stopover city on the same Star Alliance routing. Classic combos: Istanbul + Bangkok, Zurich + Tokyo, Vienna + Singapore. The stopover city must be a natural connection point on a Star Alliance route between your origin and destination.

Set a calendar alert for 355 days before your departure date. Search for business class availability on each segment separately using United.com or Aeroplan.com. Both legs need saver-level award space on the same booking.

Before transferring any points, verify that saver award space exists on both the outbound leg (origin to stopover city) and the continuation (stopover city to final destination). If either segment is unavailable, the booking will not work.

Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant) or Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days) to your Aeroplan account at a 1:1 ratio. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability on both segments.

Call Aeroplan or use the multi-city search tool online. Specify your stopover city and duration (up to the maximum allowed). The system prices it as one round-trip award. Confirm total points match expectations before completing the booking.

Aeroplan allows stopovers of up to 45 days on round-trip awards. You can stay in your stopover city for a few days or several weeks, giving you genuine time to explore rather than just passing through.

No, stopovers are only available on round-trip awards through Aeroplan. One-way bookings do not qualify for the free stopover benefit. This is one reason round-trip awards can offer better value than two one-ways.

Aeroplan has improved its online multi-city search tool, and some stopover itineraries can now be booked online. However, complex routings may still require a phone call. When calling, clearly state you want a round-trip award with a stopover and specify your stopover city and dates.

The best stopover cities are Star Alliance hub cities with strong business class availability: Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub), Zurich (SWISS hub), Vienna (Austrian hub), Singapore (Singapore Airlines hub), and Tokyo (ANA hub). These hubs offer the most consistent saver-level award space.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Aeroplan stopover is one of the most powerful tools in the travel rewards playbook. By adding a free stopover to a round-trip business class award, you can explore two world-class cities for the points cost of visiting one. It requires planning, patience at the 355-day booking window, and comfort with Star Alliance routing rules, but the payoff is extraordinary: 10-15 cents per point in value on experiences that would cost thousands in cash. For the FI community member who has mastered basic award bookings and is ready to level up, this is the redemption that changes how you think about travel.

#8567. 17 Part-Time Jobs for High School Students – Starting Age & Pay for Each

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Choose a high school job by your age and school schedule first, then by pay. Federal child labor rules don’t cover casual babysitting or chores like yard work for neighbors, and they allow most store and restaurant jobs from 14. At 14 and 15, you can work at most 3 hours a school day and 18 a school week.

The Department of Labor’s rules also keep those hours between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m., or 9 p.m. from June 1 through Labor Day, which leaves out most evening shifts during the school year.

Age also decides the tasks. Until 16, you can’t bake, do warehouse work, or run power equipment such as a lawn mower. Until 18, you can’t do work the department rates hazardous, such as operating a forklift or a meat slicer.

At 16 and 17, federal law sets no limit on your hours. Your state can set its own limits, and the stricter rule applies. The Labor Department’s state-by-state table shows the hour limits states set for workers under 16 and for 16- and 17-year-olds. Many states also require minors to get a work permit, sometimes called working papers.

Each pay figure below is the median hourly wage the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported for employees in that job in May 2025, adults included. Half earned more than the median and half earned less. Federal law also lets employers pay workers under 20 a youth minimum wage of $4.25 an hour for their first 90 days. If your state or city sets a higher minimum wage, you get that rate instead, unless its law makes an exception for workers under 20.

The list covers jobs with an employer or a neighbor. Summer jobs, online work, and a business of your own are separate searches. Once the paychecks start, find out whether you need to file a tax return, and whether to put some of your pay in a custodial Roth IRA, a retirement account a parent manages for you until you’re an adult.

Childcare workers earned a median $16.82 an hour. Casual babysitting has no federal minimum age, so parents decide when you’re ready. Start with families you already know, set your rate with each one, and take a babysitting course that covers first aid and CPR before your first job.

Animal caretakers earned a median $17.00 an hour. Caring for a neighbor’s pets is one of the minor chores around private homes that federal child labor rules leave out, but Rover requires its sitters and dog walkers to be at least 18. So find clients on your own street, and meet each pet before you take the job.

Landscaping and groundskeeping workers earned a median $18.82 an hour. Mowing and raking for neighbors has no federal minimum age, but a landscaping company can’t put you on a power mower, trimmer, or edger until 16. Knock on doors in early spring with a flat price per lawn, and offer leaf raking in the fall.

Cashiers earned a median $15.81 an hour. Bagging groceries, stocking shelves, and running a register are all open at 14 under federal rules, and Publix hires front service clerks, its name for baggers, from that age. Apply on the chain’s careers site, then ask the store manager about after-school shifts.

Retail salespersons earned a median $17.03 an hour. Cashiering, selling, and stocking are open from 14 under federal rules, though a chain can set a higher minimum of its own. List the exact hours you can work after school and on weekends, since a store has to schedule you within the federal limits.

Food preparation workers earned a median $16.98 an hour. From 14, you can wash dishes, prep food, and cook on electric or gas grills without an open flame or on fryers that lower and raise baskets automatically. Baking and other cooking wait until 16, and power-driven meat slicers and dough mixers until 18. Ask for the kitchen manager when you apply.

Fast food and counter workers earned a median $15.00 an hour. Taking orders, running the register, and preparing food are all open from 14, within the same cooking limits as any kitchen job. Apply online, then stop in on a slow afternoon and ask for the manager.

The Labor Department’s O*NET database files baristas under fast food and counter workers, so the same $15.00 median applies. Federal child labor regulations name coffee grinders and automatic coffee machines among the machines 14- and 15-year-olds may run, though each café sets its own minimum age. Ask at coffee shops near your school about after-school shifts.

Waiters and waitresses earned a median $16.94 an hour, tips included, since the BLS wage survey counts them as pay. Federal law lets restaurants pay tipped workers a cash wage of just $2.13 an hour as long as tips bring them to at least $7.25, though some states require more. Serving is open from 14 under federal rules. Ask how tips are shared before you take the job.

Ushers, lobby attendants, and ticket takers earned a median $15.82 an hour. Selling tickets and working the concession stand are open from 14, and the regulations even name popcorn poppers among the machines you may run. Before 16, though, you can’t work past 7 p.m. outside summer, so ask about weekend matinee shifts.

Amusement and recreation attendants earned a median $15.46 an hour. At a bowling alley, skating rink, or recreation center, running the front counter and cleaning up are open from 14. Lead with the weekend daytime hours you can work.

Clerical library assistants earned a median $17.74 an hour. Pages put returned books back on the shelves and keep them in order, clerical work open from 14 under federal rules. Ask at the circulation desk, and check your city’s or county’s job listings.

General office clerks earned a median $21.64 an hour. Filing, answering phones, and data entry are office work open from 14. Ask family businesses, dental and medical offices, and your school’s front office whether they need after-school help.

Tutors earned a median $20.84 an hour. The federal regulations list tutoring among the work open at 14. Start with younger students you already know, in the subjects where your grades are strongest.

Web developers earned a median $44.54 an hour. The regulations also list computer programming and writing software as work open at 14. Build a portfolio first, with sites for a club, a team, or a family business, then offer to update a local shop’s site.

Lifeguards and ski patrol workers earned a median $16.14 an hour. At 15, you can guard at a pool or water park with a lifeguard certification from the American Red Cross or a group like it, and at 16 at lakes and beaches. The Red Cross requires students to be at least 15 by the last day of class, and its certification lasts two years. Ask indoor pools about year-round shifts.

Recreation workers earned a median $17.58 an hour. Camps accredited by the American Camp Association hire counselors from 16, as long as each is two or more years older than the campers in their group. Younger teens can start as counselors in training, a role that pays at some camps and costs tuition at others, so ask which kind it is before you sign up.

Before you accept an offer, ask how many hours a week the job can give you. In a school week, 18 hours at $15 an hour pays $270, while 10 hours at $18 pays $180.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That said, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like new credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most important issues for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

One step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you plan to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

In fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

Your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That said, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit quickly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

While secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

Many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

In fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

There are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an issue with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

College students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

Either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

#8564. Real vs. Nominal Interest Rates – Subtract Inflation Before You Save or Borrow

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

The rate a bank or lender quotes is the nominal rate. The real rate, roughly the nominal rate minus inflation, measures what your savings gain or your loan costs in buying power. Subtract inflation from any rate you’re offered before you choose where to keep cash or whether to borrow.

Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months through September 2026, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reports, while the FDIC puts the national average savings rate at 0.38%. A savings account paying that average has a real rate of about -3.3%, so at that pace the money in it buys about 3% less after a year.

A nominal interest rate is the rate on the account or loan itself, such as a savings account’s annual percentage yield (APY) or a credit card’s annual percentage rate (APR). It tells you how many dollars you’ll earn or owe, not what those dollars will buy. Deposit $1,000 at 4% APY, and a year later you have $1,040, whatever $1,040 buys by then.

Here, nominal means before inflation. In another sense, a nominal rate is one that leaves out compounding, the interest earned on interest, which is what separates an APR from an APY.

The real interest rate takes inflation out of the nominal rate, so it measures what your money can buy instead of how many dollars you have. If prices rise 3% in the year your $1,000 grows to $1,040, the $1,040 buys only about 1% more than the $1,000 did.

When the real rate is positive, savers gain buying power and borrowers pay for the use of the money. When it’s negative, savers lose buying power even as their balances grow, and what borrowers repay, interest included, buys less than what they borrowed.

The real rate you’ll end up with depends on inflation over the life of the account or loan, which no one knows in advance, so any real rate figured today is an estimate.

For a quick estimate, subtract the inflation rate from the nominal rate. A one-year certificate of deposit (CD) paying 4% when inflation runs 3% has a real rate of about 1%.

The exact formula divides instead, with each rate written as a decimal.

Real rate = (1 + nominal rate) ÷ (1 + inflation rate) − 1

For that CD, 1.04 ÷ 1.03 − 1 = 0.0097, a real rate of 0.97%. The quick version is close when rates are low, and the gap widens as they rise. A credit card charging 24% when inflation runs 3.7% has a real rate of 20.3% by subtraction and 19.6% by the exact formula.

The inflation figure to use depends on the decision. For one about today, such as whether your savings account is keeping up, use the 12-month change in the Consumer Price Index (CPI), the measure of consumer prices the BLS publishes each month. The October 2026 report has none, because the 2025 government shutdown kept the BLS from collecting October 2025 prices. So September’s 3.7% stays the latest figure until the November report comes out on December 10.

For a decision that runs for years, such as a five-year CD or a fixed-rate mortgage, use expected inflation, since what counts is inflation over the whole term. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland estimates expected inflation for every horizon from one to 30 years, and its November 2026 update put the next 10 years at 2.67% a year.

Run the numbers on $10,000 for a year at 3.7% inflation. In a savings account paying 0.4%, close to the national average, it grows to $10,040, but what cost $10,000 at the start of the year costs $10,370 by the end, so your balance buys about 3% less.

Move that $10,000 to a high-yield savings account paying 4%, and it grows to $10,400, a real rate of about 0.3%, so it buys a little more after a year than it did at the start.

Taxes take a cut, since interest counts as taxable income. If your interest is taxed at 22%, the 4% account earns 3.12% after tax, a real rate of about -0.6%.

A negative real rate doesn’t make saving a mistake. Money for emergencies and for costs you expect within a few years has to be safe and on hand, so keep it where its rate is highest. Money you won’t need for a decade or more is better invested, since a negative real rate compounds year after year.

On a loan, the real rate is what borrowing costs you in buying power. A 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 6% has a real rate of about 2.3% against the past year’s 3.7% inflation, and about 3.3% against the Cleveland Fed’s estimate of 2.67% a year over the next 10 years.

Inflation helps a fixed-rate borrower because the payment stays the same in dollars while prices rise, so each payment costs you less in buying power than the one before. A variable rate offers less of that help, since it moves with a benchmark rate, and benchmark rates tend to rise when inflation does.

Subtracting inflation never changes which of your debts costs the most, since the same figure comes off every rate. It shows how much each one costs you in buying power. A credit card at 24% still costs about 20% a year after inflation. A 3% fixed-rate mortgage has a real rate of about -0.7%, so inflation shrinks what you owe, in buying power, faster than interest adds to it.

Investment returns work the same way. A stock fund that gains 10% in a year when inflation runs 3.7% has a real return of about 6.3%, or 6.1% by the exact formula.

Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) and I bonds each pay a rate set up front plus an adjustment for inflation, so the set rate is a real rate, which on an I bond is called the fixed rate.

Compare an investment’s return with a savings or loan rate only on the same basis, both before inflation or both after. A 4% savings rate looks close to a stock return of 7% after inflation, but compared fairly, it’s 7% against the account’s real rate of about 0.3%.

Look up the CPI’s latest 12-month change on the BLS’s CPI page, updated each month, and subtract it from the rate on each account and debt you hold now.

For cash you’ll need within a few years, compare the best high-yield savings accounts.

Before you buy a thrift store find to resell, look up what the same item has actually sold for online, not what sellers are asking. Buy it only if that sold price, minus the selling site’s fee and the shipping, beats the store’s price by enough to pay you for your time.

That profit is taxable from the first dollar, even though selling your own used things for less than you paid isn’t. A marketplace has to report your sales to the IRS on Form 1099-K only once it pays you more than $20,000 in more than 200 transactions in a year, so report the profit yourself whether or not a form arrives.

Flip regularly as a business, and you also owe self-employment tax once your net earnings reach $400. Most flips earn a few dollars to a few dozen, so a fee or label you didn’t count can turn one into a loss.

Say a vintage Pyrex bowl costs you $6 and sells on eBay for $40, and the buyer pays $10 for shipping and $4 in sales tax while the label costs you $10. eBay takes 13.6% of the whole $54 plus 40 cents, or $7.74, so the $50 you collect drops to $32.26 after the fee and the label, a $26.26 profit on your $6.

Log each find’s cost, sale price, fees, and shipping in a spreadsheet as you go. The log shows which kinds of finds pay you, and it’s the record that proves your profit at tax time.

Choose where to list each find from the best places to sell your stuff.

#8559. Wells Fargo Routing Numbers by State – Go by Where You Opened the Account

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. Your Wells Fargo routing number depends on the state where you opened the account, not where you live now. Use that state’s number for a direct deposit or an automatic payment, and confirm it on a check or in the Wells Fargo app first. A wire coming into your account uses a separate number.

An account opened in Ohio uses Ohio’s number, 041215537, even after you move to Florida. Give an employer Florida’s 063107513 instead, and the deposit may fail, arrive late, or bounce back, as Wells Fargo’s guide to routing numbers warns.

Wells Fargo’s routing number page lists its numbers by state. Checking, savings, and money market accounts opened in a state all use that state’s number. Some states share a number, so an account opened in Massachusetts that shows 121042882, the number California uses too, is correct.

Accounts opened in Southern California may show a different number on their checks than 121042882, and Wells Fargo says either one works.

A line of credit’s number depends on the first three digits of its account number instead, and a Brokerage Cash Services account uses 102307164.

Wires coming into your account don’t use the state numbers. For a wire sent from inside the U.S., give the sender 121000248 as the routing number. For a wire from another country, give the sender the SWIFT code WFBIUS6S, which international wires use in place of a routing number.

Before you give the number to an employer or a biller, check it against your own account in any of these ways:

For a new direct deposit, create the pre-filled form in the Wells Fargo Mobile app and hand it to your employer. It carries the account’s own routing number, account number, and account type, so you never copy the numbers by hand.
